name: Mississippi Today
title: Shakespeare could have written this LSU-Ole Miss football plot
description: People walk through the Grove on the University of Mississippi campus as a crew sets up for ESPN "College GameDay" on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026.
text:
OXFORD — So I’ve heard this question several times this week: “Is this LSU-Ole Miss game the biggest college football game you have ever covered?”
Rick Cleveland
Well, no. It’s not even the biggest in the last 10 months. The Ole Miss-Georgia Sugar Bowl playoff game was bigger. The Miami-Ole Miss Fiesta Bowl was still bigger. Now then, this might be the most anticipated regular season game I’ve ever covered. No question, it would be in the first sentence of any conversation of that nature. 
This much is certain: This will be the strangest college football game I have ever covered. And by strange, I refer to all the bizarre surrounding circumstances – all the, for lack of a better term, football incest.
No. 7 LSU vs. No. 8 Ole Miss, two teams with star power and national championship hopes, make this the national game of the week. But you factor in Lane Kiffin returning to the scene of what Ole Miss fans consider his unforgivable betrayal, former Ole Miss stars now playing for LSU and so many other extenuating circumstances and you have a football tempest. Indeed, Shakespeare would have a ball with this scenario. Had football been a sport in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, Shakespeare might have written this play. This game has many of the elements of a Shakespeare masterpiece: betrayal, revenge, corruption, incest – you name it.
LSU head coach Lane Kiffin reacts during the second half of an NCAA college football game against Louisiana Tech in Baton Rouge, La., Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Matthew Hinton
Let’s put it this way: When I got into this business about a hundred or so years ago, I never imagined covering anything quite like this. How is this bizarre? Let us count the ways:
Mississippi head coach Pete Golding directs his players before the Fiesta Bowl NCAA college football playoff semifinal game against Miami, Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026, in Glendale, Ariz. (AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin) Credit: AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin

Just this Tuesday in Baton Rouge, LSU defensive end Princewill Umanmielen was served court papers pertaining to the $550,000 lawsuit Ole Miss filed against him for allegedly breaking the terms of his contract at Ole Miss. Umanmielen led Ole Miss in sacks with nine last season. He already has five for LSU.
Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, who also seems LSU’s de facto athletic director, then posted about the Ole Miss athletic director on social media: “Keith Carter could have saved Ole Miss some money and waited until Saturday. He’ll be easy to find in the Ole Miss backfield often!”
Umanmielen is one of four former Rebels who helped Ole Miss to 13 victories last season. Others are linebackers T.J. Dottery, guard Devin Harper and wide receiver Winston Watkins. All are key players. LSU fans might term them opportunists. Ole Miss fans believe them traitors.
Of course, what Ole Miss fans resent most is that Kiffin tried his best to take Heisman candidates Trinidad Chambliss and Kewan Lacy and several other Rebels to Baton Rouge with him, as well. They still play for the Rebels.
Much has been made of the former Rebels – players and assistant coaches – now at LSU. But two former Tigers now play for Ole Miss: running back JT Lindsey and offensive lineman Carius Curne. Yes, the former Ole Miss coaches now at LSU know all about Ole Miss’s personnel, but one of Pete Golding’s key off-season hires was Frank Wilson, LSU’s star recruiter and the interim head coach after Brian Kelly’s dismissal last year. 
Head coaches Kiffin and Golding both coached under Nick Saban at Alabama, and then Kiffin hired Golding away from Saban at Ole Miss. They know each other’s tendencies inside and out. Here’s the crazy part: Golding now lives in Kiffin’s old house. You couldn’t make it up. And you can bet on this: For all the nice things Golding has said about Kiffin this week and in the past, he still burns inside because of the manner in which Kiffin tried to sabotage the Ole Miss program after he left.
Want more? Landry Kiffin, Lane’s daughter, remains a student at Ole Miss and has complained on social media this week about vulgar signs around Oxford and posts on social media about her and a former Ole Miss football player and a sexual relationship that didn’t happen. ”I opened my phone this morning to pictures of banners on houses around Oxford posted on different accounts saying really inappropriate things about me,” Landry Kiffin  said. “… I think that turning a girl into the punchline of a sexual joke because you’re upset at somebody she’s related to should not be okay.” Landry Kiffin dates Whit Weeks, an LSU linebacker.
With all the intrigue, a record crowd is descending upon Oxford, with or without game tickets. Oxford’s population is about 26,600. Estimates are 200,000 – and perhaps even 300,000 – will clog the roadways, the Oxford Square and the Ole Miss campus. By midafternoon Friday, traffic was insane and getting worse by the minute. Security has been beefed up with extra officers from the state Department of Public safety and police from Mobile and New Orleans for the Mardi Gras-like weekend. From above, Oxford must look like a stepped-on ant bed.
Back to Shakespeare: The bard’s plays, while heavy on incest, betrayal and corruption, also featured much hilarity. Ole Miss coaches found some humor this week when Kiffin listed $5 million transfer quarterback Sam Leavitt as “doubtful” because of an unspecified injury. “That’s Lane being Lane,” was the general reaction, along with laughter, in the Ole Miss camp. “We can’t complain much. He did that s— all the time when he was here,” an Ole Miss athletic official told me.

Kiffin was an Ole Miss hero in this town then. He is public enemy No. 1 now. In the minds of Ole Miss fans, Shakespeare’s Brutus had nothing on Lane Kiffin. Et tu, Lane?
A crew sets up for ESPN’s “College GameDay” in the Grove on the University of Mississippi campus on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Vance rallies Iowa Republicans, says Trump’s trade policies benefit farmers
description: COUNCIL BLUFFS — Vice President JD Vance told Iowans Friday that President Donald Trump’s trade and tax policies have helped farmers and working-class families, as he worked to rally support for gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and other Iowa Republicans in the midterms. Trump’s tariff policies have been a point of concern for Iowa farmers over […]
text:
Vice President JD Vance spoke at a rally supporting Iowa Republicans including gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn at the Mid-American Center in Council Bluffs Sep. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)COUNCIL BLUFFS — Vice President JD Vance told Iowans Friday that President Donald Trump’s trade and tax policies have helped farmers and working-class families, as he worked to rally support for gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn and other Iowa Republicans in the midterms.
Trump’s tariff policies have been a point of concern for Iowa farmers over the past year. Vance said the administration’s actions were necessary to reverse “bad trade policy, let’s be honest, from both Democrats and Republicans,” which he said “made it impossible for Iowa farmers to get their food to market.”
He spoke at a midday rally hosted by the Republican National Committee at the Mid-American Center in Council Bluffs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We now have, thanks to Donald Trump’s hard work and fighting on behalf of Iowa farmers, 2 billion new consumers all over the world who are now open to American food instead of closed to American food,” Vance said. “Corn exports are up by 35%. Markets that were closed to our beef and dairy for decades are taking Iowa beef and dairy today, and China has committed to buying $17 billion (in agricultural products) from our farmers just this year.”
According to U.S. Department of Agriculture data, annual corn exports grew from $13.71 billion to $18.55 billion from 2024 to 2025, roughly returning export values to the levels seen in 2021 and 2022. Some farmers have expressed concern about Trump’s decision in August to suspend tariffs on imported ground beef to lower the cost of meat, which cattle producers said would have a negative impact on U.S. herds.
He also said the president had focused on prioritizing building domestic markets for American agricultural producers.
“What does it mean for the safety of our kids, of our grandkids, when we let foreign countries, many of which do not have our best interests at heart, when we let those foreign countries buy our food?” Vance said. “So what Donald J. Trump did when he came into office is he said, we are done with that. We are growing American food on American farms for American families. And I always tell you, ladies and gentlemen, whenever you hear me talk during this midterm campaign, I’ll say Rome was not built in a day. Because we know there’s a lot of work to do, but just two years in — not even two years in — President Trump has cut that deficit by 42%, and it’s fallen even faster this year.”
A critical component of supporting the Trump administration and Republicans’ goals on agriculture, Vance said, was electing Republicans in Iowa, including Lahn. Vance called Lahn, a businessman who owns a family farm in Belle Plaine, a “person who wakes up every single day and thinks about how we can defend the jobs, the prosperity, and the public safety of Iowans from every single walk of life.”
“Zach is going to be a fighter, ladies and gentlemen,” Vance said. “That’s what we need. We need somebody who’s willing to stand up, stand up and protect your families. Stand up and protect your farmers and your farmland. Stand up for every single Iowan who’s been told to sit down and take it, who’s been told that they’re backwards if they believe that Iowa farmland ought to belong to Iowans. Who’ve been told they’re racist for believing that Iowa schools ought to go to American citizens, and not to the foreign-born.”
Zach Lahn, the 2026 Republican candidate for Iowa governor, spoke with attendees at a rally with Vice President JD Vance at the Mid-American Center in Council Bluffs Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The vice president said Lahn “is going to be a great ally to those in Washington who are fighting for you as opposed to against you.”
Lahn spoke before Vance at the rally, where he told the crowd his campaign for governor was focused on preserving Iowa for the next generation. He said this means “defending the institutions that hold our culture together — the local communities, the church, the family, and ultimately, let me say this, ultimately, it’s the individual. This is what the West was ultimately built upon.”
“I want the next generation to grow up in the Iowa that we grew up with, the Iowa that we love,” Lahn said. “I want them to build a life here, build their families here, prosper here, and someday give something back to their children that was even better than what we gave them.”
Lahn said Vance got into politics and his current position “because he wanted to defend culture.”
“And I cannot wait to work with him, to work with Vice President JD Vance to defend the culture of Iowa and America,” Lahn said.
Vance’s Iowa event comes as the state’s elections are positioned to play a critical role in determining control of Congress. Iowa currently has an all-Republican federal delegation, but political forecasters say three of the four U.S. House seats will be highly competitive in the Nov. 3, 2026 midterms, in addition to the races for U.S. Senate and governor.
Republican incumbents in Iowa’s 1st and 3rd Districts were already projected to face tight races, but on Wednesday, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the 2nd Congressional District race to a “toss-up,” writing, “Iowa seems like enough of a potential problem for Republicans that IA-2 merits being a Toss-up, too.”
Council Bluffs is located in the state’s one congressional district not expected to be competitive in 2026. The seat in Iowa’s 4th District, a longtime conservative stronghold, is open in 2026 as current U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra ran for Iowa governor — losing in the primary to Lahn. Political forecasters favor Republican nominee Chris McGowan to win against Democrat Dave Dawson in the general election. McGowan, who spoke to the crowd of roughly 400, told voters to “ignore the polls, let’s get out and vote.”
Republican voters in the region could play a large role in statewide elections, like the gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races. “What we’re gonna do, and especially in Iowa 4, we’re gonna turn out to make sure the rest of the state carries Zach Lahn to victory,” McGowan said.
Lahn faces Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand in the election.
Vance made critical comments about Sand in his speech, saying he was falsely presenting himself as a moderate candidate — a line of attack used by other Republicans on the campaign trail.
The vice president said Sand was “a man who is cut from the exact same cloth as Adam Hamilton and James Talarico,” referencing Democratic candidates running in Kansas and Texas. Vance said while Sand’s campaign advertisements highlight him “groaning about partisanship,” the Democratic candidate has “spent his entire life working for and donating to far-left Democrat causes.”
“Rob Sand has spent this whole campaign running away from the things he spent the rest of his career fighting for, and now he’s banking on voters being too dumb to see what’s happening,” Vance said.
On the campaign trail, Sand has said his time in the auditor’s office shows that he is willing to go against the Democratic Party, citing his decisions to have independent and Republican senior officials at the state auditor’s office, as well as his decision to reject a request from the Democratic National Committee on public records regarding the alleged “wrongdoing by (Gov.) Kim Reynolds.”
Vance also claimed Sand “is a billionaire who has repeatedly fought against tax cuts for middle-class Iowans.” Lahn released a campaign ad in August also calling Sand a billionaire. Sand’s only income is listed as his $103,000 salary as state auditor in campaign ethics disclosures. But the Lahn campaign told KCRG the comment references Sand’s wife, Christine Lauridsen, who owns the Lauridsen Group, a family-owned business with hundreds of millions in annual revenues — though the private company’s or the Lauridsen family’s net worth is not publicly available information.
Maddie Moher, press secretary for Sand’s campaign, said “after seven years as State Auditor and nearly 900 public town halls across Iowa, Iowans know Rob Sand as an independent watchdog who holds both parties accountable, protects taxpayer dollars, and fights to lower costs.”
“Zach Lahn has spent his entire campaign lying about Rob, and now he’s bringing in another D.C. insider to try to bail him out because he can’t answer for his frequent flights to Kansas or his decade-long career as a political operative,” Moher said. “The attacks Lahn has pushed have been repeatedly found false by independent fact-checkers and news outlets, and outsourcing his talking points to another Washington politician doesn’t make them true. Iowa voters know the leader who will actually show up and work for them is Rob Sand.”
Iowa Democrats said Vance’s event was a “desperate attempt to bail out Kansas carpetbagger and career political operative Zach Lahn.”
“Another insider D.C. politician is rushing in to prop up Zach Lahn because he has no answer for how he can be a full-time governor when he lives in Kansas,” IDP Chair Rita Hart said in a statement. “The truth is Lahn is a career political operative who wants to continue the worst of Kim Reynolds’ failed agenda for another four years, and his party bosses know he would be a reliable rubber stamp for the reckless tariffs and ongoing war in Iran that have sent the price of gas, utilities, and groceries skyrocketing. After years of underfunded public schools, farm bankruptcies, and record cancer growth rates, Iowans are ready for change, but Lahn is only offering more of the same.”
Vance last visited Iowa in May, when he spoke in support of U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, the Republican running for reelection in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District.
Though his visits to Iowa have been focused on the midterms, trips to Iowa often signal interest in a future presidential bid. Vance has not announced a presidential run, but is considered likely to run as a GOP presidential candidate in 2028. A recent poll from YouGov/Bowling Green State University shows the vice president holding an early lead in the field compared to other potential candidates such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz.

name: VTDigger
title: Where there’s a will, there’s a way: Pop-up clinic to offer free estate planning services
description:
Legal professionals are volunteering to provide estate planning education and services Saturday to underserved Vermont communities.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Where there’s a will, there’s a way: Pop-up clinic to offer free estate planning services.
text:
A free pop-up clinic for estate planning will be held at Community National Bank in Barre on Saturday. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger
As Vermonters age, the lawyers who can help put their final wishes in writing are getting older — and scarcer — too.
With Vermont’s large aging population and shortage of lawyers, it can be tough to find legal counsel to help a person specify who inherits the assets and objects they leave behind. The issue is compounded by the rate of aging legal professionals in Vermont.
“On one hand, you have a shrinking legal community, in terms of number of lawyers, and certainly the number of lawyers serving remote areas, and then also you have an aging population,” said Don Hayes, the director of the South Royalton Legal Clinic and a professor at Vermont Law and Graduate School.
“So it’s almost a perfect storm. Things are kind of tugging in opposite directions.”
With that in mind, the Vermont Judiciary Commission on the Delivery of Legal Services is offering a free pop-up clinic for estate planning this Saturday. It’s open to anyone, but one goal is to empower low-income and underserved populations to gain control of their estates. Vermonters can register via email to attend the event.
The clinic, from 9:30 to 11:30 a.m. at the Community National Bank in Barre, is an opportunity for Vermonters to receive free legal counseling from volunteer attorneys and Vermont Law and Graduate School students. Everyone who attends will have the opportunity to speak to an attorney, and participants whose needs the clinic can accommodate will be able to walk away with a fully drafted and executed will, Hayes said.
The benefits of having one’s estate in order are numerous, Hayes said, particularly when designating a power of attorney — someone who can act in place of a person who becomes incapacitated — or establishing enhanced life estate deeds. These deeds can be an essential step toward building intergenerational wealth, Hayes added, by ensuring that real estate can pass directly to someone’s descendants without going through probate.
But especially in lower-income households, he said, estate planning can feel like less of a necessity.
“And even if that’s not true, if the perception is that it’s a really expensive endeavor, and I don’t even have money to pay for heat this winter, it’s going to be so deprioritized,” Hayes said. 
There’s also an education barrier to seeking estate planning services, Hayes said.
“Some people think that, you know, ‘I’m a lower-income household, I don’t have anything, what could I possibly use an estate plan for?’ But there’s so many things that, if you don’t have them in place, can really be punishing,” Hayes said. For example, a person might become incapacitated without having designated a power of attorney, Hayes said, leaving their loved ones unable to take over their estate.
Hayes said estate planning, such as the type this clinic offers, can help break down barriers and make legal services feel a bit more accessible.
“It’s a cool thing to be able to give legal services to people that feel that they can’t afford it or they don’t deserve it,” Hayes said.
The clinic is part of the mission of the Vermont Commission on the Delivery of Legal Services, which formed in 2025 to address the barriers Vermonters face when accessing legal services. According to Vermont Supreme Court Associate Justice Harold Eaton Jr., the average age of Vermont lawyers is one of the major factors playing into the overall shortage of legal services.
“We have an issue with the graying of the bar,” Eaton said. “By that I mean lawyers getting older, not being replaced by younger lawyers coming in. And in addition, we have a distribution problem in the sense that many lawyers are located in the more populated areas of the state, and that leaves some places without any legal services available or very little.”
This clinic was identified as a simple way of reaching underserved populations and alleviating some of the demand for legal services in a short time, according to State Court Administrator Therese Corsones.
“They were trying to look at something that could be focused and direct that could be accomplished in one day,” Corsones said.
A review of the clinic will be part of a larger report submitted in October evaluating the key findings of the commission during its past year of operation, Corsones said.
“One of the things we hope to gain from this clinic is to see what the need is,” Corsones said. “And if so, the plan would be to replicate the clinics around the state.” 
Hayes emphasized that even if writing a will does not have a huge impact on someone’s estate, it can still be a powerful thing to do.
“I’ve done wills for people in hospice where they know that they’re going to die, probably in the very near future,” Hayes said, “and their will is not changing anything that would happen at law otherwise. But it’s just the fact that they’re making that expression, they’re putting it down on paper. 
“There’s something very dignifying about being able to do that.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: As SC diesel prices rise, so do economic impact fears
description: The rising cost of diesel fuel is threatening the livelihood of South Carolina’s truckers and forcing operational changes at the Port of Charleston.
text:
A sign at a North Charleston gas station shows the price of diesel fuel at nearly $6.20 per gallon on Friday. (Photo by David Wren/SC Daily Gazette)The rising cost of diesel fuel is threatening the livelihood of South Carolina’s truckers, driving fears of inflation spikes and forcing operational changes at the Port of Charleston as the state’s economy confronts record pump prices that are expected to continue climbing.
“It’s painful everywhere,” said Rick Todd, president and CEO of the South Carolina Trucking Association. “Diesel fuel has been characterized as the workhorse fuel for the world. I mean, literally everything is driven by diesel.”
That includes the trucks that bring groceries and consumer goods to stores, industrial equipment used in factories and on farms, container ships that call on Charleston’s port and even the cranes that move containers through the terminal yards.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The statewide average for a gallon of diesel hit an all-time high of $6.17 this week, according to AAA, driven largely by the war in Iran and Middle East supply concerns. That’s a nearly 75% increase since the beginning of this year.
Prices aren’t expected to peak any time soon. Oil flow chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait between Yemen and the Arabian peninsula — along with reduced refining capacity in the U.S. — have created the potential for diesel shortages, although incidents so far have been isolated.
Joey Von Nessen, a research economist at the University of South Carolina, said higher transportation costs will translate to more expensive groceries and other goods, potentially forcing consumers to pull back on spending that’s been resilient so far, even in the face of rising inflation.
“The bottom line is this represents another economic headwind as we head into the fall months,” he said. “It will definitely have an impact on demand if diesel prices stay elevated at their current levels.”
SC governor celebrates new law aimed at reducing insurance costs for restaurants, businesses

Todd said independent truckers and small trucking firms will feel the most pain, while large freight-hauling companies can blunt higher diesel prices by buying in bulk. Nearly two-thirds of South Carolina’s 24,000 registered motor carriers operate a single truck.
“For the average owner-operator or small fleet that doesn’t have buying power, they’re pretty much paying retail,” Todd said.
He predicts some truckers might simply park their rigs and look for other work until prices improve. Some might get out of the business altogether, as rising fuel costs and spiking liability insurance rates combine to make the occupation unprofitable.
“It’s not sustainable,” Todd said of current diesel costs. “This is uncharted territory in a lot of ways.”
Elevated fuel costs are also impacting the Port of Charleston, which relies on diesel to power most of its equipment and where trucks carry more than three-fourths of the cargo moving through container terminals.
There is a balancing act between reducing the use of diesel-guzzling machinery while, at the same time, not forcing truckers to burn more time and fuel than normal picking up or dropping off cargo, said Micah Mallace, president and CEO of the S.C. State Ports Authority.
The port reduced the number of cranes used to move containers earlier this year to cut costs. But as the year wore on and cargo volumes ticked up, so did the amount of time truckers spent idling within the terminals.
Less cargo has SC Ports Authority cutting its way toward growth

In response, the authority is scheduling more workers and crane operators during busier hours, while pulling back during less intensive times. The maritime agency also buys fuel at bulk contract prices, and as often as possible, operates its handful of hybrid cranes that require less fuel by running on a combination of electricity and diesel power.
“Weve seen inflation in our underlying costs because of diesel, but we’ve been able to mute that impact internally,” Mallace said. “But it’s a more dramatic impact for motor carriers and shipping lines, where their No. 1 or No. 2 operating cost is fuel. We’ve seen our partners really hurt by this and we are trying to think through ways to help offset their cost impact.”
The average cost to move a container from the port to a warehouse is between $395 and $595, according to BlackBridge Logistics. While that is among the lowest cost of any major U.S. port, fuel surcharges are increasing bills as much as 55%– costs that are generally passed on to consumers.
“Higher prices are the biggest short-term threat to the economic outlook,” Von Nessen, the research economist, said. “Another factor that we’ve seen emerge in the last several months is that prices are rising faster than wages, due primarily to this uptick in energy costs.”
SC Ports temporarily halts Leatherman operations in face of high costs, waning demand

When consumers lose purchasing power, it can cause an overall pullback in economic activity, he said.
It won’t take long to see if that threat comes to pass.
Historically, consumers start to reduce their discretionary spending, such as entertainment and dining out, within just a few weeks of fuel-related inflation. Fixed expenses, like housing and groceries, can start to show up as higher credit card balances or decreased savings.
“The longer we see prices rising faster than wages, the more likely we are going to see consumer spending cool,” Von Nessen said.

title: North Carolina Muslim groups push voter registration ahead of November election
description: At the Islamic Association of Raleigh’s mosque on Page Road in Durham, Nigel Edwards set up a table with voter registration information and a QR code directing people to election resources. It was part of a push Friday by Muslim organizations across North Carolina to encourage members of their community to register and vote in […]
text:
National Muslim Voter Registration Day table. (Photo: Sinthia Shabnam/MPower Change)At the Islamic Association of Raleigh’s mosque on Page Road in Durham, Nigel Edwards set up a table with voter registration information and a QR code directing people to election resources.
It was part of a push Friday by Muslim organizations across North Carolina to encourage members of their community to register and vote in the November election.
Nigel Edwards speaks with attendees at a voter registration table after Friday prayers, Sept. 18, 2026.(Photo:Ahmed Jallow/NC Newsline)
The response was mixed, said Edwards, president of the state’s Muslim American Public Affairs Council.
Some people were already registered. Others were not interested in voting. But Edwards said even registering one person who had never done so before would make the effort worthwhile.
“I had at least one brother who actually is going to register who’s never registered before,” Edwards said. “Even just one person is a success, in my opinion.”
Edwards said some people also did not know an election was coming.
“A lot of it is just simple awareness,” he said. 
National Muslim Voter Registration Day is a nonpartisan effort led by MPower Change. More than 80 Muslim organizations were participating in more than 15 states, including North Carolina, according to the organization. Events were planned in states including New York, New Jersey, Florida, Michigan, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
In North Carolina, about 12 to 15 locations were participating, said Sinthia Shabnam, who leads the group’s effort in the state.
Friday prayers are an important opportunity for organizers to reach older members of the community and others who may be less engaged in politics, Shabnam said. 
“It’s those aunties. It’s those uncles. It’s the elderly in the community. It’s the folks that don’t even know they could vote,” she said. “It’s actually the best time to reach that target audience.”
NC Board of Elections will no longer provide forms to voter registration drives

Abdul Allam, who attended Friday prayers at the Durham mosque, said voter registration efforts need to happen repeatedly to keep people engaged.
Some Muslims, he said, pay close attention to presidential elections but are less attentive to primaries and local elections.
“It has to be done multiple times, not once, because that keeps reminding people,” Allam said.
Allam said people also need help understanding how to register and participate.
“It’s not just voting for the president,” he said. “At every level it has an impact.”
The Charlotte Muslim Caucus also held registration and voter pledge events at about five locations in the Charlotte area. The group hoped to register about 50 people and get at least 500 people to pledge to vote, said Nasif Majeed, a co-founder of the caucus and the son of Charlotte state Rep. Nasif Majeed.

title: Podcast: Supporters of creating a state trust fund for unclaimed property explain Amendment K
description: South Dakota has collected over $1 billion in unclaimed property over the years, from sources including abandoned cash, stocks, bank accounts and even gold teeth. Much of that money has gone into the state budget, because not all of the rightful owners come forward to claim their property. Yet they could come forward at […]
text:
South Dakota State Treasurer Josh Haeder (left) and state Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, both support Amendment K, a ballot question that would create a state trust fund for unclaimed property. (Photos by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight; illustration by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




 
South Dakota has collected over $1 billion in unclaimed property over the years, from sources including abandoned cash, stocks, bank accounts and even gold teeth. Much of that money has gone into the state budget, because not all of the rightful owners come forward to claim their property. Yet they could come forward at any time. That’s why lawmakers decided to start putting those assets into a cash-flow fund, and use only the interest to help fund the state’s budget.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
To put the money in a trust fund earning higher returns, lawmakers need the approval of South Dakota voters.
The ballot question is part of a legislative package that passed last year. One of the bills, which was signed into law, gradually transitions all unclaimed property money into a cash-flow fund that generates a small amount of interest for the state budget. Amendment K, which is on the Nov. 3 ballot, would put the money in a higher-earning trust fund managed by the state Investment Council, like other funds such as the retirement pool for public employees.
State Treasurer Josh Haeder and state Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, joined Searchlight Report to explain their support for the amendment. No organized opposition to the ballot measure has surfaced yet.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Spanberger presents slate of data center regulation proposals, puts first directives in motion
description: Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled a package of legislative proposals to rein in the data center industry in Virginia, with goals to tighten environmental regulations, increase cost allocation for the industry, and make the proposal process more transparent by barring non-disclosure agreements between localities and data center developers. The plan d[...]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22 on Friday, Sept. 18 to kick off her data center regulation package. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Friday unveiled a package of legislative proposals to rein in the data center industry in Virginia, with goals to tighten environmental regulations, increase cost allocation for the industry, and make the proposal process more transparent by barring non-disclosure agreements between localities and data center developers.
The plan does not include a moratorium on data center development while the details of the plan are refined, a step several environmental and advocacy groups and citizens have demanded in recent weeks. 
Dubbed the “Data Center Accountability Framework,” Spanberger’s plan outlines five pillars as key priorities: transparency, environmental protections, lowering energy costs, promoting clean energy, and focusing on local workers.
“The Framework is a thorough plan to end data center secrecy, protect our environment, lower energy costs for families, bolster our clean energy economy, and make sure Virginia workers have the protections and assurances they deserve,” Spanberger said in a press conference to announce the plan at the Virginia State Capitol.
Spanberger also signed Executive Order 22,  which will kick-start her plans for clamping down on the industry ahead of the next legislative session that will begin in January 2027. 
 Transparency

Perhaps the most concrete of the directives is a measure to ban nondisclosure agreements between data centers and executive branch agencies, departments, state boards and commissions. It also bars these agencies from requiring such agreements for data center projects. 
The order does not impact the use of nondisclosure agreements by localities, but the governor said she plans to work with the General Assembly to pass a law banning the agreements at the local level. 
In the framework package, the governor also proposes eliminating by-right local approvals of data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power.
Many counties statewide have taken steps towards requiring conditional use permits,which require public hearings and a vote of approval from local leaders.
Additionally, the governor wants to remove data centers from Virginia’s fast-track permitting process that allows permit approvals for the projects to speed up when they are proposed in “business ready” locations. 
The fast-track process is a remnant of Gov. GlennYoungkin’s administration, which encouraged and supported the rapid build out of the state’s data center industry as a means to boost Virginia’s business reputation. 
 Environmental protections

The framework directs lawmakers to develop policies to create standards for energy efficiency, water use and land impacts.
Budget language that passed the General Assembly in June directed the Department of Environmental Quality to identify “water scarcity areas,” data centers’ water use for cooling could put drinking water availability at risk. Data centers located in those areas, mainly east of Interstate-95, will have to reduce their water use. 
The framework also outlines a plan to expedite noise regulations that were also in the budget language, but does not state when those regulations will be put into place. Currently, DEQ has until 2029 to research the lowest possible sound levels data centers could operate on and make that the standard across the board.
 Lower energy costs

Spanberger’s new data center plan requires utilities to allocate more of the energy infrastructure costs largely spurred by data centers onto the industry. 
Dominion Energy has already taken action on this front, after the utility created a new rate class,  GS5, which mostly includes data centers and large manufacturers. The State Corporation Commission approved the new rate class last November.
Like the recommendations in the framework from the governor, the G5 rate class includes 14-year contracts, as well as specific cost allocations for energy generation, distribution, and transmission costs. 
The SCC also recently directed Dominion to create a new tariff to directly assign the cost of high-voltage transmission lines that are only necessary due to data centers to those customers. Spanberger supported the tariff, which is reflected in her framework.
Tech giant Microsoft has already put the State Supreme Court on notice that it could appeal that order.
Microsoft representatives said in an email last week that the company hopes “any rates ultimately put in place are transparent, fair, and reflect the costs each customer creates.” 
But filing notice of appeal, they continued, “Microsoft preserves its ability to challenge any implementation that does not meet these expectations.” 
 Elevating clean energy, hiring Virginia workers

Another component of Spanberger’s plan looks to limit the amount of power data centers can produce on-site through natural gas generators and other “behind the meter” methods that don’t draw from the electric grid. 
The plan also proposes making it easier for data centers to bring clean energy options on-site by reforming utility charges for clean energy investments.
PJM, the regional grid operator for 13 states including Virginia, recently proposed a new rule to direct data centers to pay for their power generation or cover their energy needs by backstop power purchases. This would help bring more power on the grid when it’s strained on very hot and cold days.
Several recent proposals by data centers in the commonwealth show the industry’s growing interest in building its own gas turbines to power data facilities. That method skirts around the Virginia Clean Economy Act, which requires the retirement of carbon emitting power sources by utility companies by 2050. 
The framework prioritizes hiring local workers to build data centers and using local businesses for procurement and contractors. 
 Lawmakers, environmental groups, data centers react

A slate of state legislators spoke up in support of Spanberger’s framework Friday afternoon, sentiments shared by some environmental groups.   
“Governor Spanberger’s Data Center Accountability Framework is a step in the right direction,” a statement by the Virginia House Democratic Caucus read. “We look forward to continuing to work with Governor Spanberger in the upcoming 2027 legislative session to develop thoughtful legislation that holds data centers accountable.”
Many of these policies require legislative action from the General Assembly to take effect. Also many of the proposals are prospective, meaning they will apply to new data center applications rather than the more than 600 data centers that are already operating or being built statewide.
“For those that are up and running and already operating, we have the ability and intention to continue to make sure that into the future we are holding them to greater and greater standards,” Spanberger said.
Representatives from the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Sierra Club, and League of Conservation Voters joined Spanberger for the announcement and called it a strong first step towards enacting legislation to cement the framework’s goals. 
Other organizations were critical of the framework because it didn’t include an outright pause on data center development. 
“It does not address the continued connection of data centers to the grid, despite inadequate power and the many impacts on air quality, water supply, electric bills, and people and communities,” the Piedmont Environmental Council said in a statement. “Not to mention the hundreds of miles of proposed transmission lines, solely to support data centers.”
“We must stop the madness and issue an immediate pause on approvals until these protections – and more – are fully implemented,” Chesapeake Climate Action Network Director Victoria Higgins said in response to the framework.
The Data Center Coalition, the leading national group that lobbies for the industry, said they are waiting for more details on the plan.
“(We) are ready to engage with policymakers to ensure workable, balanced policies that keep Virginia competitive and honor prior commitments by the Commonwealth and its localities,” coalition representative Nicole Riley said.
Spanberger didn’t answer directly when asked why she did not impose a data center development moratorium while her package is considered before lawmakers. She reiterated that some Virginia localities are considering pausing data center development.
“While (localities are) looking at what’s available to them as a potential option, it is up to our communities… But the state has to show leadership,” Spanberger said. “We are in a place where day by day, community members are demanding action.” 
The framework, she added, “is an opportunity for us to take action and ensure that we are moving forward.”

title: Florida bar exam passage rate drops by more than 3%
description: Those pursuing admission to the Florida Bar were less successful this year than last. The summer 2026 exam was taken by 2,250 first-timers. Of that cohort, 75.2% passed, or 1,693. That passage rate represents a decrease from summer 2025, when 78.4% of test-takers passed. During summer 2024, 76% of test-takers passed. The number of test […]
text:
The Westcott Building and fountain at Florida State University on Dec. 31, 2024. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Those pursuing admission to the Florida Bar were less successful this year than last.
The summer 2026 exam was taken by 2,250 first-timers. Of that cohort, 75.2% passed, or 1,693. That passage rate represents a decrease from summer 2025, when 78.4% of test-takers passed. During summer 2024, 76% of test-takers passed.
The number of test takers in 2026 rose from 2025, when 2,152 took the test for the first time.
The highest passage rates among law schools in the state this year were Florida State University (91.8%), the University of Florida (90.9%), Ave Maria School of Law (89.8%), Florida International University (87.3%), and the University of Miami (84.9%).
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The lowest passage-rate schools were Cooley Law School (39% of 23 test-takers), Barry University (59.9%), Jacksonville University (68.8%), Nova Southeastern University (73.4%), Florida A&M University (79.7%), and St. Thomas University (79.8%).
Among accredited schools, 80.4% of test-takers passed.
“We are tremendously proud of our graduates for achieving the highest first-time bar passage rate in Florida,” FSU College of Law Dean Erin O’Hara O’Connor said in a Friday news release.
“This extraordinary result reflects the talent, discipline and determination of our students, as well as the commitment of our faculty and staff to their success. Our graduates worked incredibly hard to reach this milestone, and we are excited to see all that they will accomplish as they begin their legal careers.”
The Florida Board of Bar Examiners, an administrative board of the Florida Supreme Court, administers the test.
Earlier this year, the Florida Supreme Court agreed that students from schools accredited by organizations other than the American Bar Association could sit for the exam. A Supreme Court workgroup questioned the ABA’s “accreditation standards on racial and ethnic diversity in law schools and about the ABA’s active political engagement.”
Florida Supreme Court ends three-decade reliance on ABA, handing win to DeSantis

The Supreme Court determined that “it is not in Floridians’ best interest for the ABA to be the sole gatekeeper deciding which law schools’ graduates are eligible to sit” for the exam. 
“The ABA is a very, very partisan activist organization, and you have a right to be that, but you should not then be the arbiter of legal education,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said in January.
However, this month the ABA voted to eliminate its requirement that college pledge to diversity in recruiting and admissions to obtain accreditation. The vote was an effort to maintain its status as an accreditor with the U.S. Department of Education.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Fits All school voucher program’s review is up: Here’s how $94.7 million were spent
description: When John Arthur, a Democratic representative from Holladay, read a recent report on how the Utah Fits All funds were spent last school year, he let out a big sigh. Utah’s school choice program is one of the issues that has deeply split the state Legislature. And for him, it’s an issue that’s very close […]
text:
Students work in a math class at Wasatch Junior High School in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)When John Arthur, a Democratic representative from Holladay, read a recent report on how the Utah Fits All funds were spent last school year, he let out a big sigh. Utah’s school choice program is one of the issues that has deeply split the state Legislature. And for him, it’s an issue that’s very close to home.
A report that Odyssey, the program manager for Utah Fits All, filed to the Legislature this month discloses how $94.7 million the state allocated for the program was spent during the 2025-2026 school year. After lawmakers approved tweaks to further limit the expenses families could cover with the scholarship dollars, the report looks different than last year, when items like ski passes and chaperone expenses for field trips were allowed.  
Arthur, also an elementary school teacher, acknowledged the program has become more restricted. Still, he says the purchases are extravagant, especially when he pays for some supplies for his classroom out of his paycheck. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“On a personal note, it kills me as I go through this report and I look at the things that the money was spent on and and then I look at my own personal budget and look at the money that I spend on Kleenex boxes and food and other supplies that I bring into my classroom for my students,” Arthur said, “while this money is just going straight from the legislature either into private schools and religious schools or into the homes of the people who are receiving it.”
According to the report, 14,522 students used the program. About $57 million was spent on tuition and fees in private schools and about $27 million on educational goods, like software and applications, supplies, electronics and textbooks, among others. 
Utah Fits All voucher program will continue until Utah Supreme Court rules on its constitutionality

Some of the largest specific expenses for goods were for art supplies (about $1.9 million), learning manipulatives ($2.5 million), STEM kits ($2.3 million), curriculum textbooks ($2.2 million), laptops ($2.3 million), tablets ($1.3 million) and 3D printers ($1.1 million).
For Arthur, the electronics purchases are one of the things that make him most concerned about the program, especially since the Legislature has started efforts to keep children off screens, including a default ban on cellphones during the school day. Also, he said, because other students in the state don’t have the same opportunities.
“There’s $468,000 listed here for headphones. I had to do a donation drive to get headphones that had microphones into my classroom, so that my multilingual learners who have to take the WIDA test (an English language proficiency assessment program) every February can practice with headphones that have microphones. I had to ask for charity. I had to ask friends to donate to that fund,” he said. “Meanwhile, you’ve got the Utah Fits All voucher program using tax dollars to buy people headphones that they just get to keep.”
However, program proponents like Utah House Majority Whip Candice Pierucci, a Republican from Herriman, see the report under a much more positive light, especially since the Legislature made substantial changes to ensure expenses “have a clear nexus and tie to education.”
With reduced scholarship for homeschool students, Utah Fits All update poised to become law

“There is no other education program in our state that we audit annually and have it meet such rigid financial requirements. So, in this program we are certainly being mindful of taxpayer dollars, and we also recognize that not every child is going to fit into one system,” Pierucci said. “We do not believe in a one-size-fits-all approach. We believe in empowering parents to make decisions that are best for their kids.”
Last year, lawmakers reduced the annual scholarship amount for homeschool learners, from $8,000 to $4,000 for students 5 to 11 years old. Students 12 to 18 years old could get $6,000, while private school students are still eligible for $8,000 a year to help cover their tuition or other expenses. 
That led to a change in the proportion of students who use the vouchers for homeschool education. About 80% of recipients last year were homeschooled. This year, that number went down to almost 48%, while the remaining 52% of students went to private schools.
There was also a 20% cap for extracurriculars and physical education, and the clear exclusion of ski passes, furniture, musical instruments, apparel and other items from the allowable expenses. 
Amid the fracturing debate in the Legislature, Pierucci finds the notion of the Utah Fits All program taking away from public schools disingenuous, she said.
“Over the past five years, the state legislature, we in the majority caucus, have increased state funding for public education by 1.8 billion, which is a 44.2% increase. So we have increased education funding, despite the fact that enrollment is declining as fertility rates start falling,” she said.
She also contested a major argument program detractors make: that not all Utah children have access to it. She said that any family in the state can apply for the scholarship, and that regular school districts offer similar programs, like speech therapy, art or gym classes.
“I’m not seeing the disconnect here on kids in this program getting something different than kids whose families are choosing to go to a district or charter school,” she said.



Let us know what you think...


 


That question is expected to be answered in court, when the Utah Supreme Court makes a decision on the program’s constitutionality. 
A 3rd District judge declared last spring Utah Fits All was unconstitutional, saying it was a “program within the public education system that is not free and is not ‘open to all the children of Utah,’” and diverts constitutionally appropriated funds from already underfunded public schools. 
The program was allowed to continue as Republican state leaders appeal that decision and wait for a final say from Utah’s highest court.
Utah’s largest teacher union, which filed the lawsuit against the program, didn’t comment on the report’s content. But, leaders said they hope to prevail in court.
“Public money belongs in public schools. Last year, Utah’s Third District Court ruled the state’s voucher program unconstitutional and we will continue defending that ruling,” UEA President Renée Pinkney said in a statement. “Our tax dollars should support public schools, where more than 90% of Utah students attend.”
Apart from tuition and goods, over $10.6 million of the scholarships were used for services, including after-school or summer programs, educational therapies and tutoring services. 
Under Odyssey, the cost of administering the program for the 2025-2026 year was $4.8 million, about half of the $9 million the Utah State Board of Education awarded last year to ACE Scholarships, the past Utah Fits All program manager, before terminating the company’s contract “for convenience” after just one year.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Judge rules EPA illegally ended $7B solar program for low-income Americans
description: Trump illegally terminated a program intended to make solar power accessible to 900,000 lower-income Americans, a R.I. federal judge ruled.
text:
The Trump administration illegally terminated a $7 billion Solar for All program intended to make solar power accessible to more than 900,000 lower-income Americans, a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled Friday.
The Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the Solar for All funds in August 2025 after President Donald Trump’s massive tax and spending law passed in Congress a month earlier, with Administrator Lee Zeldin calling the Biden-era grant program a “boondoggle.”
District Judge Mary McElroy wrote in the ruling that Congress clearly intended the EPA to continue administering the Solar for All grants that were already obligated. The EPA acted contrary to this intent and without any other statutory authority when it terminated the program, McElroy wrote. She vacated the termination.
The EPA did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday.
The lawsuit filed in Rhode Island by the Rhode Island AFL-CIO labor organization and others — including the public interest law center Rhode Island Center for Justice and the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors — highlighted the importance of the program for local workforces and lower-income communities seeking access to clean-energy project funding.
Patrick Crowley, president of the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, called the decision “a big victory” for states across the country.
“If and when the program does get up and running, there will be thousands and thousands of union jobs created across the United States,” he said Friday. “We were proud to be the lead plaintiff.”
Clean, affordable power like solar shouldn’t be a luxury, said Alex St. Pierre, vice president for environmental justice at Conservation Law Foundation, one of the nonprofit legal advocacy groups representing the plaintiffs.
“Communities have waited long enough,” St. Pierre said in a statement. “Nearly every family is looking for ways to cut their energy bill. These dollars should go where Congress intended: toward lower energy bills, less climate pollution, good jobs and cleaner air.”
In May, for the first time, solar supplied more of the nation’s electricity than coal.
The Trump administration has targeted a host of programs and policies dedicated to clean energy. The $7 billion Solar for All program was part of the $27 billion “green bank,” formally known as the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund. It was established in the Democratic-backed climate law passed in 2022 under former President Joe Biden. The attorneys general of more than a dozen states also sued over the canceled solar program funding. A federal judge in Washington dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction in June. The plaintiffs have appealed.
The other $20 billion, also canceled by the Trump administration, was slated for eight community development banks and nonprofit organizations for tens of thousands of projects to combat the effects of climate change, such as residential energy efficiency projects to larger-scale investments such as community cooling. A divided federal appeals court said last month that the Trump administration improperly terminated the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, handing a win to a coalition of nonprofits picked to run the effort.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: David Jolly: A complete ban on data centers in Florida should be ‘on the table’
description: CLEARWATER — David Jolly has already made it clear he’s a critic of large-scale data centers, for which Floridians continue to express disapproval up and down the state. The Democratic gubernatorial candidate had already said that if elected in November, he’d issue a one-year moratorium on construction of these facilities. But after visiting a region […]
text:
David Jolly walking outside a section of the Vantage VA2 Data Center in Sterling, Virginia, on Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo via Jolly campaign)CLEARWATER — David Jolly has already made it clear he’s a critic of large-scale data centers, for which Floridians continue to express disapproval up and down the state.
The Democratic gubernatorial candidate had already said that if elected in November, he’d issue a one-year moratorium on construction of these facilities. But after visiting a region of Northern Virginia this week with the highest density of data centers in the country, he says he’s seen first-hand the economic and public health disruption they inflict on communities and that it’s not what he wants to see in the Sunshine State.
“I visited a family with a home, you open the door and you’re hit with the noise pollution,” he said Friday after attending an event with Habitat for Humanity in Pinellas County. “You walk outside, you see the turbines that are fueling the energy. Down the street, there were four kids who developed respiratory conditions who had to seek medical help.”
Data centers also are deflating real estate prices in their communities, Jolly said. He learned of a home near a massive data center that sat on the market for nearly a year and ended up selling for $80,000 below list price.
“Let’s be honest about what’s happening in Florida,” he said. “Big tech, big data, the utilities are rushing into a relatively unregulated environment, or at least a favorably regulated environment. And that’s why you’re seeing voters who feel like they don’t have the economic or political power to push back, stand up, and say, ‘Please don’t do this.’
Local communities in Florida continue to say they don’t want data centers. This week, the Orange County Commission advanced a plan to temporarily ban data center development. Commissioners reached a consensus for a 6-to-18 month moratorium, depending on how long county staff need to research the potential harms, according to Orlando Weekly.
Three local governments in Florida have permanently banned construction of data centers, and 19 are pausing such development, according to FloridaDataCenters.org.
Already operating
However, 12 data centers are already operating in Florida and another eight are planned, according to Cleanview, a marketing intelligence company. The Florida Legislature approved and Gov. Ron DeSantis signed legislation earlier this year that bans public utilities from passing the electricity costs of data centers onto residential and small business customers. It also preserved local authority over zoning, permitting, and land use for such centers, and gives local governments authority to set strict standards or deny projects.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds has expressed support for letting local governments decide whether they want to construct data centers. He has dismissed Jolly’s one-year moratorium as “politics.”
And Donalds said in Tampa earlier this month that construction of data centers would not resemble what Jolly visited this week.
“In Northern Virginia, they built them next to apartment complexes and residential neighborhoods,” he said. “We’re not going to allow that in Florida. … If you’re going to do it, just do it a couple of miles down the road. Don’t do it in residential neighborhoods.”
Advocates for data centers say they are needed in the United States, lest this country lose the race for AI superiority to China. The strongest advocate for that position is President Donald Trump. The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing data center-related proposals covering at least 17,600 acres of public land across six states  — Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming, the Washington Sun reported Friday.
Jolly says he’s perfectly fine if the other 49 states build data centers — just not Florida.
“There is no long-term economic impact from the data centers. There is the upfront construction jobs, but that there’s not the legacy economic impact that actually justifies the disruption of a community,” he said.
“Look I do think that our national policymakers do need to work through some things to the extent that it’s a national security strategy. Let the White House and the Congress figure it out. But as Florida and Florida voters, we’re saying don’t build them here, let the other 49 states build them. It doesn’t hurt our national security strategy to say no to data centers in Florida.”
The Donalds campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Federal judge says AI deepfake election law violates First Amendment
description: A federal judge ruled in favor of a political action committee accused of breaking a new election law regulating the use of AI deepfakes this week. U.S. District Judge Susan Watters said that the new Montana law violates the First Amendment and infringes on the most protected speech of all – political speech. However, the ruling […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.A federal judge ruled in favor of a political action committee accused of breaking a new election law regulating the use of AI deepfakes this week. U.S. District Judge Susan Watters said that the new Montana law violates the First Amendment and infringes on the most protected speech of all – political speech.
However, the ruling was narrow and only impacted thethe plaintiffs in the case.
The case centers on mailers that were sent out in Montana before the June primary that used AI to alter images of candidates, and several lawmakers targeted by the political action committee filed complaints with the Commissioner of Political Practices.
Artificial-intelligence assisted programs can create realistic-looking images, video and audio of a person, something lawmakers across the country have looked to address.
Rep. Eric Albus, a Hi-Line Republican; former legislator Jennifer Carlson, running for a state House seat in the Bozeman area; and Rep. Llew Jones, running for state senate, filed the complaints earlier this year. 
The committee, which lists Dan Bartel, a former Republican legislator, as its treasurer, ran mailers depicting some of those candidates with Pride flags and buttons.
Watters ruled in favor of Bartel and the PAC, saying that because the law treats “identically deceptive media differently based solely on whether its message is weaponized or deployed to elevate a candidate” that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in establishing that it constitutes “viewpoint-based” discrimination.
She went on to write that it was “presumptively unconstitutional.”
Yet, the ruling only applies to Dan Bartel and his PAC, and does not impact the law for the rest of the state. The decision, and its limited reach, Watters said is part of recent Supreme Court case law, calling on federal court judges to limit or curtail the use of broad preliminary injunctions to strike down laws.
 Injunction, or not?

A recent Supreme Court case, Trump v. CASA, which dealt with a presidential executive order regarding immigration, drastically changed how injunctions are handled in the country’s highest court.
In that case, the conservative majority said that a district court should have decided the case in favor of only the organizations that were party to the case, not to the general public. The court held that the Judiciary Act of 1789 doesn’t give federal courts the right to impose universal injunctions.
Watters mentioned both Trump v. CASA and the Supreme Court’s ruling on injunctions in her decision.
The state, which defended the bipartisan AI law passed by the Legislature, argued that a preliminary injunction “be no more burdensome than necessary,” and asked Watters to limit the scope of the ruling, pointing to Trump v. CASA. The Plaintiffs in the case had asked for an injunction which would have made the new law moot.
Watters wrote the court lacked authority under the Judiciary Act of 1789 to issue a “universal injunction” and, “to comply with the mandate that equitable relief be no more burdensome than necessary, relief must be limited to the named plaintiffs.”
Plaintiffs in the case were represented by the Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute and Montana attorney Matthew Monforton.
“This is an important victory for political speech and the First Amendment,” said Adam Schulman, a senior attorney at the law institute. “The government cannot censor speech just because that speech uses AI technology.”

name: National
title: Rural women who got C-sections more likely to be prescribed opioids at home, study finds
description: Women giving birth in rural communities were more likely than peers in urban areas to receive oral opioid prescriptions for pain upon leaving the hospital after a cesarean section, according to a new analysis of data from half a million C-sections. The study was conducted by researchers at Truveta, a health data and analytics company […]
text:
HIALEAH, FL - SEPTEMBER 23: Mary Arguedas, who does not have insurance because she can not afford it, waits to be examined by her OB/GYN, Vivian Chona, at the Jessie Trice Community Health Center, Inc. on September 23, 2009 in Hialeah, Florida. A new census report showed that 53.1 percent of adults ages 18-64 in Hialeah lack health insurance -- almost three times the national average.   (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Women giving birth in rural communities were more likely than peers in urban areas to receive oral opioid prescriptions for pain upon leaving the hospital after a cesarean section, according to a new analysis of data from half a million C-sections.
The study was conducted by researchers at Truveta, a health data and analytics company owned and governed by 30 health systems across the nation. Researchers compared pain-management prescriptions from more than 540,000 C-sections between January 2018 and July 2026.
While hospital pain medication use was consistent across groups, the researchers said it varied after patients were discharged from hospitals: For every 100 women who underwent a C-section, roughly 10 more women living in rural communities received an opioid prescription than women in urban communities. Women in rural communities were also more likely to receive prescriptions for acetaminophen and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen. 
More rural hospital closures would mean long drives for pregnant women seeking obstetric care

About 1 in 3 births across the nation is delivered by C-section. Typically, several types of pain medications are used together. 
The researchers evaluated three groups of pain medications including acetaminophen (Tylenol), NSAIDs and opioids, such as oxycodone and fentanyl.
While managing pain for recovery after a C-section is crucial, some hospital systems have been trying to curb opioid prescriptions amid the nation’s opioid epidemic to lessen addiction risks. Opioid medications also come with many side effects.
Substance use disorder and mental health conditions are the leading underlying causes of maternal death, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. They contributed to more than 1 in 5 pregnancy-related deaths, according to CDC data from 38 state maternal mortality review committees.
The Truveta researchers also examined prescribing by race, ethnicity and documented history of substance use disorder. Unadjusted findings showed somewhat higher opioid prescribing after discharge among Black or African American women and among women with a documented history of substance use disorder. However, the team didn’t determine whether these differences were statistically significant or account for other factors that might help explain them.
“The fact that we’re seeing kind of more open prescriptions upon discharge, given that recommendation, especially within the context of substance use disorder in maternal health specifically — it does raise a very important question about what’s driving that difference in prescribing, and what happens after women are going home,” said Madhura Vachon, lead researcher of the analysis and a former epidemiologist at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

text:
Sen. Jonathan Dismang discusses tax legislation House Speaker Matthew Shepherd and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders listen during a press conference on March 30, 2023. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)A special election to fill the Senate District 18 vacancy resulting from former Sen. Jonathan Dismang’s resignation this week will be Jan. 5, 2027, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced Friday. 
A special primary election for eligible parties will coincide with the Nov. 3 general election. 
Dismang, who stepped down Tuesday, was named vice president of external affairs for Arkansas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. The former Republican lawmaker, will join the organization next month and succeed former state Rep. Bill Gossage as chief of external affairs following his retirement in January 2027, according to a press release.
Sen. Jonathan Dismang, an architect of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion, stepping down

Candidates have from noon Monday until noon Thursday to file to run for the vacancy in Senate District 18, which includes White County and parts of Faulkner and Cleburne counties. 
Independent candidates can circulate petitions of support between Sept. 28 and Oct. 1. Petitions must be submitted to the secretary of state’s office by noon Oct. 1. 
Will Moore, a Republican and Searcy’s city attorney, announced his intention to run for the seat Tuesday.
The vacancy leaves Republicans with a 27-6 majority in the Senate.
Five legislative vacancies are being filled in 2026. Republican Sen. Brad Simon and Democratic Rep. Alex Holladay won special elections in March to represent Senate District 26 and House District 70, respectively. 
Republican Bill Teeter won the House District 44 special election in August to replace the late Republican Rep. Stan Berry.  
Eudora Mayor Tomeka Butler, a Democrat, and Rison Republican Harrell Wilson are vying for the Senate District 1 seat in a special election that coincides with November’s midterms. The winner will replace former Republican Sen. Ben Gilmore who resigned in June to work for Attorney General Tim Griffin.  
Sanders has also scheduled a special election during November’s midterms to fill Rep. Austin McCollum’s seat, which became vacant when the Bentonville Republican resigned following domestic violence charges.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Revolution Wind completes installation of all 65 turbines
description: Despite Trump’s attacks, Revolution Wind is nearing completion off the coast of R.I. The 704-MW project will be fully operational this year.
text:
Another offshore wind project just wrapped up turbine construction in the U.S., despite the Trump administration issuing not one but two stop-work orders against the installation.
The $6.2 billion Revolution Wind farm has installed its 65th and final turbine. The project has been producing carbon-free power for Rhode Island and Connecticut since March, but at partial output. It will be able to deliver up to its full 704-megawatt capacity ​“later this year,” per one of its developers, the beleaguered Danish energy giant Ørsted.
“The completion of Revolution Wind is an important milestone for Rhode Island, Connecticut, and the broader New England region,” said Hillary Bright, executive director of offshore wind advocacy group Turn Forward in a Thursday statement. ​“As electricity demand continues to grow, the region needs more generation that can strengthen reliability, diversify the power supply, and provide greater certainty for consumers.”
Offshore wind was once meant to anchor Northeast decarbonization plans. But, at least for now, the Trump administration has dashed those hopes. President Donald Trump has pursued a relentless line of attack against the sector and managed to essentially halt new development.
When Trump was elected in November 2024, research firm BloombergNEF expected the U.S. to build 39 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2035. By the end of 2025, it had slashed that figure to just 6 GW — an amount that assumed only the five offshore wind projects already underway would get built.
Trump tried to stop these in-progress projects, too. The Interior Department issued a stop-work order to Revolution Wind in August 2025 due to unspecified national security threats. That order was thrown out by a federal judge one month later. The agency had issued — and then revoked — a similar order to the Empire Wind project in New York months earlier.
In late December, the Trump administration threw a Hail Mary pass and issued new stop-work orders to all five projects underway. Project developers and state attorneys general challenged each one in court, and beginning in January, judges struck down the orders, one by one.
The Trump administration has since shifted from trying to stop these projects to offering refunds to energy developers who are willing to forfeit the offshore wind leases they had previously purchased. So far, the administration has agreed to hand out nearly $4 billion in taxpayer funds via these deals — moves that serve only to, as one analyst put it, ​“shoot a corpse.”
Along with Revolution Wind, two other large-scale offshore wind projects are fully complete in the U.S.: the South Fork Wind project near New York and Vineyard Wind 1 off the coast of Martha’s Vineyard. The Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind installation — a whopping 2.6-GW project — began delivering power to the grid in March and should wrap up construction next year. Two others, Empire Wind and Sunrise Wind, are both expected to be fully operational in 2027.
Revolution Wind will help bolster New England’s constrained grid.
During the historic Winter Storm Fern earlier this year, Vineyard Wind 1 showed up big for the region even before the project was fully operational. The South Fork Wind farm performed well for New York during the same frigid stretch. No surprise there: Offshore wind is known for its strong winter performance.
Then offshore wind came through again when record-setting heat descended on New England this summer. During the July heat wave, carbon-free electricity from Vineyard Wind 1 and Revolution Wind allowed utilities to rely less on dirty, expensive oil-burning peaker plants.
As President Trump continues to try and thwart the industry’s prospects in the U.S., Revolution Wind and the other projects that make it across the finish line will keep proving their worth: They provide clean electricity that states, particularly in the Northeast, desperately need. 
This story was first published Sept. 18, 2026 by Canary Media.
