name: Daily Montanan
title: Planned Parenthood endorses independent in Montana Senate race
description: Planned Parenthood’s political arm has endorsed the independent candidate in Montana’s U.S. Senate race, a rare departure by the organization that almost exclusively backs Democratic candidates.  Montana is uniquely positioned as a state that has all-Republican elected officials at the state and national level, but just two years ago voted to enshrine aborti[...]
text:
Planned Parenthood signage is seen in the Financial District neighborhood of Manhattan on April 16, 2021 in New York City. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)Planned Parenthood’s political arm has endorsed the independent candidate in Montana’s U.S. Senate race, a rare departure by the organization that almost exclusively backs Democratic candidates. 
Montana is uniquely positioned as a state that has all-Republican elected officials at the state and national level, but just two years ago voted to enshrine abortion rights in the state constitution by a 15-point margin. 
With the national GOP platform holding to an anti-abortion stance, groups focused on women’s reproductive healthcare have had two options in the Senate race for alternatives to Republican Kurt Alme — Democrat Alani Bankhead and independent Seth Bodnar. 
“Montana voters across the political spectrum overwhelmingly chose to protect reproductive freedom in their own constitution,”  said Alexis McGill Johnson, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Action Fund. “We know Seth Bodnar will meet this moment with the same clarity and represent the will of Montanans in the U.S. Senate.”
As of Friday, Bodnar is one of two candidates Planned Parenthood has endorsed who is not a registered Democratic candidate — Bill Hill, a nonpartisan in Alaska,  also received the endorsement. 
Planned Parenthood’s endorsement of Bodnar follows a recent poll by the Montana Free Press/Rutgers Eagleton showing him gaining ground in a three-way race, pulling 30% of the vote behind Alme’s 38%. Bankhead earned 16%.
Seth Bodnar during a 2025 military reunion event by alumni at the Canyon Club on the University of Montana on Friday, Sept. 12, 2025. (courtesy photo)
In the 2022 Dobbs decision, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a longstanding precedent set in Roe v. Wade that said the constitution included the right to make a decision to have an abortion. The court had shifted to the right under President Trump’s first term, when he was able to appoint three justices to the bench. 
Non-GOP candidates see abortion as one way they can connect with voters in Montana. 
In a press statement, Bodnar used the endorsement to double down on his independent status and show his support for women’s decisions about their own bodies. 
“The government has no place in a Montanan’s doctor’s office, whether that government sits in Helena or Washington, D.C.,” Bodnar said in a statement. “Montanans already settled this at the ballot box, Republicans, Democrats, and Independents voted to protect it in our own constitution …That’s exactly the kind of decision I’ll always answer to Montanans on, not a party.”
Bankhead has also earned the support of national women’s rights groups. 
Earlier this week, her campaign announced an endorsement from the National Organization of Women Political Action Committee, which exclusively backs candidates with pro-choice policy positions. 
“NOW has been in this fight for 60 years, and they’ve never treated women’s rights as one issue,” Bankhead said in a statement to the Daily Montanan.  It’s reproductive freedom, it’s what you earn, it’s whether you can see a doctor, it’s whether you’re treated equally. That’s how I see it too.”
Kim Villanueva, chairperson for NOW PAC, said in a statement that this election “is personal” for women everywhere. 
“Our rights are being stripped away day by day, and the answer is simple — elect feminist candidates who won’t back down,” Villanueva said. 
Bodnar’s campaign used its endorsement to take additional shots at Bankhead, questioning her stance on reproductive rights and blasting associations she’s had with the conservative McLean Bible Church in Virginia and other conservative organizations in the past. 
“She belonged to a pro-MAGA megachurch whose pastor called abortion ‘a sin against God’ and who celebrated the overturning of Roe v. Wade,” said Kelly Webster, spokesperson for the Bodnar campaign. “While Bankhead may be comfortable with these far-right views, Montanans believe that a woman should have the right to make her own personal health care decisions without interference from politicians or anyone else.”
Bankhead’s policy stance as a candidate has always been pro-choice.
Alani Bankhead, a candidate for the United States Senate, speaks at the 2026 Montana Democratic Party Convention on June 20, 2026 at the Northern Hotel in Billings (Jenna Martin for the Daily Montanan)
In previous interviews with the Daily Montanan, she said everyone is allowed the freedom of religion, but that she does not believe in bringing religion  into politics. 
Bankhead said she attended McLean Bible Church while stationed in Washington D.C., until 2017.
Lon Solomon, who was the pastor at the time, has a sermon on his website titled “Abortion: the American holocaust,” but Bankhead said she never heard him preach any “anti-abortion rhetoric,” while attending the church. 
“I would never have gone to a church like that,” she told the Daily Montanan. “All I heard from him was to do the right thing.”
Bankhead said she is personally pro-choice, and her work with sex trafficking victims while in the military has given her a front row seat to the importance of allowing women to have agency over their bodies.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri train ride led to Kansas City-area measles case that’s exposed 250 people so far
description: It was the call Ray Dlugolecki had been dreading. And one he and other public health officials have been expecting. The assistant director at Jackson County Public Health learned on Sunday afternoon about a confirmed case of measles, not just in his agency’s jurisdiction, but in one of its own buildings. The previous week, an […]
text:
Jackson County health officials are still working to trace potential exposures to a single measles case reported Sept. 13. (photo submitted).It was the call Ray Dlugolecki had been dreading. And one he and other public health officials have been expecting.
The assistant director at Jackson County Public Health learned on Sunday afternoon about a confirmed case of measles, not just in his agency’s jurisdiction, but in one of its own buildings.
The previous week, an infected resident of eastern Jackson County had been inside the health department’s Lee’s Summit facility at 3651 N.E. Ralph Powell Road on two separate occasions.
Dlugolecki understood that the highly contagious virus, which has been spreading with increasing success in communities around the country, had finally reached his doorstep.
The welcome mat — a countywide vaccination rate too low for herd immunity — seemed to have made the scenario almost inevitable.
County officials said the person likely contracted the virus on an Amtrak train traveling from Sedalia to Chicago on Aug. 27.
And now, that single case has exposed more than 250 people in Jackson County to measles, a dangerous virus that had been all but eliminated in the United States only a few years ago. That number doesn’t include anyone across the state line in Johnson County who could have also been exposed.
“If we have pockets of individuals who are unvaccinated or can’t receive vaccines,” Dlugolecki said, “it gives the virus the opportunity to enter those communities and spread like wildfire.”
 A link to another case

Immediately after learning about the Lee’s Summit exposure, a team of six Jackson County Public Health employees came into the office to begin trying to trace the infected person’s movements and figure out where they could have been infected.
They worked into the night tracking down and notifying anyone who was in the room when the infected person was there or during a window after the person left. The measles virus can linger in the air as long as two hours.
So far, the health department has identified 251 people who had been exposed in Jackson County by this one case, including at least 10 who now have to quarantine for 21 days because they were not vaccinated or did not know their vaccination status.
And area health officials expect the number of people exposed to grow.
The team also traced the infected individual’s movements to public spaces in Overland Park, where the Johnson County Department of Health and Environment also opened an investigation.
Johnson County Health Director Charlie Hunt said no new cases had been identified by Sept. 16, but that could change, as symptoms can take seven to 14 days to show up.
Jackson County Public Health investigators said the local case is directly connected to another recent measles case of a Missouri resident who boarded Amtrak train 318, the Missouri River Runner, in Sedalia on Aug. 27 and rode to Chicago. Dlugolecki said evidence, including the timing of travel, symptom onset and epidemiologic information available, means the cases are likely linked.
According to state officials, two other measles cases have also stemmed from that person on the train — one in another person on board, and one in someone who lived in the same household — bringing the total cases related to the Amtrak exposure to four.
 A recipe for an outbreak 


To achieve herd immunity for measles, at least 95% of people must be vaccinated. But across the country growing distrust in public health and misinformation about vaccines has caused that number to fall below that threshold.
According to most recent data, in 2025 only 89.5% of Missouri kindergartners and 90.26% of Kansas kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
Recent data show a sharp rise in the number of parents seeking exemptions so their children can attend school without getting required shots. Missouri’s exemption rate jumped to 6.3% in the 2025-26 school year from 5.2% a year earlier, while Kansas’ jumped to 4.5% from 3.6%.
Growing fear stoked by misinformation about the safety of vaccines — including some coming from the White House — is likely partially to blame. And, since the COVID pandemic, public health guidance of almost any kind has been greeted with more skepticism overall.
But whatever the cause of declining vaccine coverage, the result is a population potentially ripe for an outbreak, KC-area public health officials said.
One infected person walking into a room with unvaccinated people could quickly spiral into a dangerous situation. In fact it is almost certain nine out of 10 unvaccinated people who are exposed will get sick.
“People have to realize there are constant sparks getting thrown,” said Nathan Koffarnus, an epidemiologist with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. “It’s just where they land, that’s the luck of the draw. … Now that there are more people walking around unprotected or underprotected, it’s a larger issue again.”
 How measles spreads

The measles virus spreads through the air when someone who is infected coughs, sneezes or talks. It can also be picked up from a contaminated surface like a countertop or table.
Two shots of the MMR vaccine, the recommended dose, are 97% effective, meaning if 100 vaccinated people are exposed, only three might develop the virus. That makes the MMR vaccine one of the most effective out there. For comparison, the influenza vaccine is typically only 30% to 50% effective, in large part because influenza, like the virus that causes COVID, mutates, creating a changing target that is more difficult for a vaccine to hit.
So far this year, of the 3,294 people known to have contracted measles in the United States, 95% were not vaccinated.
But rarely, people who get an MMR vaccine still get sick.
That was what happened in the recent Lee’s Summit measles case. Dlugolecki said the person at the center of the case had been vaccinated.
Catherine Satterwhite, executive director of the Center for Population Health and Equity at Kansas City University, said breakthrough cases happen with all vaccines. But in the case of measles, they are exceedingly rare.
“For somebody to have a breakthrough case, a lot of things have to happen,” she said.
Rarely, a person’s immune system doesn’t respond as expected to the vaccine, leading them to have less protection. It is also possible a vaccine could be somehow corrupted, possibly because it wasn’t stored at the proper temperature, causing it to provide less protection.
But even people who experience one of those extremely rare problems and get a breakthrough case of measles will still benefit from having been vaccinated, Satterwhite said. A breakthrough infection is usually less severe, comes with fewer serious side effects and is less easily passed on to others.
Satterwhite also said the Lee’s Summit breakthrough case provides a perfect illustration of why widespread vaccination is so important.
“We recommend vaccines on the population level to protect the people who either aren’t getting the (immune) response that we expect,” she said, “or who can’t get vaccinated.”
The few exceptions include infants. The first MMR dose isn’t recommended until a child turns 1, and the second is given around 5 years old. Some immunocompromised people also can’t receive the vaccine.
 The cost to health and taxpayers

Health officials hope that incidents like the recent exposure in Missouri cause more people to understand the risks of not getting the shots.
Just being exposed, even without symptoms, will require someone who is not vaccinated to quarantine for 21 days. And developing measles can cause serious illness, including pneumonia, encephalitis and, in rare cases, death. An ongoing outbreak in Pennsylvania is linked to four deaths so far.
The virus, which was responsible for 500 deaths every year before vaccines became available, was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. But that status, achieved when there was no continuous spread for more than 12 months, is at risk.
Beyond the health costs of a measles outbreak, responding to infections costs tax money. The Washington Post reported that investigating a Colorado outbreak involving nine children and one adult earlier this year cost taxpayers half a million dollars.
Jackson County Public Health could not yet offer an exact price tag for their recent case, but  Dlugolecki said the agency has already dedicated more than 150 staff hours to the response. That includes epidemiology and communicable disease investigators, leadership, communications, nursing and staff temporarily reassigned from other areas of the health department to help identify and contact exposed individuals, verify immunity, provide quarantine guidance and coordinate follow-up, he said.
“That redistribution of staff also means other important public health work has had to pause or slow while the response is underway,” Dlugolecki said
Each exposed person may require multiple calls, vaccination record review, coordination with healthcare providers or employers, symptom monitoring and follow-up over the 21-day monitoring period.
“The larger point is that a measles response can become very resource-intensive very quickly, even when it starts with a single case,” Dlugolecki said. “Much of that burden comes from the number of people who may have been exposed and the amount of work required to make sure they are identified, informed and appropriately managed.”
 The vaccine worked too well?

Declining vaccination rates are the biggest reason the country is seeing more measles cases this year — the most in three decades. In some ways, said Koffarnus of the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the vaccine may have been too effective.
“Cases have gone down so much over the past few decades that most people can’t remember ever knowing anyone that had it,” he said. “When you don’t see it and you don’t hear about it you think, ‘Well, that’s not something we have here in the United States.’ It’s tough for people to take that seriously and think, ‘Well, yeah, I probably should get the shot.’”
A popular meme often circulated among people who oppose the MMR vaccine involves “The Brady Bunch,” a 1960s sitcom. In a 1969 episode, the TV family happily navigates a measles outbreak, gleeful about time off school, appearing to experience very little distress.
People cite the show as an example of why measles isn’t much to worry about, an inaccurate view, health officials said.
But the truth is, the virus wasn’t much to worry about in recent years when vaccination rates reached 95% or higher. That wasn’t because the virus was no big deal — health experts are quick to point out —  but because the virus wasn’t spreading.
Clearly, that reality has changed, said Dlugolecki, something he didn’t expect when he began his public health career 13 years ago. He didn’t think waiting for the next report of a measles exposure would be part of his regular workload.
“I was shocked to see it come back as it has over the last couple of years,” he said. “I didn’t expect to see massive outbreaks in dozens of states with deaths being reported.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: More CT kids, youths accessing shelter services in 2026
description: The number of Connecticut youths accessing emergency shelters has increased by about 5% from 2025 to 2026, and resources are stretched.
text:
The number of Connecticut youths accessing emergency shelters has increased by about 5% from 2025 to 2026, and resources for that population are thin, homeless service providers said.
More than 970 children have accessed emergency shelter services in 2026, an increase from 928 in 2025 and 844 in 2024. Another 365 people aged 18 to 24 have accessed these services, according to data from the Connecticut Coalition to End Homelessness.
This comes at a time when the state has minimal shelter services for people under 18, said Stacey Violante Cote, of the Center for Children’s Advocacy. Late last year, the New Haven-based Youth Continuum shuttered under financial stress. This left only two youth shelters in the state — both in Fairfield County.
“It’s unsafe that we have minors that don’t have a place to go if they are kicked out of their house, or if they leave home,” Violante Cote said.
This has particularly posed problems for LGBTQ+ kids who might not be comfortable going into adult shelters, Violante Cote added.
Most children are accompanied by their parents, said Sarah Fox, chief executive of the Connecticut Coalition to End Homelessness. The increase is partly driven by rising costs of living and broader problems for families in making ends meet.
“All of these issues impacting our families have a direct impact on youth, and I do think that there’s a lot of areas that we need to focus on, including having resources ready for youth,” Fox said.
She added that the Connecticut Department of Education, which defines homelessness differently from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, likely has the more complete count.
In the education world, homeless students include those who are “doubled up” or sleeping on a friend or family member’s couch. The Department of Education also counts students who are living in hotels, where HUD typically does not.
This means that the state’s count of homeless students far outpaces numbers of youths accessing emergency services.
In the 2025-26 school year, state data shows that there were about 4,800 students experiencing homelessness. That made up about 1% of the total student population. That’s actually a slight decrease from 2024-25 when there were about 5,100 students experiencing homelessness.
Fox said that could be the result of an undercount. The students reported in the state’s data are those who come to the attention of the school district — they typically seek services and tell a school employee that they don’t have a stable place to sleep.
Violante Cote said for those students who are doubled up, sometimes it can be hard to get housing aid because many state services require that people be actually homeless — living on the streets or in shelters — before they can access the help. This can be a particular challenge for kids aging out of foster care, she said.
“We need to focus on housing and stability earlier and make sure that young people and families are connected to resources faster, so we can prevent housing instability,” Fox said.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware wins $16 million to strengthen charter schools
description: Five-year federal grant will support new and expanding programs while adding oversight and accountability measures DOVER, Del. — Delaware has secured a five-year, $16 million federal grant to expand access to public charter schools while strengthening the oversight, financial monitoring and support intended to ensure those schools deliver results for student[...]
text:
Photo: Classroom at the Sussex Academy, a charter school in Georgetown.
Five-year federal grant will support new and expanding programs while adding oversight and accountability measures
DOVER, Del. — Delaware has secured a five-year, $16 million federal grant to expand access to public charter schools while strengthening the oversight, financial monitoring and support intended to ensure those schools deliver results for students.
Grant could add about 1,900 seats
The Charter Schools Program grant begins Oct. 1. At least 90% of the money — approximately $14.4 million — will be distributed through competitive subgrants supporting the planning, opening, replication and expansion of charter schools.
Proposals will be evaluated based on educational quality, demonstrated community need, organizational readiness, financial sustainability and evidence of demand. If enough proposals meet those standards, the initiative has a five-year goal of increasing Delaware’s charter school enrollment capacity by approximately 10%.
About 19,000 students currently attend Delaware’s 23 charter schools. A 10% capacity increase could create room for approximately 1,900 additional students, although actual growth will depend on the proposals received and approved.
“Expanding opportunities for students cannot be about adding seats for the sake of adding seats,” Delaware Secretary of Education Cindy Marten said. “We have to start with what students and communities need and be equally focused on quality, strong implementation and accountability.”
Grant targets unmet educational needs
The Delaware Department of Education said the grant will target educational needs that are not being fully met by existing programs. Potential areas include alternative and therapeutic education, career and workforce pathways, rural education, dual-language instruction, literacy programs and flexible options for students who are older than their classmates or have not earned enough credits to graduate on schedule.
The initiative also seeks to improve charter school access for economically and educationally disadvantaged students, multilingual learners, students with disabilities and other groups that have faced barriers to educational opportunities.
“Charter schools are one part of Delaware’s public education system,” Marten said. “This investment gives us an opportunity to support strong educational models where there is documented need, learn from what is working, and use those lessons to expand opportunity across public education.”
Priority for underserved students and communities
Existing charter schools applying for replication or expansion funding will be judged partly on their academic performance and operational track records.
Proposals serving underserved communities, addressing transportation barriers or expanding opportunities for multilingual learners and students with disabilities may receive priority consideration. Programs offering workforce-connected education or replicating successful school models also may receive additional consideration.
State officials emphasized, however, that priority status will not allow an applicant to bypass the program’s quality, readiness or financial requirements.
Investment extends beyond individual schools
A portion of the federal award will be used to provide charter schools with technical assistance in governance, board development, fiscal management, regulatory compliance, leadership development and program implementation. The state also plans to establish peer-learning programs and professional communities where educators and school leaders can share successful practices.
The grant also calls for stronger charter-authorizing practices, including annual reviews of each participating school’s academic, financial and organizational performance.
“We are grateful for the partnership between the Delaware Department of Education and the Delaware Charter Schools Network,” said Kendall Massett, the network’s executive director. “We are equally grateful for this investment in our education system, and for what it makes possible for students across our state.”
Massett said the grant reflects “a shared vision for collaboration, flexibility, and support for the people and strategies best positioned to make a difference for students statewide.”
Schools will face continuing monitoring
Schools receiving subgrants will undergo continuing fiscal, program and performance monitoring. That process will include progress reports, budget reviews, site visits, performance evaluations and reviews of implementation milestones.
The Department of Education said it will use those findings to identify risks, direct additional assistance to struggling programs and take corrective action when necessary. An independent outside evaluator also will assess the initiative throughout the five-year grant period.
Lessons and successful practices identified through the program will be shared with both charter and traditional public schools through professional development, peer networks and other cross-sector programs.
First competition planned during opening year
The Community Funding Accelerator assisted Delaware with identifying the federal funding opportunity, determining the state’s eligibility and preparing the application.
During the grant’s first year, the Department of Education plans to establish its management and accountability systems, consult with education stakeholders and provide technical assistance to prospective applicants. It also will release the first competitive funding opportunity, train application reviewers and select the first group of grant recipients.
Details about eligibility, application requirements, available award amounts and deadlines will be announced as the first competition is developed.

Potential uses: Planning and opening new charter schools and replicating or expanding successful schools
Statewide goal: Increase charter enrollment capacity by approximately 10%, subject to qualified proposals

How to apply: The Delaware Department of Education will release eligibility requirements, application instructions and deadlines as the first funding competition is developed
Learn more: Visit the Delaware Department of Education website at education.delaware.gov

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘I plant seeds’: Harrisburg teacher named South Dakota teacher of the year
description: A third-grade teacher for the Harrisburg School District was recognized as South Dakota’s 2027 teacher of the year at a banquet Wednesday in Fort Pierre. text:
Christina Berger teaches a class of third-graders at Liberty Elementary School in the Harrisburg School District. Berger was recognized as South Dakota's 2027 teacher of the year. (Courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Education)A third-grade teacher for the Harrisburg School District was recognized as South Dakota’s 2027 teacher of the year at a banquet Wednesday in Fort Pierre.
Christina Berger has taught at Liberty Elementary School for the last eight years, though she has more than 20 years of experience in elementary education. She started her career in North Dakota.
In a video recognizing Berger as a regional teacher of the year, Berger said she loves teaching “because who wouldn’t love organized chaos?”
Berger said helping children learn, especially in reading, and connecting with each of her students on a personal level brings joy to her career. That drive to create lasting relationships extends to parents and community members through her involvement in the district’s Parent-Teacher Organization and by hosting student teachers throughout her career.
“I plant seeds,” Berger said of her role as an educator, “and you get to see the result years and years later.”



 Christina Berger, South Dakota’s 2027 teacher of the year, is featured in a video when she was honored earlier as a regional teacher of the year. (Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Education)
Liberty Elementary Principal Aaron Weaver said in a news release that Berger’s influence reaches beyond the classroom.
“She leads with heart, integrity and an unwavering commitment to doing what’s best for kids,” Weaver said.
The teacher of the year recognition means she’ll serve as a representative for South Dakota public education across the state and country, including attending the National Teacher of the Year Program Orientation, Space Camp, Washington Week, and the Impact and Influence Virtual Conference.
South Dakota Secretary of Education Joe Graves said in the news release that Berger earned the award because she’s “crafted her own legacy in the Harrisburg School District.”
“Her colleagues, students, and parents positively compliment her and her teaching style with a common takeaway of every child feeling seen, valued, and supported,” Graves said.

 Catching Our Eye

• Farmers, water, and data centers. The Reporting Project’s Alan Miller reports, “Farmers raise concerns about long-term protection of water resources in wake of Ohio Chamber of Commerce study on data-center demand.”
A key finding in an Ohio Chamber of Commerce study of water and electricity resources available for data center growth in central and southwestern Ohio is that those corridors are “broadly well positioned to support additional data center growth from a water-resource perspective through 2030.”
That’s a little more than three years from now. What about water resources 13 years from now? Or 23 years from now?
Some folks involved in agriculture and food production, which add an estimated $124 billion to the economy annually and are the state’s largest industry when combined, are concerned that not enough is being done to include them in discussions about water or to protect Ohio’s water resources far into the future.
• Well, disaster. The Athens County Independent’s Dani Kington reports, “Operator fights to reopen injection wells linked to disaster.”
A fracking waste injection company is fighting to reopen two suspended Noble County wells that the Ohio Department of Natural Resources linked to a 2021 environmental disaster.
The wells were initially suspended by order of the chief of the Ohio Department of Natural Resources Division of Oil and Gas Resources Management in January 2023. The division found the wells were responsible for a 2021 incident in which toxic waste injected into the ground by DeepRock Disposal Solutions burst to the surface via an oil and gas production well two miles away. The incident contaminated Noble County land and waterways, killed hundreds of animals, and cost the state nearly $1.3 million to clean up.
• Starting with love. In Matter News, Jack Shuler writes, “If you start from a place of love, you can’t go wrong: A vigil for an unhoused community member who recently died in Newark served as a call to not look away.”
“You know, the world has a way of overlooking people,” said Pastor Peter Borhauer of First United Methodist Church in downtown Newark, Ohio. “If you don’t fit whatever the expectations are, no one cares.”
He was speaking to a knowing crowd of 50 or so people gathered in the church basement to memorialize a friend named Daisy, a loved one who died on the streets of this small city. The room is filled entirely with church volunteers, outreach workers, and people who are unhoused or have been. The man across from me, “Mm-hmms,” in affirmation.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Feds drop appeal that sought to block funding for Gateway tunnel project
description: The Trump administration dropped a bid to revive a funding freeze that a federal judge found "flagrantly" violated law.
text:
NEW YORK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 17: Construction continues on the Hudson Gateway Tunnel project to connect New Jersey to Penn Station on October 17, 2025 in New York City. President Donald Trump recently said he "terminated" the $16 billion Hudson River tunnel project and the Second Avenue subway extension project. White House budget director Russ Vought has said that the spending was based on "unconstitutional" diversity, equity and inclusion principles. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)The federal government dropped an appeal that attempted to again block federal funding for the Gateway tunnel and other infrastructure projects in the region just weeks after asking a federal court to overturn a lower decision that found the funding freeze flagrantly violated law.
In a mandate issued by the U.S. 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals, court clerk Catherine O’Hagan Wolfe said New York, New Jersey, and the federal government agreed to dismiss the appeal. The federal government said just last month that it was moving forward with an appeal.
The $16 billion Gateway project will add new rail tunnels under the Hudson River, and is considered one of the most important infrastructure projects in the nation.
The court’s order does not detail how the parties came to an accord, but the Gateway funding freeze threatened political consequences in competitive House districts in New York and New Jersey, including in the 7th Congressional District. There, Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) faces former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot Rebecca Bennett (D) in what is expected to be the closest House contest in the state.
The Trump administration first froze funding for Gateway last September.
Russel Vought, the director of the federal Office of Management and Budget, at the time said the freeze was meant to ensure funds did not flow to “unconstitutional DEI principles.”
Trump, meanwhile, repeatedly said the freeze was meant as political punishment for Democrats amid a federal government shutdown.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Teachers’ unusual classroom supplies expose another ClassWallet snag
description: Senior student Anyla Clayborn, left, and Yazoo City High School librarian Katie Erwin sort a few of the books Erwin has collected for the depleted library, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Yazoo City.
text:
Every morning for a week, the fifth-graders in Hannah Bagwell’s science class at Florence Elementary School check on the apples.
Under their watchful eyes, three apples — one whole, one halved, one sliced — will decay. The students will take notes, predict what will happen and analyze the success of their guesses the next day. Bagwell uses the lesson to introduce the students to the scientific method. It’s a unique way to teach the idea, and she’s found it’s the most successful. 
“Science is so real-world, so having hands-on experiences really helps the students see that science is everywhere,” she said. “It’s hard for them to think about in theory, but when they see it in practice, it makes it more relatable to students.”
Teachers across subjects use all kinds of supplies and methods to teach students — think building toothpick-and-straw contraptions in physics class to prevent falling eggs from cracking, or using shaving cream for a sensory word spelling experience in kindergarten. 
But these nontraditional items have become harder to access, according to some Mississippi teachers. 
The Mississippi Department of Education rolled out a new digital platform this year for the Education Enhancement Fund, or procurement card program. The program, which was established in 2012, gives every K-12 public school teacher $748 a year — around $25 million in total — to buy supplies for their classrooms. But educators have long said they get the money, traditionally in the form of a physical card, too late for it to be useful. 
Florence Elementary School students in Hannah Bagwell’s class observe apples decompose in a science investigation.  Credit: Courtesy of Hannah Bagwell
To make the process easier for teachers, the agency switched to ClassWallet this year, a digital platform that allows teachers to purchase supplies online from pre-approved vendors. Teachers can also file for reimbursement for purchases from vendors that are not included, and local vendors can apply to join the marketplace.
“The decision to move to the digital platform … was driven by frustration we were hearing from teachers by way of business managers,” said Kymberly Wiggins, the state education agency’s chief operating officer. “This was not a decision made in a vacuum. We heard pretty sound concerns that drove us to examine the way we were delivering those funds.”
According to Wiggins, the change has been successful. More than 35,000 teachers are using the program, she said, thousands more than at this point last year. 
They are also spending more money. Last year, in the first month of activating the cards, teachers spent $8.5 million of the $25 million allocated for the program. This year, they spent almost $10.5 million in the first month. 
“We’ve come a long way,” said Lance Evans, Mississippi Superintendent of Education at a state board of education meeting Thursday. “We’re excited about where we are.”
But educators say the new platform forces them to plan lessons far ahead and makes it more difficult to buy uncommon teaching supplies and subscribe to online teaching modules. 
“I haven’t tried to be reimbursed because it’s not a ton of money,” Bagwell said, of the apple experiment. “The new process is definitely more complicated than just going to the grocery store. For someone who is not thinking weeks in advance, especially when it comes to a science investigation, I’m going to have to spend more of my own money now.”
Yazoo City High School students, from left, Kursactys Owens, A’drisia Martin and Carrington Clark, are shown by librarian Katie Erwin how to bind their report projects using a Cover One book binding machine, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Yazoo City. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Wiggins said the agency is trying to respond in real time to teachers’ concerns. People work over the weekend to approve teachers’ purchases, she said, and they’re accepting more nontraditional items, such as a convection oven for a science class or fidget spinners for special education students. 
Out of 70,000 transactions, the agency has only rejected 448, she said. 
“We are aware of those niche kinds of specialized teacher populations,” Wiggins said. “We see the program working because they’ve spent half the funds, but we know there are areas we can gain some efficiencies.”
‘Another rock in the road’ with ClassWallet
Katie Erwin is one of those educators who requires unique supplies. The Yazoo City High School librarian says the ClassWallet online marketplace offers beaucoup books, but it’s missing what she really needs: Book repair equipment.
She would typically buy those through Amazon, but her account is frozen because it’s linked to her old physical EEF card. Erwin has two options, and she’s not pleased with either: She could buy the supplies elsewhere and file for reimbursement, but she’s uncomfortable linking her bank account. Or she could request that another vendor is added to the marketplace, but she’s not sure how long that would take. 
For now, she’s stuck borrowing supplies from teachers and relying on her principal to help her get what she needs.
Read more: Mississippi teachers say new state-mandated process for buying classroom supplies is ‘insane, cumbersome, frustrating’
“It’s just another rock in the road with this new system, another something to go around,” Erwin said. “I feel like I have very little control or say over where I buy from or what I buy. It almost feels like I’m being doubted. 
“If I say the library needs something, it needs it.”
Yazoo City High School students are shown by librarian Katie Erwin how to bind their report projects using a Cover One book binding machine, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Yazoo City. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
State officials weigh a solution
Erwin has run into another problem frustrating educators across the state: Paying for subscriptions. 
Previously, educators were able to use their physical cards to pay for subscriptions to teaching platforms or teacher supply magazines. The new ClassWallet marketplace doesn’t account for subscriptions. Teachers have no choice but to pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement, which many prefer not to. 
Erwin, for example, subscribes to her local newspapers and keeps them in the library for students. Other educators, such as music teacher Michelle Cook in Laurel, need subscriptions for curriculum. 
Cook has for years subscribed to a music magazine, ordering songs for students that come with a digital download, making it easy to project lyrics onto her screen. The subscription is about $150 a year. 
As the only music teacher at her elementary school, she has the same group of students from year to year. She uses the subscription to keep the songs fresh, keep her class fun. 
Now, without being able to pay for the subscription with state funds, she’s going to reuse old songs. 
“Some of the kids might remember it,” she said. “It’s just been frustrating. I would love to be able to get access to the stuff I need.”
Bagwell, the science teacher, is splitting a subscription to a science video service with other science teachers at her school. One teacher pays $300 for the subscription at the beginning of the year, and the others send her their share via Venmo. 
Ronald Jeri, a Spanish teacher at West Jones High School, relies heavily on subscriptions to teach his students. The platform Señor Wooly, for example, allows his students to watch educational videos, answer questions and learn how to correct their mistakes. 
Jeri estimates he spent around $400 on subscriptions each year. In early August, he said he wasn’t sure what he would do this year. 
“I’m hoping that in the following weeks, somebody will try to correct this huge mistake,” he said. 
Wiggins said the agency is aware of educators’ issues paying for subscriptions and acknowledged reimbursement is currently their only option — but it may not be for long. 
Yazoo City High School librarian Katie Erwin talks about using personal funds to equip the library with needed items, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Yazoo City. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
State Education Department officials hope to introduce a hybrid model for the program in the future, she said. Part of the $748 in EEF funds would go to a physical card that teachers could use for subscriptions or last-minute supplies at their local store. 
Agency officials deployed a new feature on Aug. 31 that allows businesses enrolled in the direct pay program to be paid directly from ClassWallet. That way, teachers don’t have to file for reimbursement. Currently, 20 vendors are enrolled. 
Wiggins wants to hear from more teachers in the future to improve the program. 
“Our thought was not ever making this a more cumbersome, complicated process,” she said. “We had little to no visibility into what teachers were purchasing. For us, this has been really informative to establish benchmarks about what teachers need. 
“We just continue to listen to all feedback and figure out how to make this experience as efficient as possible for teachers while also finding the balance of being good stewards of $25 million in state funds.” 
Erwin, though, wishes educators were more involved in the process from the start. 
“Where’s our voice in all of this?” she asked. “Are we being consulted before the big decisions are being made, or are people just throwing Band-Aids at us afterwards?”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Tenant right to purchase bill closer than ever on Beacon Hill
description: The House and Senate each tucked a version of the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act, or TOPA, into its economic development bond bill this summer. A six-member conference committee is now negotiating a single version of the omnibus bill to send to Gov. Maura Healey.
text:
IF THE LANDLORD of a large Massachusetts apartment building decides to sell it off, the tenants inside have few options other than hope the next owner doesn’t have plans to price them out. Occasionally a local community organization or city partnership will manage to step in to buy and preserve the building as affordable units. 
More often, the waves of the market wash the housing out of reach for longtime, lower-income tenants.  
Housing advocates say working to build new homes, including subsidized affordable housing, is essential, but can’t make up for the loss of existing lower-cost units. “We like to say trying to solve the housing crisis without preserving affordable housing is like trying to fill up a bathtub with the drain open,” said Ann Jochnick, a housing attorney with the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute. 
The social justice advocacy group is one of the organizations backing legislation that advocates say could go a long way toward preserving existing lower-cost housing by giving tenants a chance to band together and buy a building being put up for sale.  
The House and Senate each tucked a version of the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act, or TOPA, into its economic development bond bill this summer. A six-member conference committee is now negotiating a single version of the omnibus bill to send to Gov. Maura Healey.  
Broadly, the policy would let renters in a multifamily building being put on the market organize to match an outside buyer’s offer and purchase the property themselves, or hand that right to a nonprofit or community land trust. 
Right to purchase laws for tenants first arose in the late 1970s, with one of the strongest measures now on the books in Washington, DC, which adopted the policy in 1980.  
Advocates credit it with preserving more than 16,000 units of affordable housing in DC, and a government study found that housing production continued apace, but real estate groups say it needlessly extended the period of time it took to sell buildings and drove away third-party bidders. They argue that recent changes to DC’s policy were necessary because the tenant right-to-purchase rules were slowing down the sale process and putting landlords in a bind. 
Sen Pat. Jehlen, a Democrat from Somerville, who put forward tenant right-to-purchase legislation in Massachusetts, said it “would allow communities to slow displacement and gentrification by removing some homes from the for-profit, speculative, escalating market, and making them permanently affordable.” 
Legislative opponents, however, say the policy will harm the housing market.  
Rep. David DeCoste, a Norwell Republican, said he is concerned that the measure “will have a severely detrimental impact on small property owners.” He said it will “diminish the value of existing properties and discourage potential investors from buying existing properties or building new multifamily homes.” 
State Sen. Lydia Edwards, a Democrat from East Boston, who is one of the measure’s Senate co-sponsors, points out that tenant right-to-purchase laws are nothing new in Massachusetts.  
Since the 1990s, residents in manufactured housing like trailer parks have had the right of first refusal to buy the land if it will be sold, and a law has been on the books since 1983 requiring most landlords who plan to convert apartments into condominiums to give the tenants the right of first refusal to buy their unit. 
“We’ve always had an option to purchase,” Edwards said, “but we’ve just narrowed it to specific kinds.” The new forms of legislation target tenants in large rental buildings, she said, “because they’re being displaced.” 
Advocates say the types of buildings that TOPA tends to cover — unsubsidized low-cost units known as naturally occurring affordable housing — are much cheaper to preserve when compared with the cost of building new subsidized affordable housing. And the units, which make up almost half of the affordable housing in the state, are dwindling and often in the sightline of investors. 
The Legislature passed a tenant opportunity to purchase measure at the very end of its 2019-2020 session, as part of an economic development bill. Then-Gov. Charlie Baker signed the rest of the roughly $627 million package, but line-item vetoed the tenant right-of-first-refusal section, saying he was concerned “that making multifamily sales transactions less predictable will result in less investment and construction of fewer rental units.”  
This session, the policy came back as standalone legislation in both chambers, put forward in the House by Democratic Reps. Jay Livingstone and Rob Consalvo and by Jehlen in the Senate.  
Cassie White, director of policy and community organizing for the community development organization Fenway Forward, testified in favor of the on the standalone bills. The policy would have helped her group preserve affordable units, she said. 
Fenway Forward twice made offers to buy a 55-unit apartment building in Boston’s Fenway neighborhood, with the support of tenants, but were outbid in 2019 and rejected in favor of a lower but faster-closing offer when it was put up for sale again in 2022. The group said Fenway Forward had planned to make the units affordable to households making between 30 to 60 percent of area median income, or between $40,000 to $80,000 for a two-person household. 
The version of the policy that the House adopted would only have the measure take effect in cities and towns that opt in to the tenant purchase policy. Landlords would have seven days to notify tenants of a planned sale, and tenants would then have 15 days to form a tenant association and make an offer. If there is no offer from the tenant group or their partner, the landlord can find another buyer. Once an outside offer is made, tenants would have another 15 days — up to 30 in some circumstances — to match that offer, then 160 days to secure financing and close.  
Landlords who own six units or fewer in a participating municipality are exempt. 
The Senate version is narrower, creating a five-year pilot in five communities, with the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities writing the regulations. 
The Massachusetts Law Reform Institute is part of the TOPA Coalition, a roughly 70-organization alliance of tenant groups, affordable-housing developers, and preservation nonprofits that has pushed the policy for more than a decade. Jochnick, the housing attorney, said the coalition would like to see the most comprehensive version make it through conference committee, but if it is a pilot, she would like to see at least 10 communities covered to include a wider array of cities. 
MassLandlords, which represents owners and managers of rental property statewide, opposes the policy “in all forms.” 
The group argues TOPA’s main beneficiaries are nonprofit community development corporations who would own the buildings, and that the added delay discourages sales altogether. It points to Washington, DC, as a cautionary tale. Lawmakers in the nation’s capital overhauled the statute last September, exempting multifamily buildings constructed in the past 15 years and some two- to four-unit buildings, along with adding a 45-day “cooling-off period” during which tenants can’t sell off their rights under TOPA to a third party. 
For Edwards, the idea of starting out with a pilot program addresses a few major concerns. Because the state housing office would be in charge of regulations, there would be opportunities for feedback on the final program. It would also let a small number of willing Massachusetts municipalities be the testing grounds, and the five-year pilot could be renewed if the communities want to apply again and take more time to test the policy. 
“If it doesn’t work, we’ll learn with limited damage,” she said. “If it does, then everyone wins.”

text:
The Boney Courthouse in downtown Anchorage, across the street from the larger Nesbett Courthouse, holds the Alaska Supreme Court chambers. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Court System is now offering automatic reminders by text message for people with upcoming court hearings, part of an effort to reduce the number of missed appearances.
The court system announced the service Wednesday. State courts already offer automatic text notifications for jury duty and upcoming criminal cases. 
To sign up for the new service, text a case number to (575) 222-8484. The system will ask for a confirmation. Reply yes. Reminders go out at 4 p.m. the day before the hearing.
People who receive notifications do not need to be part of the case, and there is no limit to the number of signups per phone number.
The court system, which operates the service, will not sell your phone number to a third party, and it will not share it, the court system says in its terms and conditions.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: US Sen. Roger Marshall leaves paper trail in Florida while calling Kansas home
description: TOPEKA — U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall established deeper roots than previously disclosed in Sarasota, Florida, where he had a vacation home that he traveled to on official business and said he used for visiting family. Marshall and his wife put down roots in Sarasota, hosting fundraising events, obtaining real estate and fishing licenses and filing […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall prepares to speak to a group of Kansas business leaders on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall established deeper roots than previously disclosed in Sarasota, Florida, where he had a vacation home that he traveled to on official business and said he used for visiting family.
Marshall and his wife put down roots in Sarasota, hosting fundraising events, obtaining real estate and fishing licenses and filing paperwork from the coastal Florida town while the senator worked in Washington, D.C., and claimed Kansas as home. 
The Republican senator’s residence has been fodder for campaign attacks as he faces a midterm election against the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Kansas City-area United Methodist pastor, who Marshall has pointed out owns four homes.
Marshall has faced persistent scrutiny throughout his time in the Congress for his transience in Kansas. Public records show his wife has held a Florida real estate license for half of her husband’s Senate term and has another license application pending. Records also show Roger Marshall has held fishing licenses in Florida since 2019 and used a P.O. Box in Kansas as his primary personal mailing address.
He appeared Saturday alongside Hamilton at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson in the first senatorial debate of the season, where he addressed his residency.
“My home is a short hour’s drive down a gravel road here,” Marshall said.
The crowd groaned, laughed and jeered.
The St. John home is a three-bedroom house that sits on more than 300 acres, surrounded by ponds, he said. Others have described it as a hunting cabin.
He sold the Great Bend home where he said he and his wife raised their kids within days of being sworn into the U.S. Senate in 2021. He previously had a rental property in Santa Cruz, California, which he sold in 2019 for between $1 million and $5 million, according to U.S. House financial disclosures. 
The Marshalls bought the Sarasota vacation home for $1.2 million in 2019. Since then, Roger Marshall held active fishing licenses in Florida until May, according to Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission records.
His wife, Laina Marshall, held a Florida real estate license from 2021 to 2023 and currently has an application for another pending, according to records from the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation. Her main address is listed on the application as the Marshalls’ Florida home. It is unclear whether she brokered any real estate transactions.
Laina Marshall, wife of Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, attends a campaign rally for her husband on Sept. 14, 2026, at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe. It was headlined by Vice President JD Vance, who credited Marshall’s public service, faith and friendship. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
When the Marshalls sold their Great Bend home, the deed was notarized in Sarasota on Jan. 13, 2021, while Congress was on a weeklong break.
The family appears to own more valuable assets in Florida than Kansas, paying roughly five times as much in property taxes in the Sunshine state than the Sunflower state during Marshall’s time in the U.S. Senate, according to county property records in both states.
Marshall has claimed the rural Stafford County house as his home base for years, while voting records show his ballot is mailed to a P.O. Box that is also used as his official campaign committee mailing address. He also used his old Great Bend address on candidate filings until Sept. 11, when he changed it to the Stafford County address, according to Federal Election Commission records.
After initially acknowledging Kansas Reflector’s detailed list of questions, a spokesperson for Marshall’s campaign did not respond to questions about Marshall’s primary residence, personal travel to Florida and his wife’s real estate dealings.
“I only wish I had a home in Florida,” Marshall told reporters in August, according to the Topeka Capital-Journal.
He told the state fair crowd Saturday: “You’ll be glad to know it was struck by two hurricanes and has been uninhabitable for two years.”
The home is mostly rebuilt and on the market for $1.45 million, according to a real estate listing.
He said he used the home to visit his grandchildren, who live in the area.
“I don’t think anybody in Kansas would hold it against somebody for wanting to go visit their grandchildren,” Marshall said.
Members of the crowd heckled Marshall throughout his explanation, and a chant swelled from the bleachers.
“You don’t live here,” the crowd shouted like they were in a basketball arena.
Hamilton encouraged Marshall to “spend all the time you can in Florida with your grandkids,”
The Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, and Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall appear on the debate stage on Sept. 12, 2026, at the Kansas State Fair in Hutchinson. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector
Even after the hurricanes’ destruction, Marshall’s ties have remained in Sarasota. He hosted a “Sarasota retreat” fundraiser in conjunction with his own political action committees and the Kansas Republican Party in 2024 and 2025. Politico in 2025 published the invitation to the second annual retreat at the St. Regis Longboat Key Resort. 
Janette and Stan Gray, a couple from Paola who own an internet company that serves rural areas of Kansas and Missouri, said Marshall’s time in Florida won’t factor into their vote for him in November.
“Come wintertime, anybody that’s smart and has the money heads south,” said Stan Gray, 61.
Janette Gray, 54, said she would “probably do the same” as Marshall.
The couple attended a campaign rally Monday in Olathe, where Vice President JD Vance and half of Kansas’ congressional delegation stumped for Marshall.
Stan Gray said it has remained apparent that Marshall is from Kansas.
“He still is from here,” he said. “You don’t leave Kansas. You just spend some time away from the cold.”
Reporting by the Kansas City Star revealed Marshall took official trips from Washington, D.C., to Sarasota, spending more than $18,000 in taxpayer funds from 2021 to 2024. The trips reportedly stopped after a hurricane destroyed the area. It is unlawful for a senator to use taxpayer money for personal travel.
Marshall has criticized Hamilton for owning four homes. Hamilton is registered to vote in Stilwell, where he said he and his wife live. He also owns a lakefront vacation property in the Missouri Ozarks and two additional houses, which he said he bought for his adult daughters, in Lawrence and Kansas City. The Hamiltons’ trust has owned the Climax Springs home since 2012, according to Camden County property records.
Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton’s campaign said Marshall’s ties to Florida “are more evidence Marshall abandoned Kansas, doesn’t care, and simply isn’t doing his job.”
“Kansans have taken note of his absence and deserve to know what exactly the ‘official business’ was that cost them $20,000 for routine trips to his home in Florida,” he said.

title: SC regulators file to take over Charleston insurance companies, alleging high-risk debts
description: SC regulators are seeking an emergency takeover of a retirement-focused insurance firm the agency argues is at risk of defaulting on customer payouts.
text:
South Carolina regulators are seeking an emergency takeover of a retirement-focused insurance firm the agency argues is at risk of defaulting on customer payouts. (File photo/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — South Carolina regulators are seeking an emergency takeover of a retirement-focused insurance firm the agency argues is at risk of defaulting on customer payouts.
The state Department of Insurance filed suit in Richland County this week to take control of Atlantic Coast Life Insurance until the company turns around its investment portfolio.
In court filings, the agency said the company overextended on high-risk, underperforming investments beyond what state law allows. If these ventures fail, as many as 50,000 customers who rely on the company for retirement income could lose their life savings. It could also affect more than 100,000 funeral and life insurance policyholders from the legacy arm of the business.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“If the Department of Insurance allegations prove true and the company is allowed to keep operating this way, tens of thousands of people could see their retirement income disappear,” said Bob Hartwig, a University of South Carolina finance professor who studies the insurance industry. “We’re talking about promises that are literally meant to last a lifetime.”
The company declined to comment beyond its court filings.  In those filings, the company denies these allegations, says it’s fiscally sound and accuses the department of overstepping its authority. It also counter-sued state Insurance Director Michael Wise, alleging he publicized confidential information that could harm the company.
Company history
A private equity firm bought Charleston-based Atlantic Coast Life in 2015. Since then the company has gone from selling life insurance and funeral policies to largely offering a form of investment vehicle, known as an annuity.
Under the business model, insurance companies sell annuities to policyholders in exchange for investment proceeds. Income is tax-deferred, so people often use them when they’re planning to retire. Sometimes their payouts are used to pay off a mortgage, finance a grandchild’s college education or are taken in intervals to cover living expenses.
But the financial backstop for the policies sold by Atlantic Coast Life involves a complicated web of businesses and includes investments in companies facing bankruptcy and fraud charges.
While Atlantic Coast Life focuses on investment, it’s still an insurance company and falls under the state insurance agency’s purview.
SC Director of Insurance Michael Wise on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. (Screenshot of SCETV legislative livestream)
The filing by the agency this week is the latest in a lengthy legal dispute dating back to at least 2024. The department is asking a circuit court judge to overturn earlier rulings by the state court that hears cases involving South Carolina’s regulatory agencies.
The company wants the judge to deny the department’s requests, citing the 2025 findings in Administrative Law Court. In those proceedings, retired Supreme Court Justice Kay Hearn, who was acting as the hearing officer, found the companies were “paying their obligations as they come due” and “the department has conceded that it has identified no risk that the companies might default.”
Furthermore, the company, in court filings, called the department’s allegations “speculative” and said a takeover would “cause immediate and irreparable harm” to the business and its policyholders.
In January, the national insurance ratings agency AM Best downgraded the company’s financial strength from a B++ (Fair) to B (Good.)
Exception not the rule
Hartwig called a failing annuity company “very much the exception rather than the rule.”
Hartwig said state insurance regulators have the authority to intervene before a company fails. To say regulators should wait until a company is in default would be like telling the Federal Aviation Administration not to act until after a plane crashes, he said.
“In my opinion, (Department of Insurance) would be derelict in its duties if it didn’t get involved,” Hartwig said.
Since the Great Recession, private equity firms’ involvement in the insurance industry has increased, especially in the life and annuity sectors. These insurers are predictable investments and boast large pools of capital that appeal to private equity, the Department of Insurance said in court filings.
When Advantage Capital took over Atlantic Coast Life, income from insurance premiums jumped from $25 million in 2015 to $102 million a year later, court filings say. By 2024 it had reached a high of $1 billion, according to a company financial report.
But these deals also tend to involve more risk. As a result, state law puts limits on the level of risk companies can take.
Under the arrangement, Advantage Capital Management, a subsidiary of Advantage Capital, managed the insurance company’s investments and collected fees for doing so. The deal further involved Advantage Capital sub-advisers also collecting fees.
None of this is unusual in this line of business. What is outside the norm, according to state insurance regulators, is the size of the fees charged compared to the success of the underlying investments the advisors made.
The firms invested heavily in private bonds rather than publicly traded ones, choosing those less regulated investments at a rate double the industry average, the insurance agency said.
Meanwhile their fees grew to more than double the industry standard, the agency’s lawyers said in court filings, despite performance that was only ordinary.
Some of those investments involved distressed or insolvent companies, the agency said: a struggling low-cost Canadian airline, European professional soccer clubs that have never turned an operational profit and a film studio still recovering from a failed Bollywood merger.
Hartwig called private equity involvement in the insurance sector a source of growing concern among industry watchdogs. The companies’ investment strategies are a major pivot from the past, when insurers stuck to investment-grade corporate bonds.
“Life insurance has been around for hundreds of years,” he said. “Over that history, most would never imagine backing the retirement dreams of thousands of Americans with these types of investments.”
Risky investments
As Atlantic Coast Life took on riskier ventures, it needed a way to balance that risk on its books.
That’s where another Advantage Capital subsidiary, Southern Atlantic Reinsurance, comes in.
Reinsurers are designed to help insurance companies take risk off their balance sheets so the insurance company doesn’t have to keep as much capital on hand.
The reinsurer took on $2.4 billion in reserves and associated investments from Atlantic Coast Life. But Southern Atlantic’s investment portfolio wasn’t much better, according to the state Insurance Department.
It loaned tens of millions to companies that later filed for bankruptcy. To recoup losses, it foreclosed and took over those companies, but insurance regulators aren’t convinced the insolvent companies will perform any better under Advanced Capital’s control.
In other cases, it let loans grow and linger beyond their original due date without collecting payments or interest.
777 Partners
Furthermore, the insurance companies are entwined on multiple levels with a family of companies accused of mismanagement and financial crimes.
Those companies, known as 777 Partners, got their start purchasing legal settlements and lottery payouts from cash-strapped recipients. Whenever courts award someone legal winnings but the awardee can’t afford or doesn’t want to wait for payments to roll in over time, they can sell it for a discounted lump sum. The company gets all future payments and the recipient gets cash up front, though less than they would have received over time.
The 777 Partners took out loans to finance these purchases and invested the funds in assets “not traditionally found in insurance portfolios,” the state Insurance Department said, such as airlines and sports teams, in addition to an insurance business.
The company is now in bankruptcy court and former executives have pleaded guilty to or face charges of federal fraud.
Atlantic Coast Life, through its parent company, holds investments in 777 companies. The company told state insurance regulators it was distancing itself from 777 but the two remain entangled. In all, 777 owes $1.3 billion to Advantage Capital affiliated companies, loans that are now in default, according to court filings.
Whether the state Department of Insurance steps in to shore up Atlantic Coast is again up to the courts.
While the insurer is a small operator compared to industry giants with hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of policy holders, the company’s failure would be no less devastating to those involved, Hartwig said.
