name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Shellfish farmers warn overregulation could drive NJ aquaculture to ‘extinction’
description: Shellfish farmers pleaded with New Jersey legislators to ease restrictions on aquaculture. An Assembly panel approved four measures Thursday.
text:
Shellfish farmers pleaded with New Jersey legislators to ease restrictions on aquaculture. An Assembly panel approved four measures Thursday. (Photo courtesy of New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection)Legislators advanced a package of bills Thursday intended to help New Jersey’s aquaculture industry, with shellfish farmers complaining that state regulations stifle expansion and have driven some to move out of state.
The Assembly’s agriculture and natural resources committee listened to an hour of testimony during an afternoon hearing at the Statehouse, where shellfish farmers blasted a common boogeyman: the Department of Environmental Protection.
Oyster farmer Matt Gregg, co-founder and operator of the Barnegat Oyster Collective and president of the New Jersey Aquaculture Association, likened the department to a villain from a Scooby-Doo cartoon. Like Scooby’s gang of teenage detectives, shellfish farmers have had to band together to fight foes like the pandemic, marine predators, and extreme weather, Gregg said.
“But more often than not, the foe is the New Jersey DEP,” Gregg said. “If we don’t do something, we will die a death of a thousand cuts. We will regulate everyone into extinction.”
Larry Hajna, a department spokesman, declined to comment.
One of the industry’s biggest challenges, farmers testified, has been the state’s longtime narrow definition of aquaculture, which specifically bars “construction of facilities and appurtenant structures” from the definition. That has set aquaculture farmers up for zoning and permitting hurdles that land-based farmers don’t face and also discouraged commercial investors from investing, Gregg and other shellfish farmers testified.
“It’s like telling a farmer that the barn that he’s built and owns isn’t part of his farm,” said Scot Mackey, executive director of the Garden State Seafood Association.
So one bill the Assembly panel considered would expand the state’s definition of aquaculture beyond in-water operations to include land-based hatcheries, processing facilities, storage sheds, and other structures that support the industry. It passed unanimously.
Bill sponsor Assemblyman Alex Sauickie (R-Ocean) called it “a minor change but it is a game-changer.”
“These folks are treated like second-class farmers right now, from my point of view,” he said.
The panel also passed a bill that would get more industry voices on the Aquaculture Advisory Council in the state Department of Agriculture. Shellfish farmers complained that public officials now pack the council, which has had longstanding vacancies and sometimes flouts its statutory mandate of meeting four times a year.
“It’s hard to advise anyone on aquaculture matters if the aquaculturists aren’t involved in the discussion,” said Matthew Williams, who owns the Cape May County-based South Bay Shellfish Company. “In recent years, about half of the current industry-related seats have been vacant, and there’s been little industry attendance at the meetings. I think many members of our industry have been disenfranchised because of how things work at the council. Meetings get canceled. Members of the industry have literally been shushed, and the most recent aqua-development plan was six years late.”
The bill would expand the council’s membership from 13 to 18 members, at least eight of whom would have to be residents experienced in the aquaculture industry.
Committee members also passed a bill that would task the council, the agriculture and health departments, and other agencies with developing guidance on aquaculture agritourism. And they approved a resolution to recognize the work of Rutgers University’s Haskin Shellfish Research Laboratory. Scientists there have developed disease-resistant, hardier, and faster-growing oyster strains, the legislation notes.
Assemblywoman Andrea Katz (D-Burlington), the committee’s chair, said the bill package arose out of a visit she and other legislators made earlier this summer to see shellfish farmers in action in Barnegat Bay.
“What became pretty clear quickly is that our laws hadn’t quite caught up with what these farmers are actually doing,” she said.
Most of the aquaculture in New Jersey is shellfish production, with more than 50 mollusk farms in coastal bays here that primarily harvest hard clams and Eastern oysters, according to Rutgers. Farmers here also harvest trout, baitfish, koi, and aquatic plants, according to Sauickie.
One clam farmer said he hopes the legislative package passed Thursday is just the start.
William Mayer of Brigantine-based Clam Daddy’s told committee members clam farming is the backbone of New Jersey’s aquaculture industry but remains “microscopic” compared to its competitors down South because of “the red tape and the government restrictions.”
He urged lawmakers to consider giving aquafarmers financial assistance to offset skyrocketing labor and utility costs and persuading state environmental officials to expand the coastal acreage where they’re permitted to work.
“We have difficulty accessing commercial working waterfronts, never-ending electrical rate hikes, and labor costs that never seem to stop rising,” Mayer said. “The cost of doing business is a boatload of clams. As the marine commercial waterfront is erased by mega mansions, clam farmers are stuck with nowhere to go.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s literacy gains inspired me to postpone retirement
description: I’ve worked in education for 30 years, which means I can now retire and receive my full benefits.  But I’m not writing this from my favorite spot on my patio with my dogs beside me and my feet up; instead, I’m writing from my office as an elementary school principal in Phelps County, where I’ve […]
text:
(Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)I’ve worked in education for 30 years, which means I can now retire and receive my full benefits. 
But I’m not writing this from my favorite spot on my patio with my dogs beside me and my feet up; instead, I’m writing from my office as an elementary school principal in Phelps County, where I’ve returned for my 31st year in education.
I delayed retirement because my school is on a roll. I know it sounds crazy. So many headlines are about teacher shortages and learning recessions and other problems plaguing public schools. But my small school in rural Newburg is achieving hard-earned progress through a program that’s expanding across Missouri, and I’m not ready to go.
Where does our momentum come from? The stars aligned. That’s what it feels like. Over the last few years, Newburg recruited another educator with more than 30 years of experience to serve as superintendent. She installed me as principal of the elementary school. My school was chosen to participate in the Rural Schools Early Literacy Collaborative, a philanthropy-backed initiative to increase reading skills in Phelps County. 
Being a part of the Early Literacy Collaborative means our grade K-1 teachers receive intensive support from national experts. These experts are former teachers who have taught the same grades and implemented the same curriculum they’re coaching my teachers on. And they’ve flown to Missouri once a month for the last two years to visit our classrooms, ask about our students, and help us improve our instruction. 
The difference has been transformative. After the first year of the Collaborative, 100% of our kindergarten and first-grade students demonstrated growth on reading tests, and on average those students made gains that more than doubled our typical annual growth. The official data hasn’t been released yet for the second year, but the number of students who need improvement and are on Reading Success Plans has gone way down – they’re meeting their goals and moving on. Now we have students who are scoring Advanced Proficient. That just wasn’t happening before. 
Like a lot of schools across Missouri and across the country, we struggled with building our students’ foundational reading, writing, and math skills. As a rural school serving low-income students, it’s harder to recruit and retain teachers. That means we have more teachers with less experience. Some were still working their way through college while they were trying to learn how to manage a classroom. Others didn’t have research-backed curriculum for teaching kids how to read. In other words, our teachers weren’t set up to succeed, and — not surprisingly — our students weren’t having lots of success.
Being a part of the Early Literacy Collaborative has made all the difference. Over the last two years, we’ve purchased and implemented materials and lesson plans that build on each other and support both teachers and students. Our teachers have received consistent, actionable feedback from fellow educators who have experience with their grade-level dynamics and instructional materials. We’ve received training, both as an individual school and as a part of the Collaborative, on how to set up systems to make this work sustainable. 
I believe we’re almost at a tipping point, and that’s why I’m still here. This year we’re prioritizing data – helping our teachers learn how to keep track of each students’ progress with different skills and adjust their instruction accordingly. This is really hard work, but after seeing what we’ve been able to accomplish over the last few years, I know we can handle it.
I’m not the only one who knows we have a good thing going. The state sees something special happening in Phelps County, and aspects of the support we’ve received through the Early Literacy Collaborative are now being put into practice across the state. I’m thrilled that more schools have access to this same type of coaching.  
So yes, I could be sleeping in on weekday mornings and not stressing about the wellbeing of dozens of educators and hundreds of students. But I’ve worked in education long enough to know that these moments when everything falls into place – with experienced administrators overseeing prepared teachers using effective materials and receiving constructive feedback – are few and far between. They’re moments I want to be here to experience. 
And when I do retire, it’s going to be a good feeling. What a way to go out.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: National screen time debate reaches Oklahoma schools
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — As questions swirl nationwide about the appropriate role of technology in children’s education, some Oklahoma parents, lawmakers and districts are calling for a reduction to in-school screen time. The nation’s two largest districts, New York City Public Schools and the Los Angeles Unified School District, rolled out policies this year curtail[...]
text:
Jenks High School students use laptops and paper worksheets in an advanced chemistry class at the Jenks Public Schools Math and Science Center on Nov. 13, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — As questions swirl nationwide about the appropriate role of technology in children’s education, some Oklahoma parents, lawmakers and districts are calling for a reduction to in-school screen time.
The nation’s two largest districts, New York City Public Schools and the Los Angeles Unified School District, rolled out policies this year curtailing use of personal devices and artificial intelligence in the classroom. Similar discussions are now burgeoning in Oklahoma.
Parent groups in multiple Oklahoma districts have started advocating for limits on education technology, like laptops, touch-screen tablets and lessons delivered digitally. State lawmakers have taken notice as they consider which bills to pursue in the next legislative session.
The state House passed a bill this year that sought to limit children’s screen time in elementary schools at no more than an hour a day, but the legislation didn’t survive the Senate.
One of the bill’s authors, Sen. Ally Seifried, R-Claremore, said she’s considering filing legislation on school screen time again. Seifried, the vice chair of the Senate Education Committee, also wrote laws banning student cellphone use in schools and implementing regulations on AI in education.
“I do think the time is ripe to make this a priority this upcoming session,” she said.
Sen. Ally Seifried, R-Claremore, speaks to another senator ahead of the chamber’s organizational day on Jan. 7, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
After the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, many Oklahoma districts purchased a laptop or tablet for each student, a concept known as “one-to-one” devices, in an attempt to maintain instruction during a time of school closures and individual quarantines.
Those devices have largely remained, and some traditional, brick-and-mortar districts have incorporated digital or AI-based lessons into daily classroom instruction.
The chief question, Seifried said, is whether education technology better supports student learning than traditional teaching methods.
To Katie Smith, a mother of two children in Edmond Public Schools, the answer is a clear “no.”
Too many medical associations and academic studies have raised concerns about the negative impact screen time and digital media consumption can have on children, she said. Other studies suggested digital tools are less effective for learning. Meanwhile, national reading and math scores have declined since education technology became adopted more widely.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends parents consider the quality of their children’s digital media interactions, not only the amount of time spent consuming it.
Smith founded Pencils Over Pixels-Edmond Public Schools in June to advocate for limits on AI and screen time access, borrowing the name from a similar parent group in Pennsylvania. 
She said her opposition to excess screen time isn’t based on a “bad feeling” about it, but rather experts and data.
“I think the evidence is in, and I think it’s clear and convincing,” said Smith, an attorney.
Laptops fill cubbies at the Jenks Public Schools Freshman Academy on Nov. 13, 2024. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Her sons in pre-K and fourth grade each received school-assigned devices, and she said she found it worrying that no district policy limits daily use while they’re in the classroom.
In a statement to Oklahoma Voice, the Edmond district said it will convene a committee this year to look at overall technology integration in its schools, including screen time, and whether it needs to make any changes to its practices.
Smith has urged the Edmond Board of Education to adopt a resolution affirming support for pencil-and-paper instruction, physical learning materials like printed textbooks and use of digital devices only when they offer “clear, evidence-based instructional advantages that cannot be achieved through traditional methods of learning.”
About 500 Edmond parents have signed a petition supporting the resolution, Smith said. Even more have expressed support from other districts — Stillwater, Norman and Oakdale — where parent groups are advocating against overuse of screen time and “gamified” online lessons, she said.
Smith has supported an even more rigorous policy than her resolution’s language. Social media pages for Pencils Over Pixels-Edmond have promoted elementary schools being 90% to 99% screen-free, middle schools having no more than 50 minutes of screen time per day and high schools allowing up to 15 minutes of personal device use per class.
“I’m not totally anti-technology at school by any means,” Smith said. “I just think it needs to be put in its place. I think it’s just taking over everything. We need reasonable limits. We need a policy. We need breaks. We need balance.”
Oklahoma Teacher of the Year Kasey Bennett also has been advocating for a reduction in one-to-one devices, particularly at the early elementary level. Students miss out on critical interpersonal interaction and fine motor skill development when they spend too much time behind a screen, she said. 
Bennett teaches elementary science, technology, engineering and math in Durant Public Schools through hands-on, tactile lessons. Use of screens in her classroom is intentionally “very, very limited,” she said. 
“I know we have to take assessments,” Bennett said. “I know we have to have computer class. That is fine. Everything in moderation. There’s no reason a 6 year old needs their first grade work delivered to them sitting in their classroom behind a one-to-one device.”
Durant Public Schools teacher Kasey Bennett is the 2026 Oklahoma Teacher of the Year. Bennett, who also runs a small business, stands at her vendor stall at the Affair of the Heart show on June 11 at the Oklahoma County Fairgrounds in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Long before the pandemic, Putnam City Public Schools started purchasing iPads for students K-12, and it still does so today.
The touch-screen tablets and Apple software bolster the district’s emphasis on project-based learning, said Putnam City’s chief technology officer, Cory Boggs. He said the district, based on the west side of the Oklahoma City metro area, hasn’t seen any advocacy within its community against the devices.
Elementary and middle school students are mostly expected to leave their iPads at school while high school students can take them home, he said.
Unless they’re enrolled in online courses or credit recovery, Putnam City students don’t have lessons delivered to them through a digital platform, Boggs said. Classes are led by teachers, who decide how much they want to involve the iPads, and students are assigned both physical and digital copies of their textbooks.
The devices are still essential, though, because state-mandated assessments and academic screeners are taken electronically, Boggs said.
“We just have to look at the day and we look at their situation and make sure it is being used in the most appropriate manner,” he said. “I would be the first one to say you shouldn’t be using your technology all the time for everything you do. Never. It’s just a tool when it makes sense.”
In far northeast Oklahoma, Welch Public Schools has gone in the opposite direction. The district discontinued its one-to-one Chromebook program this school year.
Superintendent Jeremy Ramsey said the district now relies more on teacher-directed, hands-on learning, though Chromebooks are still available in school buildings when needed.
Ramsey said he hopes higher literacy scores will result from students reading physical books and taking notes on paper. The policy change also wiped away a $30 Chromebook fee that each family had to pay to cover repairs.
The district school board voted unanimously in favor of the change, and the Welch community gave “zero negative feedback about not using electronic devices,” Ramsey said.
“I’m a firm believer that districts need to do what’s best for their community,” he said. “If they have a good curriculum surrounding (devices), then I say more power to them.
“Do whatever you feel you need to do within your community. In my community, it was strongly positive.”

name: WyoFile
title: Destructive ventenata — arguably worse than cheatgrass — sweeps west across Wyoming
description:
The noxious invasive grass has been detected west of the Bighorn Mountains for the first time. 
The post Destructive ventenata — arguably worse than cheatgrass — sweeps west across Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
MEETEETSE RIM—Josh Shorb’s internal dialog upon learning that the destructive nonnative grass ventenata was found growing along the highway shoulder south of Cody spanned four letters and one syllable.
Because his gut reaction needn’t see print, the Park County Weed and Pest District supervisor pondered a more poignant way of describing his thoughts. 
“How do I say this?” Shorb said. “I was dejected, but not surprised. Then it was just time to get to work.” 
Late Tuesday morning, Shorb was getting to work. He was standing near where his colleague, Jake Jarrett, found the African grass growing along a Highway 120 ditch between Cody and Meeteetse earlier in the summer. 





Click to enlarge: A cured blade of slender, aggressive ventenata grass rests in Josh Shorb’s palm on Sept. 15, 2026. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Shorb was overseeing an aerial mission to douse ventenata with a chemical that would kill it: Rejuvra. Make no mistake, he knew he wouldn’t get it all, even though his contracted pilot was putting down the herbicide on 420 acres and well beyond the patches where the noxious grass was found. 
“This is day one,” Shorb said. “This is a plant where, if you turn your back for a few years, you’re going to be in trouble.” 
In the right conditions and the right place, ventenata can be even more destructive than cheatgrass, the most widespread annual invasive grass overtaking Wyoming. It has similar properties: Also called wiregrass, ventenata germinates in the fall, overwinters and cures out into tinder by summer. It’s even less palatable to livestock and wildlife, providing almost no nutrition to foraging critters. 
But until now, ventenata was more confined to eastern Wyoming. It showed up in North America in the early 1950s and Sheridan County in 1997, but distribution maps show it has been most widespread in the Pacific Northwest and Idaho. 
Seth Herby watches his father, Tony Herby, take off during an all-day Sept. 15, 2026 operation to kill off ventenata that was detected in a Park County highway right-of-way. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
Shorb was standing and talking at the first detection site in Wyoming west of the Bighorns. His counterparts at weed and pest districts around the Bighorn Basin and broader western Wyoming are now on high alert. 
Shorb guesses that ventenata seed was given an accidental ride into the area from Carbon County, Montana, which has a bunch of it. 
“Something got kicked out of a tire, like a piece of mud,” Shorb said. “Now here we go.” 





Click to enlarge: Cheatgrass (left), Japanese brome (center) and ventenata (right) are all easily found in the Highway 120 right-of-way south of Cody. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Heightening costs and declining resources will make responding more difficult. Envu-manufactured Rejuvra is already notoriously expensive — about $1,100 a gallon — but in 2026 the cost of spraying “has really gone up,” Shorb said. With fuel and herbicide costs on the rise, he’s now paying roughly $75 an acre. That means just on Tuesday, the Park County Weed and Pest District was looking at a $32,000 bill. 
While one-time grant money allocated by the Wyoming Legislature helps, other funding streams have suffered. Property tax-reliant weed and pest districts around Wyoming have taken a hit, and now the Bureau of Land Management is scaling back its own spending to spray cheatgrass — and now ventenata. In 2026, the BLM’s Wind River/Bighorn Basin Field Office invested a whopping $1.2 million on cheatgrass spraying in Park County alone. 
In 2027, however, Shorb’s bracing for vastly reduced assistance from the federal government. 
“The BLM, they still have some money for noxious weed control, but specifically for cheatgrass control, we’re told that they’re out,” Shorb said. “This is just a perfect storm of what we don’t need right now.”

name: WyoFile
title: What politicians could learn from horses
description:
Wyoming still has what other states sold off. Rescission of the Roadless Rule could take what’s left of our backcountry, writes guest columnist Dan Smitherman.
The post What politicians could learn from horses appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

Riding out of the Bridger Wilderness after dark, leading a pack string, tired and impatient, suddenly my horse stopped and refused to budge. Aggravated, I dismounted to lead the string only to discover I was about to ride off a cliff band. The lesson is, sometimes we need to pay attention to information being given to us. This applies to riders and politicians alike.
The Trump administration wants to rescind the Roadless Rule, opening millions of acres to road construction. They claim it’s about access and fire management. As someone who’s spent years guiding hunters and riders through Wyoming’s wilderness areas and now volunteers with Back Country Horsemen of America maintaining these trails, I can tell you they’re solving the wrong problem.
Access doesn’t require roads. Every season, Back Country Horsemen and outfitters pack into our national forests with crosscut saws and shovels. We clear blowdowns, maintain trails and pack supplies for the Forest Service. This system works well and will continue to work.
What doesn’t work is the math. The Forest Service already has a backlog of $6.4 billion needed to maintain existing roads. Backcountry roads aren’t interstate highways. They wash out every spring, need constant grading and require endless culvert replacements and bridge repairs. Adding more miles of backcountry roads while existing roads go unmaintained is like a homeowner taking out a second mortgage while the first house collapses.
The fire argument doesn’t hold either. Humans cause 90% of wildfires. Research consistently shows fires are more likely near roads than in roadless areas. The Roadless Rule already allows temporary roads for legitimate fire suppression. What it prevents is permanent roads that become permanent ignition sources.
I learned terrain and threat assessment in the Marines. You identify what needs defending and what threatens it. After guiding hunters and families through these mountains for years, I know what threatens Wyoming’s backcountry: not a lack of roads, but too many of them.
Working with Citizens for the Wyoming Range, we fought hard to pass the Wyoming Range Legacy Act, protecting these mountains from drilling. We understood that some landscapes generate more value intact than fragmented. The outfitting economy, the hunting heritage and the clean water flowing to downstream communities all depend on keeping some country unroaded.
The horsemen I ride with are ranchers, veterans, teachers, folks who’ve lived here all their lives and newcomers who moved here precisely because Wyoming still has what other states sold off. We maintain trails not for pay, but because we believe the backcountry should remain accessible to anyone willing to earn their way in.
Politicians look at roadless areas and see untapped resources. I see the last places where elk bugle without traffic noise, where you can ride all day without crossing pavement or gravel, where the skills I’ve learned still matter. These aren’t locked lands. They’re intact working landscapes that work precisely because they’re roadless.
The Roadless Rule has functioned for nearly 25 years. Like that smart horse at the edge of a cliff, it’s kept us from making an irreversible mistake. Once you punch roads through migration corridors and pristine watersheds, you can’t undo it. The wildness doesn’t come back. We’re not making any more wilderness.
Wyoming’s congressional delegation needs to hear from people who actually use these lands — veterans who found peace in these mountains after serving; outfitters whose livelihoods depend on wild country; horsemen who keep trails open with sweat and saddle leather— not just from those who want to extract and develop them. 
Some information is worth heeding. When every major hunting organization, conservation group and backcountry user says these protections work, that’s information. When the only voices calling for more roads come from those who profit from extraction, that’s information too.
After all my years riding in Wyoming’s high country, I know the best parts require effort to reach. That’s not a bug in the system. That’s what makes them worth protecting.
This is information that our politicians need to hear and take to heart. 
The draft environmental impact statement was released for public comment in late August. The comment period is currently open and closes on Oct. 6.  Please submit your comments opposing the rescission of this rule.

name: WyoFile
title: Enjoying my backyard on a beautiful September day
description:
WyoFile’s Jared Steinman celebrates the value of an unsuccessful hunt.
The post Enjoying my backyard on a beautiful September day appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
I didn’t grow up hunting like many of my peers and neighbors here in western Wyoming. I didn’t learn at the feet of a parent or a mentor but rather alongside friends who have been selfless enough to indulge my questions and blunders. 
I consider myself fortunate to have not tasted success in the field my very first season. Walking through the woods quietly and with intention, spending time in wide open spaces, and appreciating the natural resources that surround us is always worth waking early for, regardless of the outcome. 
On Tuesday, a friend and I were able to get out for much of the day in search of mature mule deer. Though we came up short in our search, the day had new meaning for me. As a new father, with far less free time and sleep — things I took for granted last hunting season — the day re-affirmed for me just how lucky I am to live near open skies, steep mountains, clean water and people who appreciate those things as much as I do. 
Whether my son will grow to enjoy hunting remains to be seen, but I hope he’ll appreciate where he lives and learn the virtues of a tired body and a fulfilled spirit after a long day exploring his backyard.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Blackburn camp blasts Registry for seeking AG probe
description: That tree you heard falling in the forest produced no sound, except for a subsequent grating from U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign. Blackburn’s people ripped the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance this week after it forwarded a complaint by a Blackburn surrogate to the Attorney General’s Office for investigation, as board member Tom La[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, photographed on Aug. 6, 2026, will be the Republican gubernatorial candidate in November (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)That tree you heard falling in the forest produced no sound, except for a subsequent grating from U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign.
Blackburn’s people ripped the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance this week after it forwarded a complaint by a Blackburn surrogate to the Attorney General’s Office for investigation, as board member Tom Lawless speculated, “It’ll be buried there.”
The board could have subpoenaed people, which would take months, if not years. Besides, it doesn’t have the resources to find the people behind a dark-money group’s ad that targeted Blackburn during the gubernatorial primary. And, she won the Republican nomination anyway after demanding the ad be pulled because, clearly, it was gaining traction.
That didn’t stop campaign spokesperson Abigail Sigler from issuing a scathing comment, “This shady, dark-money group failed to meet basic transparency requirements defined in Tennessee law, and this morning, the Registry failed to fulfill its most basic responsibility to Tennesseans, who deserve to know who is actually funding these AI deepfakes. By refusing to do its most basic job, the Registry is complicit in concealing the truth from Tennesseans.”
Heaven forbid. Or should we ask: Why such anger?
Blackburn’s campaign must have forgotten that the Registry board, Tennessee’s campaign finance watchdog, took no action on a complaint filed by Knoxville Republican activist Gary Loe against Blackburn saying she used federal campaign funds to supplement her gubernatorial campaign. 
Loe said Blackburn’s spending was “deceitful” and noted that voters could see what happened.
Lawyers for U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn demanded a group pull ads calling her “queen pharma mama” and filed a complaint with the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Yet the Registry board dropped the matter in March after receiving word that no transfer of money took place. Blackburn spent more than $10 million to capture reelection to the U.S. Senate in 2024, then spent another $3.2 million from December 2024 to August 2025 when she announced a run for governor, according to Federal Election Commission records.
Back to Blackburn’s complaint. Chip Buck of Pall Mall filed the complaint in July against Alexandria, Virginia-based American Exceptionalism Institute, a dark-money group that pounded Blackburn with TV ads calling her “queen pharma mama,” in reference to “60 Minutes” and Washington Post reports on a pharmaceutical law — written by a pharmaceutical lobbyist — she co-sponsored. It was designed to make sure patients received their medication but wound up stopping DEA agents from intercepting large drug shipments with opioids during a national epidemic. 
Blackburn’s campaign demanded TV stations stop running the ad during the gubernatorial primary, which she captured by 10.5 points over U.S. Rep. John Rose with state Rep. Monty Fritts playing a spoiler role with 23.5% of the vote.
Even though Buck filed the complaint, Blackburn campaign attorney Brandon Smith made the argument before the Registry to go after the dark-money PAC for using AI-generated ads and failing to disclose required information such as the identity of those controlling expenditures.
Blackburn’s legal people sent “takedown letters” to various news stations raising questions about the ad, as well as potential violations of the Tennessee Political Public Transparency Act, Smith said. 
The web is getting tangled here.
According to campaign finance records, didn’t a political action committee operated by officers of the conservative pro-private school voucher group Club For Growth spend $4.81 million backing Blackburn’s gubernatorial bid, months after she donated a nearly identical amount to the organization’s primary PAC?
Smith failed to mention that tidbit.
Instead, he called the Virginia PAC a “straw” group made up of people who pump out such misleading ads frequently. He also said the Federal Communications Commission told Blackburn’s campaign it launched an investigation into TV stations owned by Sinclair Broadcast Group, E.W. Scripps Company, Gray Media and Nexstar Media Group related to “improper reporting” on PAC expenditures and ads.
Registry board member Paige Burcham Dennis warned him to use the words “possible improper,” since the matter remains an allegation. 
The FCC did not respond immediately to questions by the Lookout.
But Registry board member Hank Fincher, a former Democratic lawmaker, was miffed, to say the least, by the Blackburn campaign’s statement.
Maybe the board should have forwarded the case to the state agriculture commissioner’s office instead, Fincher surmised.
“We sent this to the chief law enforcement officer of the state to investigate it,” Fincher said. “I must assume that the staff member who made this ridiculous assertion doesn’t understand what the attorney general does or how powerful his office is.”
Fincher said he would ask the board at its next meeting to investigate all the dark-money campaigns involved in this year’s Republican primary “where both sides seemed to benefit.”
“Dark money has no business in Tennessee, and the beneficiaries of it have very little moral standing to complain about its use by others, in my opinion,” Fincher said.
David Hatley, an independent candidate running for governor, talks with voters at a campaign event in Franklin, Tenn. on Sept. 12, 2026. (Photo: J. Holly McCall/Tennessee Lookout)
Selective editing?
While the Blackburn campaign is going after the PAC that ran the “queen pharma mama” ad, it started attacking independent governor candidate David Hatley recently with online posts of him wearing jail fatigues in reference to a 1998 bank fraud conviction. We’re not sure if AI was used in the attack or if someone used paint by numbers to put him in black-and-white striped clothes.
Either way, Hatley, who reported on his legal problems at length in a book, has turned it around well enough with a hot tub business to put $7 million into his campaign and could wind up being a thorn in Blackburn’s side at the ballot box.
If he wins 20% or more of the vote and Green grabs 40%, the leading Republican could be in trouble.
If you can’t beat ’em …
Democratic state Rep. T.J. Hardaway announced this week he will not continue his write-in candidacy for the District 93 House seat in Memphis, saying instead he will back Kyler Gilkey in a new write-in campaign.
Hardaway was appointed this year to complete the term of his father, Rep. G.A. Hardaway, who died in April. T.J. Hardaway said in a release he will pursue a law degree and drop his election campaign. He took office shortly before the legislature held a special session to redraw congressional districts and slice the majority-Black city of Memphis into three seats.
Gilkey lost to former Rep. Joe Towns in the August primary and was passed over for a spot on the ballot last week. Just one member of the Shelby County Democratic Party’s executive committee selected Matthew Szalaj as its nominee for the November general election following Towns’ resignation to serve as Shelby County Criminal Court clerk. He won that election in August.
Officials said executive committee member Coleman Thompson chose Szalaj because he called him first, which is always critical.
State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a Memphis Democrat, will start running campaign ads on Fox News for his 2026 U.S. House campaign. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Conservative viewers beware
State Rep. Justin Pearson started running two TV ads this week for his 9th Congressional District campaign on Fox News and Newsmax. He plans to follow up with cable channels and digital and streaming sites in his campaign against Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor of Shelby County.
But hitting ultra-conservative folks immediately is an interesting strategy. Will he be wasting money on people who wouldn’t vote for him if he were the last candidate on the planet, or will he be able to woo MAGA voters to his side? The latter is not likely.
Cowboys country
A group of Tennessee GOP state senators visited President Donald Trump’s midterm rally in Dallas last week, including Shane Reeves, Jessie Seal, Ed Jackson and, interestingly, two Senate speaker candidates, Majority Leader Jack Johnson and Paul Bailey. 
The prez proffered all sorts of ideas to keep Republicans in control this November. Most notably, Trump said he would give $5,000 to everyone in the country if Republicans regain the House and Senate, setting off a firestorm of criticism. 
The proposal largely fell on deaf ears, though some would say Trump’s policies have cost them a lot more than five grand over a year and a half.
“I understand the appeal of putting 5K back into American pockets, but with a $40 trillion national debt, it doesn’t seem very fiscally responsible,” Reeves said.
Bailey, who paid for the trip out of his campaign account, took a similar view, saying he’s “not a fan” of the proposal.
“If we’re going to pay out $3.3 trillion, we should be paying it toward the national debt,” Bailey said.
Likewise, Johnson used his campaign account to make the trip, and even though he hasn’t taken a position on Trump’s $5,000 giveaway, he has “serious concerns about the impact it would have on the federal deficit,” spokesperson Molly Crawford said.
Tennessee lawmakers love to brag about balanced budgeting every year while Congress just passes spending resolutions to keep the money flowing. The difference is the Tennessee Legislature is required by law to balance the budget, which is why it hides a boatload of money in every department.
“Don’t you ever feel guilty when you come up short / Man you better be careful, you’re gonna get caught” – Tom Petty and The Heartbreakers – “The Criminal Kind”

text:
Part of the 10 acres the state wants to lease would include the parking lots above the Boring Company’s Music City Tunnel. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee officials will take another crack at speeding up the process of choosing a developer for state-owned land near the Capitol in Nashville.
The Department of General Services wants to select a master developer to turn several parking lots surrounding the Tennessee Capitol into a mixed-use development with housing, hotel, retail and state employee parking. The lots include the one on which Elon Musk’s Boring Company is building the first phase of its underground tunnel for Tesla vehicles.
Last week, the department brought a waiver before the State Building Commission that would allow General Services to skip the legislative disclosure process for the project. For public-private partnerships, the department is required by law to submit plans during the budget cycle, which the state legislature typically approves in April each year. The department did not submit anything during the 2026 legislative session.
State Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat who is not on the commission, opposed waiving the legislative disclosure during the public comment period of the commission’s meeting.
After her comments, the commission deadlocked in a 3-3 vote, then agreed to meet Monday after taking more time to review the proposal. 
TN officials want waiver to speed up process to choose developer of Nashville parking lots

 
Campbell said in an interview Thursday, she isn’t opposed to redeveloping the lots, but she worried the department would try to steer the contract to a specific person. 
“This is 10 acres of potentially the most valuable land in the state,” Campbell said. “Why aren’t we going through the normal process?”
The Department of General Services is also seeking a request for qualifications as part of the waiver. This type of deal differs from a request for proposals, giving the department more say in selecting the developer, something that also caught Campbell’s attention. 
Michelle Parks, a department spokesperson, said the RFQ allows the department to “identify developers with the experience and financial capacity to complete this long-term project.” 
The state would retain ownership of the property through a lease agreement with the master developer.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and Washington show key strategies for effective wildfire funding
description: Wildfire is no longer a seasonal surprise across the Mountain West. It is a recurring fiscal challenge that threatens communities, public lands, infrastructure, air quality, and state budgets. As Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and Washington confront increasingly costly fire seasons, policymakers should rethink not only how much they spend on wildfire, but how tho[...]
text:
Wildland crews implement firing operations to remove unburned vegetation between a fire’s edge and containment lines on the 2026 Three Queens Fire in Washington. (Photo courtesy of the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest)Wildfire is no longer a seasonal surprise across the Mountain West. It is a recurring fiscal challenge that threatens communities, public lands, infrastructure, air quality, and state budgets.
As Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and Washington confront increasingly costly fire seasons, policymakers should rethink not only how much they spend on wildfire, but how those dollars are structured.
Idaho’s wildfires: The risk doesn’t end where insurance does for our small businesses

The central challenge is that wildfire costs are unpredictable. A state may experience a relatively mild season one year and face extraordinary suppression expenses the next. Yet preparedness, forest management, equipment and community resilience require steady investment long before smoke fills the skies.
A more resilient wildfire funding system should therefore have two distinct components: predictable baseline funding for preparedness and mitigation, paired with flexible reserves and emergency authorities for suppression and recovery.
States in our region offer useful examples of how to build such a system.
Montana has taken important steps through its Wildfire Suppression State Special Revenue Account. Established in 2008, the account can support suppression, preparedness, equipment and mitigation. In 2023, House Bill 883 provided a $152 million one-time General Fund appropriation, increased the amount available for mitigation and preparedness, and established a balance target tied to General Fund revenues.
In 2024, Montana’s suppression costs were approximately $39.1 million, while the account was projected to hold roughly $145 million at the end of fiscal year 2025. That reserve provides stability, but the state should continue evaluating whether its funding structure encourages the most effective long-term investments.
Idaho has emphasized a combination of dedicated funding and partnerships. Its Fire Suppression-Deficiency Warrants Fund helps address unexpected suppression costs, while programs such as Shared Stewardship and the Good Neighbor Authority support work across ownership boundaries. That approach recognizes a basic reality of Western wildfire: Fires do not stop at property lines, and neither should prevention efforts.
Wyoming provides another model through its Emergency Fire Suppression Account, Fire Protection Revolving Account, legislative appropriations, federal grants, and emergency authorities. The state authorized approximately $176.9 million for wildfire suppression and recovery during the 2025–26 biennium. Wyoming’s approach illustrates the importance of maintaining access to emergency resources while using the regular budget process to provide oversight and accountability.
Washington has pursued a more comprehensive strategy. Its Wildfire Response, Forest Restoration, and Community Resilience Account commits $125 million per biennium for eight years, or $500 million total, to connect response, restoration and community resilience. A public dashboard also helps track how funds are being used. That kind of transparency can improve public confidence and help policymakers determine which investments are producing results.
These approaches differ, but they point toward a common lesson: Wildfire funding should not be treated as a single line item. Suppression is essential, but it is often the most expensive and least predictable part of the system. Preparedness and mitigation can reduce the severity of future fires, protect communities, and lower pressure on emergency budgets. Recovery funding is also necessary, because the costs of a fire continue after the flames are extinguished.
Still, mitigation spending should not become a blank check. A recent analysis from the Property and Environment Research Center found that fuel treatments can generate substantial benefits, including reduced federal firefighting costs and avoided smoke and property damages. But returns vary by project. Larger, strategically selected projects produced stronger estimated benefit-cost ratios than smaller projects. The implication is clear: states should prioritize targeted treatments where they are most likely to reduce risk, rather than measuring success simply by dollars spent or acres treated.
The same principle should apply to the way wildfire funds are budgeted and spent. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation’s analysis of “use it or lose it” federal spending raises concerns that agencies may accelerate spending at the end of the fiscal year simply to preserve future appropriations. Although not specific to wildfire funding, the analysis reinforces the need for wildfire dollars to be tied to measurable outcomes and long-term risk reduction rather than incentives to spend funds before they expire.
The Mountain West also needs to recognize the limits of state-only solutions. Wyoming, Idaho, Montana and Washington all contain significant federal land, meaning state investments can be undermined when federal, state, tribal, and private landowners pursue disconnected strategies. Better coordination, shared data, and cross-boundary projects can stretch scarce dollars further.
A smarter funding system would establish a reliable preparedness and mitigation baseline, maintain reserves for severe suppression seasons, preserve legislative oversight, and require clear performance measures. Policymakers should ask not only how much money was spent, but whether communities were better protected, response costs were reduced, and forest conditions improved.
Wildfire will remain part of life in the Mountain West. The question is whether states will continue paying primarily after disaster strikes or invest more deliberately before the next fire begins.
Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, and Washington are experimenting with different answers. Their experiences suggest that fiscal responsibility and wildfire resilience are not competing goals. With predictable funding, targeted mitigation, transparent reporting and regional cooperation, they can reinforce one another.

title: As September weather turned in 1876, campaigning in Colorado reached a fever pitch
description: The U.S. Army Signal Service recorded a high of 56 degrees Fahrenheit in Denver on the rainy afternoon of Sept. 18, 1876, and the next day the Front Range was “white with snow,” reported the Denver Times. Along with the first state elections, scheduled for the first Tuesday in October, the changing weather brought the […]
text:
Guard's Hall, at 15th and Curtis streets in Denver, is pictured in this photo from the 1870s. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-18553)The U.S. Army Signal Service recorded a high of 56 degrees Fahrenheit in Denver on the rainy afternoon of Sept. 18, 1876, and the next day the Front Range was “white with snow,” reported the Denver Times.



← Sept. 10–16
Sept. 17–23 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

Along with the first state elections, scheduled for the first Tuesday in October, the changing weather brought the return of evening programming at many of the city’s social clubs and its handful of entertainment venues. At Guard Hall, at 15th and Curtis streets, the Forresters, a family theater company, opened a run of shows on the 18th, with Mrs. Forrester starring as Lady Isabel Vane in a stage adaptation of Ellen Wood’s “East Lynne.”
“The playing of Mr. and Mrs. Forrester in ‘East Lynne’ was very fine, and was so acknowledged by all,” raved the Times. “Mrs. Forrester is a charming actress, and wins the hearts of her audience at the start.”
After brief residencies in Idaho Springs, Georgetown and Golden, the Forrester troupe’s arrival in Denver meant “a fair prospect of a somewhat extended season of dramatic amusements,” said the Rocky Mountain News. General admission was 50 cents, with reserved seats available for an extra 25 cents.
“It is hoped that sufficient encouragement will be given Mr. Forrester to warrant him in running his new enterprise through a greater part of the winter,” the News continued. “It has long been known and asserted by theatrical managers that if there was an opera-house in this city, capable of seating enough people to make it a paying venture for troupes to visit here, they would come oftener and bring stronger companies.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Meanwhile, “the canvass” in Colorado’s 1876 election, as the newspapers called the month-long sprint of campaigning leading up to Oct. 3, reached a fever pitch, with candidates for statewide office appearing nightly for public addresses in cities across the state. Partisan newspaper editors urged voters to make sure they were registered before the deadline — Sept. 26, one week before Election Day.
“The Democrats are actively hunting up their men and the name of every one of them will be on the list,” warned the pro-Republican News. “There is an undoubted Republican majority in Denver. The one thing necessary is to bring it out, and the first step to secure that result is to register.”
Despite some earlier confusion, state and county officials clarified in mid-September that two different elections for Colorado’s at-large congressional seat would be held in the coming weeks. Democrat Thomas Patterson and Republican James Belford would face off in the Centennial State’s inaugural Oct. 3 election to fill the seat for the remaining months of the 44th Congress. Coloradans would then vote again on Nov. 7 to elect a member of Congress for the full two-year term set to begin in March 1877.
Before either election, however, Coloradans were scheduled to gather in Denver for their first-ever state fair — technically, the annual exposition of the Colorado Industrial Association, the forerunner of the event that would be incorporated in Pueblo in 1886. The News congratulated “our merchants and mechanics (for) taking such an interest in the Fair this season.”
“It is known that there are several who will make large displays of their goods,” the paper reported. “Dealers in agricultural implements will also take advantage of the occasion, to make an extensive exposition in their line to the most appreciative crowd that could possibly be brought together.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: How soybeans took over the American diet – without anyone noticing
description: U.S. farmers will produce a record-breaking harvest of 4.52 billion bushels of soybeans in 2026, according to projections from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. At 60 pounds to the bushel, that is roughly 800 pounds of soybeans for every American. Most people don’t think of themselves as soybean consumers. Few sit down to a plate […]
text:
A combine harvests soybeans in Phillips County, Arkansas, in this undated photo. (Photo by Robert Goodson/U of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture)
U.S. farmers will produce a record-breaking harvest of 4.52 billion bushels of soybeans in 2026, according to projections from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. At 60 pounds to the bushel, that is roughly 800 pounds of soybeans for every American.
Most people don’t think of themselves as soybean consumers. Few sit down to a plate of soybeans, but soy is hiding in plain sight throughout the American diet. Soybean oil appears in salad dressings, mayonnaise, baked goods, infant formula, snacks and fried foods; soy lecithin emulsifies chocolate and bread; and soy protein fortifies energy bars, breakfast cereals and canned soup.

As an environmental historian who studies agriculture and food, I seek to understand a peculiar transformation: How did a plant that most Americans barely ate a century ago become a ubiquitous food ingredient without people noticing?
A Chinese crop becomes a North American commodity

	
Chinese farmers domesticated the soybean (Glycine max) from its wild ancestor, Glycine soja, between 6,000 and 9,000 years ago. By the first millennium B.C.E., it ranked among the “five grains,” the staple crops recognized in early Chinese texts.
Soybeans came to North America much later. In 1764, an English sailor named Samuel Bowen arrived in Savannah, Georgia, with a handful of soybeans, a souvenir from several years spent in China. The following spring, Georgia’s surveyor-general Henry Yonge planted Bowen’s unfamiliar “Chinese vetches” and harvested three crops in a single season. In 1767, Bowen received a British patent for his method of producing soy sauce, a fermented condiment resembling the soy sauce already imported from Asia. The enterprise faded into obscurity after Bowen’s death, and soybeans remained little more than a curiosity in North America.
Tyler Stafslien shows off his soybeans at his Ryder, North Dakota farm on Nov. 14, 2025. (Photo: Gabrielle Nelson/Buffalo’s Fire)
That changed around 1900. U.S. Department of Agriculture plant explorer Frank Meyer collected dozens of soybean varieties in China, many of which government researchers Charles Piper and William Morse planted at the department’s Arlington Experimental Farm in Virginia. They compared imported varieties for such traits as maturity, yield, plant form and suitability for seed or hay, selecting strains that showed promise for cultivation in the United States. Piper and Morse then distributed promising varieties to agricultural experiment stations around the country, where researchers determined which ones performed best under local conditions.
At first, Americans mostly grew soybeans as forage and livestock feed. The emergence of industrial crushing in the 1910s transformed the crop. Initially, processors squeezed oil from the beans mechanically. Over the next few decades, they increasingly used chemicals to extract the oil, which efficiently separated the bean into two valuable commodities: protein-rich meal for livestock, and oil for a wide range of uses, including margarine, paint and soap.
Henry Ford’s vegetable interest

	
No industrialist embraced the soybean more enthusiastically than Henry Ford. In 1933, Fortune magazine marveled that Ford was “as much interested in the soya bean as he is in the V-8” engine.
Ford believed that industry and agriculture were “natural partners.” Farmers sought new markets for their crops, and auto factories needed raw materials. On 8,000 acres in Michigan, Ford’s researchers planted 300 soybean varieties and searched for ways to incorporate the harvest into automobiles.
They succeeded. Soybean oil went into Ford paints, and soybean meal into molded plastic parts. By 1935, Ford was using roughly a bushel of soybeans in the manufacture of every automobile. Six years later, he unveiled a lightweight “Soybean Car,” built from 14 soy-derived plastic panels attached to a tubular steel frame.
Ford, whose enthusiasm for agricultural experimentation coexisted with a virulent antisemitism that earned him honors from Germany’s Nazi government, also wanted Americans to eat his wonder crop.
His scientists investigated soy milk, soybean “cheese” and soy breads, with mixed results. One employee remembered the experimental soy biscuits as “the most vile-tasting things you ever put in your mouth.”
Soybeans being loaded from a grain bin onto a truck on June 13, 2018 in Dwight, Illinois.  (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Undeterred, Ford served 30 reporters a soybean luncheon at Chicago’s 1934 Century of Progress Exposition. The menu featured soybean purée, soybean cheese, soybean bread, soybean coffee and even apple pie baked in a soybean crust. The journalists were skeptical. One later recalled, “Nothing we newsmen ate that day led us to foresee that soybeans were destined a few years later to become an ingredient in many popular food products, some of them delicious.”
They could more readily imagine the bean becoming cattle feed or an industrial raw material – which is exactly how its use evolved, at first.
Soy disappears into the American diet

	
Ford’s soybean cuisine never conquered America’s kitchens. Something much more consequential happened. Soy became ubiquitous precisely by becoming invisible.
World War II accelerated the transformation. Cut off from imported fats and oils, U.S. processors turned to domestic vegetable oils, especially soybean oil. After the war, booming livestock production drove demand for protein-rich soybean meal. But crushing all those beans also produced a river of cheap oil. Processors needed markets for what was, in effect, the crop’s increasingly abundant second product.
Food manufacturers found them. Adding hydrogen turned soybean oil into solids such as shortening and margarine. The low cost, neutral flavor and abundance of soybean oil made it ideal for processed foods. Between 1942 and 1972, federal figures show the amount of American butter in the market fell from 16.4 to 5 pounds per person, while margarine rose from 2.9 to 11.1 pounds. Cheap soybean oil helped make this transition possible.
By 2008, soybean oil accounted for approximately 80% of the 18 billion pounds of edible oils Americans used annually. It appeared as cooking oil, frying fat, shortening, salad dressing, mayonnaise and an inconspicuous ingredient in packaged foods.
Americans never needed to fall in love with tofu to become ravenous consumers of soy.
From food to fuel

	
The latest soybean headlines bring the story full circle. Henry Ford dreamed of erasing the boundary between farm and factory. Ninety years later, something remarkably close to that vision has emerged.
Soybeans feed livestock and humans, but their oil also flows into an energy economy shaped by several decades of federal renewable-fuel mandates. A new federal rule finalized in March 2026 increased the amount of renewable fuel that refiners and importers must incorporate into the nation’s transportation-fuel supply. These mandates have helped draw growing quantities of domestic soybean oil toward biomass-based diesel production.
Soybeans in a Cass County, North Dakota, field on Sept. 10, 2025, turn color as harvest approaches. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
Soybean oil becomes biodiesel and aviation fuel, powering school buses and commercial airplanes.
Federal scientists helped transform soy into a viable American crop. Agricultural policies made it cheap and plentiful. Livestock producers created enormous demand for soybean meal. Wartime shortages favored domestic oils. Processors found new uses for the oil. Food manufacturers slipped it into an expanding range of products. Americans still made choices in supermarkets and restaurants, but the menu of cheap possibilities had been shaped long before they arrived.
Soy conquered America not because Americans craved the bean, but because it was remarkably versatile. Its protein could feed a chicken or a pig, its oil could fry French fries or propel a truck, and its lecithin could emulsify chocolate or mayonnaise. It could ship easily, too, with Chinese purchases of American soy becoming an element of the trade war between the Trump administration and China.
That flexibility put the soybean at the intersection of food, agriculture, industry, energy and geopolitics. Ninety years after Ford tried to persuade skeptical reporters to eat soybean pie, his obsession with the crop looks less eccentric than prophetic.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Lawmakers punt on data center concerns
description: For the moment, set aside the question of whether huge data centers are good or bad for North Dakota. For now, stay clear of the clutter of conflicting information about water usage, the effects on consumer electricity rates, the potential for sound pollution and health problems, and the prospect of gigantic buildings standing empty in […]
text:
Members of the North Dakota Senate participate in a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 4, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)For the moment, set aside the question of whether huge data centers are good or bad for North Dakota. For now, stay clear of the clutter of conflicting information about water usage, the effects on consumer electricity rates, the potential for sound pollution and health problems, and the prospect of gigantic buildings standing empty in a few years should the rapidly evolving technology for data storage change yet again.
Instead, focus on the failure of North Dakota legislators to seize an opportunity to pause the rush to build data centers, so that those very questions could be discussed, and possibly answered. Instead, realize that majority party lawmakers in a special session in early September not only further opened the door to this unregulated and extraordinarily powerful industry, but also betrayed the public’s trust by refusing to pass a ban on nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) between billion-dollar, out-of-state companies and local elected officials.
It should be stressed again and again that questioning the potential effects of data centers is not anti-data center. Rather, it is reasonable to demand pertinent, honest information from the powerful and wealthy corporations that want to do business in the state. After all, some of these companies make the oil industry look like the corner store.
Data center nondisclosure bill dies in North Dakota Senate vote

It might be too late. The horse is out of the barn. It’s water over the dam. That ship has sailed. When the Legislature meets in regular session in January, it will be a day late and a dollar short. Pick your idiom. They all ring true.
Majority lawmakers said they will pick up the dropped ball in the 2027 session. The effect of their legislative nonfeasance will be to have given the data center companies a full four months to continue and even accelerate the building of the gigantic complexes throughout the state. They are quite capable of precisely that, given the speed at which the sprawling buildings have been constructed in Ellendale and Harwood. Rapid planning and development is underway for at least two more massive installations.
The special session’s failure to redefine the limits of nondisclosure agreements between the industry and elected local leaders is especially troubling. Fargo Democratic Sen. Tim Mathern couldn’t muster support for his reasonable proposal during the brief Senate floor debate. Other legislators seem to have bought into the nonsense that any business development is good. They argued that the state’s open meetings and open records laws, and freedom of information tools, are sufficient to let the public know what is going on, despite the NDAs. Not so.
It is not possible to use those methods to inform the public when the NDAs and meetings between the companies and individual public officials are not revealed. The press and public can’t possibly demand information when they don’t know what to ask for because the deals have been signed and sealed at secret meetings. Furthermore, an unannounced one-on-one sit-down between a mayor and a company executive does not constitute a public meeting under the law. It’s a cunning way to circumvent the law.  
Violations of the state’s sunshine laws happen all the time. But when a township fails to announce a meeting where supervisors buy a few loads of gravel, it’s not a major matter. The data center stratagem, however, has successfully blacked out the transparency that is fundamental to local government. The data center phenomenon is a very big deal, and it has happened without required public participation. The backlash is accelerating, and it’s aimed not only at the companies, but also at the tone-deaf Legislature.
Are data centers good for North Dakota? They might very well be. Bad? Maybe. But if the impact is bad, North Dakotans might not know until it is too late. The blame for that circumstance will rest with majority lawmakers who failed to apply the brakes, and with local elected officials who signed NDAs.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Tierra Walker died after she couldn’t get an abortion. Her family is suing Ken Paxton.
description: This story was originally reported by Shefali Luthra of The 19th. Meet Shefali and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. The family of a woman who died after she could not get an abortion in Texas is suing doctors and state officials including Attorney General Ken Paxton. It is the first […]
text:
(Stock photo via Getty Images)
This story was originally reported by Shefali Luthra of The 19th.  Meet Shefali and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
The family of a woman who died after she could not get an abortion in Texas is suing doctors and state officials including Attorney General Ken Paxton. It is the first lawsuit over a death linked to an abortion ban.
“It’s horrible that she’s gone and she was taken from us this way. It’s horrible that she’s not here anymore,” said LaTanya Walker, Tierra Walker’s aunt and the lead plaintiff in the case, in a press conference Wednesday. She added: “I want justice for her. I want it to not happen to anyone else. It needs to stop.”
The case, filed Tuesday in state court by a malpractice firm and the abortion rights group Amplify Legal, argues that Texas’ abortion bans violate both the state and U.S. Constitution. This case is also the first to directly sue Paxton, who has taken a leading role in enforcing Texas’ ban. Paxton is locked in a tight race for the U.S. Senate.
“Tierra Walker is dead and those responsible must be held accountable,” the suit reads. “At every turn, Texas’s political and medical establishments not only failed but actively harmed Ms. Walker.”
Walker is one of the numerous women whose deaths have been linked to abortion bans. Other deaths have occurred in North Carolina and Georgia, states with bans less restrictive than Texas’. Texas’ near-total abortion ban provides exceptions only if staying pregnant puts someone “at risk of death or poses a serious risk of substantial impairment of a major bodily function.” In 2025 — after Walker’s death — the state passed a law meant to clarify what constitutes a risk of death. But the penalties for violating the state’s ban remain onerous, and many doctors have said it is not obvious what care they can provide or how sick a patient must be before they can intervene.
Walker, whose case was first reported on last year by ProPublica, died December 30, 2024, when she was 37 years old and 20 weeks into her pregnancy. Her medical history of chronic conditions — including diabetes, hypertension, obesity and severe asthma — made her pregnancy particularly high-risk. She was hospitalized multiple times during her pregnancy and repeatedly asked for an abortion. According to the lawsuit, doctors did not give her information on how she could get an abortion, instead dismissing her after telling her “your baby is fine.”
“They just kept saying, ‘It’s not the baby, the baby’s fine,’” LaTanya Walker said.
Walker died days after being discharged from the University of Texas Science Center at San Antonio, also known as the University Health System, according to the lawsuit. Her son discovered her dead on his 15th birthday.
After Walker’s death, a medical examiner ruled that she died of hypertensive cardiovascular disease with preeclampsia, the latter of which is a dangerous pregnancy-related high blood pressure condition that doctors had identified in Walker.
Some Texans have been able to get abortions by leaving the state or ordering abortion medication online. Walker’s illness — which included seizures and frequent hospitalizations — prevented her from traveling out of state, said Molly Duane, one of the family’s attorneys. LaTanya Walker considered ordering abortion pills for her niece, she said, but she ultimately did not because she worried about whether they could exacerbate medical conditions.
“That’s the problem. You should be able to get healthcare from your doctor,” Duane said.
Medical records cited in the suit note that on her last hospital visit, her blood pressure was dangerously high and only temporarily responsive to medication. According to those records, the doctor caring for her at that point, who is a named defendant in the suit, wrote that “delivering the baby” — which would terminate the pregnancy — ”may be the best treatment for preeclampsia.”
Doctors who reviewed the case for ProPublica all told the news outlet that, given Walker’s medical risks, she should have been offered an abortion.
The suit names Paxton and Stephen Brint Carlton, the executive director of the Texas Medical Board, in their official and individual capacities, as well as Bexar County District Attorney Joe Gonzales in his official capacity. It also names the University of Texas Science Center at San Antonio and three of the doctors who cared for Walker.
The 19th reached out to Paxton’s office and Senate campaign, Carlton, the University Health System and the Bexar County District Attorney’s Office for comment, but received no immediate reply.
Paxton has been a staunch defendant of Texas’ abortion ban. In another case, he threatened legal action against anyone who gave an abortion to one woman — despite a court saying she qualified for an exception to the state’s ban. He has also sought to dismiss a case brought by women who had been denied abortions in medical emergencies, and who were pushing for greater clarity over when someone could receive an abortion in Texas.
The plaintiffs, Walker’s family, are seeking a jury trial and pursuing both damages and a judgement finding that Texas’ abortion laws violate the state constitution.

title: Alabama withdraws objections to federal marijuana rescheduling
description: Alabama’s public health officials on Thursday withdrew their objection to the federal rescheduling of marijuana, a move officials characterized as procedural, following a July public hearing.  The governing body of the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) in May voted to delay the rescheduling so that officials could have more time to determine how to[...]
text:
Mock medical cannabis lozenges in a display case at Callie's Apothecary in Montgomery, Alabama, on May 14, 2026. The governing body of the Alabama Department of Public Health on Thursday voted unanimously to withdraw its objection to the rescheduling of marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III after a procedural public hearing. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s public health officials on Thursday withdrew their objection to the federal rescheduling of marijuana, a move officials characterized as procedural, following a July public hearing. 
The governing body of the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH) in May voted to delay the rescheduling so that officials could have more time to determine how to implement it, but noted that they “fully intended” to reschedule the drug.
State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris said Thursday morning that he did not see any issues with the change, and the public comments did not reflect the impact of rescheduling but rather marijuana itself.
