name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: How did China get wrapped up in the competitive race for Wisconsin’s 17th state Senate District?
description: Both the Democratic and Republican leaders of the Wisconsin Senate have said of their efforts to win control of the chamber that their candidates are staying focused on issues close to home. However, this week the focus of the race for the 17th Senate District turned to a country 6,000 miles away: China. The race […]
text:
Rep. Jenna Jacobson ran a campaign ad claiming Sen. Howard Marklein "invested thousands of dollars in Chinese corporations."   (Photo of Jacobson courtesy of campaign. Photo of Marklein by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner) Both the Democratic and Republican leaders of the Wisconsin Senate have said of their efforts to win control of the chamber that their candidates are staying focused on issues close to home. However, this week the focus of the race for the 17th Senate District turned to a country 6,000 miles away: China.
The race in Wisconsin’s 17th Senate District, a key district that will help determine control of the body, pits Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green), the incumbent in the race, against Rep. Jenna Jacobson (D-Oregon), a two-term state representative. Marklein was first elected to the seat in 2014 after serving two terms in the Assembly and has served for the last two sessions as the co-chair of the powerful Joint Finance Committee, which drafts the state budget.
The subject of China entered the race when the Jacobson campaign began running an ad last week that claimed Marklein had “invested thousands of dollars in Chinese corporations” while voting against a “measure that would have made Wisconsin buy more American made products.” The ad displays an image of Marklein’s face beside the Chinese flag. 
“While Marklein was making money off of his Chinese investments, he was stealing money from American workers like me,” a man dressed as a construction worker says in the ad. “Someone who sold us out like that should never be in the state Senate.” 
The ad led to Sen. Patrick Testin (R-Stevens Point), head of the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate, to call a press conference to defend Marklein Tuesday. Testin called the ad “deceptive” and a “sick smear campaign.”
Barry Burden, director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison Elections Research Center, told the Wisconsin Examiner in an email that it’s “quite unusual for China or another other foreign country to be much of an issue in a campaign for a state legislative seat.” 
Burden said the “focus on China in the 17th district is a kind of proxy for other issues,” including concerns about politicians “enriching themselves unethically because of investments” as well as worries about the construction of new data centers that some Wisconsinites see as drain on resources and harmful to the environment in addition to being related to U.S. AI developers’ competition with China. 
The ad, however, is seeking to tie some of Marklein’s prior reported investments to his lack of support for a Democratic bill in 2013 that would have required state and local contracts to give preference to materials manufactured in the United States.
Wisconsin public officials and candidates are required to file a Statement of Economic Interests under state law to disclose financial relationships and prevent conflicts of interest. 
According to his 2022 statement of economic interest, Marklein had over $50,000 in a WisdomTree Emerging Markets Fund as well as between $5,000 and $50,000 in investments in the JPMorgan Emerging Markets Fund. According to Sofi, investing in emerging market funds means owning shares in companies from India, Brazil, South Africa and China with the latter representing a large portion of many emerging market index funds.
Marklein’s most recent statement of economic interest included no emerging market funds.
In his press conference defending Marklein, Testin appeared to think the ad was related to investments made through the Wisconsin Retirement System, saying Jacobson, and every state employee, has similar investments. (The Wisconsin Retirement System is not prohibited from making investments in businesses in China, though Republicans have proposed barring the State of Wisconsin Investment Board from doing so in the past.)
Testin said Jacobson was “trying to be tough on foreign adversaries now that it might be politically beneficial for her.” 
“The truth is that Jacobson could have spent months standing up to our nation’s adversaries like China, but when she had the opportunity to support meaningful legislation that would protect Wisconsin from foreign influence, she voted no,” Testin said, referring to bills that would have restricted business with China. 
Testin proposed and Marklein co-authored a bill that would have barred Wisconsin agencies from contracting with certain foreign businesses, including China. Two other bills would have prohibited China from buying Wisconsin land and prohibited the University of Wisconsin system from providing study abroad and research there.
“Jacobson has no backbone, only a slick eye for political gain. She’s quick to point a finger at people like Sen. Marklein when it benefits her, but when she has the chance to help Wisconsin, she’s only interested when there could be gains for her,” Testin said. 
Jacobson voted against the two bills that passed the Assembly. Both were vetoed by Gov. Tony Evers. The issue has also come up in the race for governor, with Republican candidate Tom Tiffany saying he would have signed at least one of those bills as governor.
Burden said connecting politicians to China could “tarnish” their reputations. According to a Nov. 2025 Marquette Law School Poll, 65% of Americans held an unfavorable view of China and its leader, President Xi Jinping, while 19% said they had a favorable view of China. 
Burden said of Jacobson’s ad that “a connection to Marklein’s potential support for Chinese businesses and government is a way for her to point out to voters without a strong partisan preference why he should be defeated.”
Will Karcz, a spokesperson for the state Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, said in a statement to the Examiner that the ad was meant to provide voters in the 17th with “the truth of Howard Marklein’s personal foreign investment history.”
“Howard has repeatedly voted against protecting Wisconsin manufacturing while cashing in on tens of thousands of dollars he invested in Chinese-owned corporations,” Karcz said. “He got rich on the backs of Wisconsin workers. Jenna Jacobson is running to make Wisconsin stronger while Howard has spent the last 10 years putting his bottom line ahead of his constituents.” 
Whether the message resonates with voters is unclear. 
Todd Allbaugh, a former Republican who grew up in Richland Center and formerly worked for Sen. Dale Schulz, told the Examiner in an interview that he was confused when he saw the ad about a week ago. He lives in Madison, but still has family in the district. 
“I’ve seen this ad now probably somewhere around 20-ish times. It was baffling,” Allbaugh said. He said he didn’t understand what it was trying to get at until he looked it up using Claude, the AI assistant developed by Anthropic. “If you have to go to Claude to figure it out, it probably isn’t a really effective ad.”
Allbaugh acknowledged that Marklein has some advantages in the race given his status as an incumbent. Marklein won his 2022 race with 60% of the vote, though the district has changed considerably under the new maps. It now represents Iowa, Lafayette, Green, Crawford and Grant counties as well as parts of Dane County. 
“I know the 17th Senate District pretty much like the back of my hand because it’s home,” Allbaugh said. “With the newly drawn maps it’s certainly become more competitive for Democrats, probably the most competitive in a very long time.” 
Allbaugh said that he thinks Marklein is “scared for his political life,” as he is suddenly running in a competitive district and that can be seen in his campaign. One of Marklein’s recent ads positioned him as a bipartisan “bridge builder” and as “your man in the middle” and highlighted tax cuts that have been made while he’s been in office as well as some investments that have been made into local EMS and into the Lone Rock Bridge, which opened this year after two years of construction. 
In Allbaugh’s opinion, Jacobson’s campaign should focus on local issues that Marklein has had some say over. He noted the closure of the UW-Platteville Richland Center campus and the UW-Platteville Baraboo Sauk County campus that have happened while Marklein has chaired the Joint Finance Committee as well as the struggle that public schools in the district have had. 
“I think she’s a super strong candidate. She’s affable. She is enormously more likable and connects to people better than Howard Marklein, and I would if I were advising them, which I’m not, I would lean into that,” Allbaugh said. “Be authentic instead of listening to consultants with boilerplate things that they’re using in the other races. It doesn’t seem like a smart use of money when there are so many more easily understood issues that are particular to the 17th Senate District.”
Jacobson’s economic statement of interest from 2022 and 2024 does not list any emerging market funds.
Her 2024 statement lists an investment in the American Funds The New Economy Fund. According to the Capital Group website, it is mainly invested in the U.S. though it has a mix of investments abroad. About 15% of the fund is in Asia, including China.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: In another new age of college admissions, high school seniors call the shots, more than ever
description: When my son and his friend, another Kansas teen, visited Trinity University this April in San Antonio, they got a preview of today’s shifting, psychedelic world of college admissions. Along with dozens of other parents and high school students, we sat in an auditorium to hear an admissions rep talk about standard stuff: campus life, […]
text:
The admission process for selective colleges has changed as fewer students apply in a post-pandemic world. (Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)When my son and his friend, another Kansas teen, visited Trinity University this April in San Antonio, they got a preview of today’s shifting, psychedelic world of college admissions.
Along with dozens of other parents and high school students, we sat in an auditorium to hear an admissions rep talk about standard stuff: campus life, academics and meal plans. Everyone sat up a bit straighter and listened a bit more intently when it came time to hear the admissions requirements.
The school’s admission standards snagged our attention because Trinity, a small, liberal-arts college, only admits 25% of applicants. Like generations of American students before him, my soon-to-be college son wondered: “What would it take to get in?”
Within the borders of Kansas, there are few, if any, schools that college counselors would label as selective in the same way as Trinity. Most, including the six major state universities, post clear admissions requirements allowing students to know whether they will be admitted before applying.
The mystery remains for Kansas students looking outside the state at more selective schools.
To find the answers in 2026, high school seniors schedule time with their college counselors, study scatterplots on college admission websites and scroll social media. Each post, graph or expert claims to know the alchemic recipe required to earn a spot in next year’s freshman class at selective universities. This GPA. This kind of essay. These test scores.
The high school graduating class of 2027 enters a unique admissions landscape. Selective universities are wriggling in their seats, shifting their posture on standardized tests and student writing samples at a time when the number of potential college students is falling.
As an instructor at the University of Kansas, I knew all of this as we sat in the auditorium in San Antonio. I knew that declining American birth rates during the late 2000s financial crisis have resulted in fewer potential college freshmen next fall. I knew that some colleges would be poised to offer better incentives to attract students. And I knew that artificial intelligence has roiled higher education — admissions included.
Standing at the lectern, the admissions rep told the students that Trinity is test-optional. That, on its own, is pretty standard. Along with other schools, test-optional admissions allows students to choose whether to submit standardized test scores — ACT and SAT — with their application. Maybe the score would help my son’s application. Perhaps it would ding his chances. It’s often difficult to discern from one school to the next.
As the admissions rep pointed to the PowerPoint slide, full of ACT scores and average GPAs, things got trippy. 
“If you are unsure about test-optional, about whether or not to submit your scores,” the rep said, “just call us or email us to tell us your test scores. We will get back to you, letting you know whether you should include them in your application. Whether it’s in your best interest.” 
I looked around to see if anyone else registered the bizarro logic.
Why would an admissions department receive information about a student and then pretend to forget that same information when making the decision about admitting that very same student?
Or, perhaps more confusing, why is a score really useful in evaluating a student, but if that same metric is a few points lower, the score is irrelevant?
No wonder parents and students feel bewildered by applications, rejections, deferrals and admissions to selective schools.
The usefulness of standardized testing for college admissions departments seems to have swung back and forth — from vital to misleading — during the last few decades. Concerns about racial and income disparities first led schools to de-emphasize the scores. Then, the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown made ACT and SAT testing impossible because of lockdown provisions.
In reaction, the number of students taking the ACT, the most popular college admissions test in Kansas, fell each year from 2016 to 2021 before leveling out in 2022 and 2023, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. By 2023, nationwide participation on the ACT had fallen 21 percentage points over seven years to 37%. 
Similarly, the national average composite score on the test fell every year between 2017 and 2023. 
For their part, Kansas students did not excel in 2024, the most recent year for which scores are available. During that year, 72% of the state’s high school graduates took the ACT, earning an average 19.3 composite score. That ranks 35th nationally among the states, plus the District of Columbia.
In many states, 100% of high school seniors take the ACT. That makes it especially concerning that the 2024 ACT scores in Kansas approached the bottom, while omitting 28% of students (likely students who would have pulled scores down even more). 
In this way, schools that are test optional give students exactly what they want: an admissions process that shrugs at testing. No need to spend this Saturday morning — a national ACT testing day — bubbling in answers on a standardized test.
Clearly standardized tests reveal bias in our society. Our family was able to pay an excellent math tutor to help my fortunate son with his preparation. He felt a bit less fortunate to have me, his lame dad, helping him with the English portion. The American education system, whether student-to-teacher ratio or ACT prep, ruthlessly separates students by class.
Even with privilege baked in, count me as confused about test-optional policies. If having the data (in this case, test scores) is helpful for one student, why not every student?
Testing data also feels more valuable at an educational moment when other reliable information seems elusive.
High school transcripts have become less and less useful as grade inflation continues. A few years ago, a friend who teaches in a Kansas City area school told me that the 50th percentile of students at that school averaged an A- across their transcripts. If most students earn A+ after A+ after A+, how useful can that information be?
You might assume this climate of grade inflation and optional testing would point admissions departments toward emphasis on college essays. However, this year many selective schools eliminated “supplemental” writing from their applications. These extra questions — in addition to the standard college essay about your personal strengths and weaknesses — had also become less useful. 
Admissions reps explained to the New York Times that many students likely use artificial intelligence on such questions in a way that pollutes student writing samples. If students cannot be supervised writing, we suspect that it isn’t them writing at all.
For the class of 2027 and beyond, authentic writing is surveilled writing.
Most Kansas universities, including the six major state universities, don’t require any writing samples. They also remain test-optional, asking that students clear either a high school GPA threshold or a minimum test score on the ACT or SAT. These policies have been in place for years. 
The collective effect of so many other admissions decisions shifting at once gives students more leverage. They don’t want to take tests. If they do, they might not want to report their scores. They earn straight A’s. They can’t be trusted to write themselves.
Meanwhile, they are increasingly precious to student-starved universities.
We have arrived — yet again — in a new age of college admissions.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Review of $71 million AES Indiana rate hike to stretch into 2027
description: The rest of the increase is scheduled to take effect in January, despite the pending case.
text:
AES Indiana's downtown Indianapolis headquarters are pictured Sept. 15, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The parties to a $71 million rate increase for AES Indiana gathered Thursday for the first meeting in a controversial reconsideration and rehearing that is scheduled to stretch into the springtime.
The utility serves more than 500,000 customers in the Indianapolis metropolitan area.
Attorneys for AES Indiana, the Indiana Office of Consumer Counselor, ratepayer advocacy group Citizens Action Coalition, the city of Indianapolis and several industrial customers agreed to a procedural schedule that includes a one-day hearing in early March.
State utility regulators approved the increase in June, on a vote of 3-1. Gov. Mike Braun denounced the move and directed Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray to file for review.
Fired regulator Andy Zay has said the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission was poised to deny the request until he was dismissed and another commissioner resigned. The reconstituted IURC voted to reconsider the case earlier this month, in a 3-1 tally.
The $71 million increase will hit customers in two phases, despite the pending dispute.
The first phase — worth less than $1 monthly for an average household using 1,000 kilowatt hours of electricity per month — took effect July 27, according to IURC spokesman Ben Gavelek.
The second phase is scheduled to hit in January. It’s worth an estimated $8.50 monthly for the average household, per AES Indiana.
“Rates go into effect, even with an appeal pending, unless a request to stay the rates is made to the appellate court, and (are) subject to refund if the court eventually determines to overturn the Commission’s order,” Gavelek wrote. “The OUCC did not request that the rate increase be stayed pending their request for reconsideration and their notice of appeal.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio now has over 125 active moratoriums on data centers. See where they are.
description: At least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships have active moratoriums on data centers as of Sept. 17, local government records and news reports show. Meanwhile, 23 communities have effectively banned data centers, with at least 23 more across seven counties considering similar proposals. Many villages and small townships do not publish ordinances or meeting[...]
text:
Construction of a data center. (File photo from Getty Images.) 
At least 138 Ohio municipalities and townships have active moratoriums on data centers as of Sept. 17, local government records and news reports show.
Meanwhile, 23 communities have effectively banned data centers, with at least 23 more across seven counties considering similar proposals. Many villages and small townships do not publish ordinances or meeting minutes online, making the true count likely even higher as more developments happen every day.
A moratorium is a temporary pause, usually on new construction in the case of data centers. While a permanent ban can require a lengthy zoning process only available to some communities, any municipality or township can pass a moratorium.
A Bowling Green State University poll released Wednesday found that 78% of Ohioans support data center moratoriums until more information can be gathered about their effects. Seventy-five percent oppose construction in their local communities, and 63% are against construction elsewhere in Ohio.
Berea Mayor Cyril Kleem said his city’s one-year moratorium didn’t mean the local government was in favor of data centers or against them.
“We get so much information, particularly through social media. I don’t know if it’s always accurate, so we just wanted to take our time to look at it,” he said.


The data center industry responds
A lobbying group that represents major data center companies funded ads touting the benefits of data centers in seven states, including Ohio. Five of the state’s biggest data center developers announced donations to a program that helps Ohioans cover their utility bills in late August.
Pro-data center industry group behind ad campaign in Ohio, Oregon, five other states

The push comes as data centers have become politically toxic ahead of the November midterms. While only 9% of Ohioans in the BGSU poll listed data centers as the most important political issue for them, 47% said a candidate’s stance on data centers is very or extremely important to their vote in November.
A leaked memo from Republicans’ main campaign committee first reported by Axios warned that data centers could be the deciding factor against Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted if developers don’t explain “who benefits, who pays, and why a community should want one.”
Capital University finance and economics professor Saurav Roychoudhury studies the economic impact of data centers on Ohio communities. Developers used to prioritize sites that were close to power and water sources, and tax incentives encouraged big names to choose Ohio, he said.
“Because there are these hyperscalers coming in, it puts Ohio onto the map,” he said. “If Amazon, Meta, and Google are all operating in Ohio … it’s a good place to do business.”
Now, Ohio’s state tax incentives for data centers are on hiatus, and politicians on both sides of the aisle are pushing to make that permanent. Many newer data centers also use water more efficiently, he added.
A new priority second to power generation has emerged: what Roychoudhury called “de-risked land.” Those are sites where developers are less likely to face community opposition or zoning issues, he said, as they try to get data centers online as soon as possible.
“Speed to market is essential,” he said. “If you are having moratoriums for six months or up to a year, and then you decide what will happen, some of these developers will just look somewhere else where it’s a little bit more friendly.”
Some developers dropped plans to build data centers after local communities proposed moratoriums, and others have persevered. Urbana, Lordstown, and Commercial Point are facing lawsuits from developers who claim that local officials collaborated on plans for potential sites before changing course and passing moratoriums.
What can communities do during a moratorium?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Moratoriums can be good for development if communities use the time to set clear rules and build public trust, Roychoudhury added. Massillon lifted its moratorium early after passing new zoning regulations for data centers.
State and federal lawmakers have floated several ideas to rein in data centers, and candidates in Ohio’s governor and U.S. Senate races outlined plans to regulate them if elected.
So far, little has been passed into law. At the federal level, environmental regulations for data centers and the plants that power them are getting rolled back. An amendment to the state’s 2025 budget bill that received little attention when it first passed is now a roadblock against community referendums on zoning for “any property involved in a megaproject.”
Still, local governments have full control over approving data center buildings, said Michael McGovern, the president of progressive policy organization Innovation Ohio.
Findlay, which is under a moratorium until April, is considering what the director of the Hancock Regional Planning Commission called the most complex ordinance he has ever written. In addition to setbacks and noise limits, which are fairly common in data center zoning regulations, the proposal would require third-party technical reports at the developer’s expense and a case-by-case cap on electrical demand.
Communities can also require workers to be hired from the local area, McGovern said, and demand proof of a contract signed by a developer and utility company that makes the developer pay for any new electrical infrastructure.
Developers could also do more to increase transparency, Roychoudhury added. They could create data dashboards where residents can monitor data centers’ energy efficiency and provide notice before turning on emergency generators, he said.
He emphasized that data center developers have to be committed to building long-term relationships in order to gain acceptance from local communities. Otherwise, he said a lack of information and a breakdown in public trust are driving the rise in moratoriums.
“If more of those moratoriums turn into outright bans, you’ll see many of the developers will move out of Ohio,” Roychoudhury said.
Will moratoriums become permanent bans?

Voters in four Ohio cities with active moratoriums will decide whether to ban data centers permanently this November.
Sunbury resident Trey Dockendorf said he helped gather signatures for a local ban on data centers that draw over 25 megawatts of power per month, even though the city is under a moratorium until January.
Amazon Web Services announced plans to build a data center in Sunbury in November 2024. The city commissioned two independent consultants to help develop zoning and land use regulations for data centers, but Dockendorf said he worried any regulations would be ineffective.
“A tiny municipality like Sunbury might not be able to afford the logistical and equipment costs to measure certain kinds of sound waves or pollution,” he said. “We didn’t feel like there was a way to regulate it correctly.”
Townships in multiple counties are coordinating with regional planning commissions to create uniform data center regulations, and in many cases, ban them. These are usually passed as amendments to local zoning resolutions, which require a monthslong process that includes a public hearing.
Zoning across Ohio’s townships vary widely, and many in southern and eastern Ohio don’t have zoning resolutions at all. For some, zoning is governed at the county level; Butler County passed a six-month moratorium for six of its 13 townships, and Fayette County is considering a one-year moratorium for eight of its 10 townships.
Data centers are getting banned en masse in nearby Logan, Union, and Champaign counties, where nearly all townships control their own zoning. The Logan-Union-Champaign Regional Planning Commission, which provides feedback to townships that want to change their zoning codes, reviewed 28 nearly identical data center bans from April to September.
There are 43 townships across the three counties combined. The proposals would define data centers in the zoning code without specifying a use, effectively prohibiting them.
In Knox County to the east, at least four townships have proposed some kind of ban, whether by designating anything left out of a zoning resolution as prohibited or an explicit ban against data centers.

Marta Hill represents Liberty Township at the Knox County Regional Planning Commission and said township officials heard many concerns from residents about data centers. The county borders Licking and Delaware counties, both of which have data centers in development.
The township passed a resolution explicitly prohibiting data centers Sept. 3 because township officials wanted it to be clear that they weren’t welcome, Hill said.
“Until there are regulations, why would we want to permit something in here that’s not regulated?” she said.
Union County’s Jerome Township was one of the first in the state to pass a data center moratorium in September 2025, but today, it’s one of six townships in the county that has not proposed a ban. Its moratorium expired in June, and data centers are now in development under new land use restrictions passed in March.
A September 2025 report that Roychoudhury conducted for the Ohio Chamber of Commerce opened by stating that data centers have brought around $40 billion of investment to the state. Over 125 moratoriums and around a dozen bans later, that level of investment has proven to be an underestimate, he said.
“I think (data center development) is still possible in Ohio,” Roychoudhury said. “It’s growing despite the pushback.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: The real cost of Tom Tiffany’s debate dodge
description: U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, is skipping multiple debates with his Democratic rival, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley.  Asked why he decided to break the Wisconsin Broadcasters Association’s 36-year streak of hosting gubernatorial candidate debates, Tiffany said, “We agreed to do one debate. In my experie[...]
text:
One debate cancellation after another leaves little opportunity to compare the candidates' positions on real issues that affect Wisconsinites. (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor of Wisconsin, is skipping multiple debates with his Democratic rival, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. 
Asked why he decided to break the Wisconsin Broadcasters Association’s 36-year streak of hosting gubernatorial candidate debates, Tiffany said, “We agreed to do one debate. In my experience in Congress as well as the state Legislature, doing one debate is sufficient.”
That’s absurd. In this high-stakes election, as Wisconsinites confront skyrocketing costs, healthcare cuts, struggling public schools, questions about election integrity, the threats posed by artificial intelligence and data centers, among many other issues, a single one-hour forum hosted by WISN on Oct. 21 cannot possibly cover their concerns in depth.
Another planned debate, hosted by the Milwaukee County Intergovernmental Cooperation Council, featuring questions gathered from mayors and community leaders around the state, was also called off this week after Tiffany indicated he would not participate.

The jilted hosts expressed their dismay in a joint statement, saying they are “deeply disappointed” and hope that the next governor will take seriously the local government issues the candidates will not be discussing on the debate stage Oct. 8.
The loss of these debates means Wisconsinites won’t have the opportunity to get answers to real people’s questions. Instead, they’ll have to settle for scripted talking points and millions of dollars in depressing negative ads.
The moderator of the Wisconsin Broadcasters Association debate, journalism professor Jill Geisler, has for years helped gather questions that are important to voters in different parts of the state. “We had someone who came from a community that had been using bottled water because of PFAS … we had someone asking about climate change’s effect on the wild rice harvest in Wisconsin,” she says, recalling some recent debate questions.
“I do think that we’re living in a more siloed era where people prefer to speak through the channels that they know are friendliest to them,” says Geisler, a professor at Loyola University Chicago. “I think what I worry about is that people think of truly well researched debates, you know, where people are asking researched questions, evidence-based questions, that that’s some kind of gotcha trap, and it’s not, you know, it is simply not that.”
The WBA team had already been hard at work planning the debate logistics and gathering issues important to local communities across the state when the debate was canceled. Before every debate, a point person does copious research on each topic, its history, legal background and the candidates’ positions and voting records. “Then we lock up for the last two days to workshop the questions,” Geisler says. After the debate, WBA publishes its questions online with links so people can read more about the issues. “We put all that out there because we think that we can’t cover it all in an hour,” Geisler says. “And people might want to do their own research, but they could see what we used.”
The broadcasters and the local government officials who were painstakingly putting together questions were planning to ask the candidates not just what they have to say about hot-button issues, but what specifically each would do as governor to address SNAP cuts, rural hospital closures, the childcare shortage and other urgent matters confronting Wisconsinites.
All of this serious, in-depth discussion has now been lost.
As President Donald Trump’s approval numbers crash and once-safe Republican congressional districts appear to be in play, Tiffany might want to avoid tough questions about his record of supporting Trump between 93% and 100% of the time while in Congress.
He seems to be leaning on an ad campaign to recast himself from MAGA warrior to folksy midwestern moderate, while relying on his supporters to attack his opponent. 
“In Wisconsin and other states, it is more often Republicans than Democrats who avoid debates,” says University of Wisconsin-Madison political science professor Barry Burden. “There are sometimes exceptions, as when Mandela Barnes resisted doing more than one debate with Ron Johnson in the 2022 Senate race, but it tends to be GOP candidates who are distrustful of journalists or being they have something to lose by taking part.” 
“The irony is that candidates who lost probably could have helped themselves with additional debates,” Burden adds. “Barnes’ narrow loss to Johnson might have been turned into a victory had there been another debate or two. Tiffany is currently trailing in the polls and might also benefit from more face time and opportunities to question his opponent.”
While Crowley is slightly ahead in the latest polls, Tiffany is outspending his Democratic rival on advertising by a margin of  3-to-1, according to J.R. Ross of WisPolitics. Republicans and the outside groups that support them are outspending Democrats by more than $8 million. 
Even that huge financial advantage might not be enough to help Tiffany overcome his record of voting for and defending Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, his support for the U.S. military entanglement in Iran and all the other Trump policies dragging down Republican politicians across the U.S.  
It will be interesting, in the single candidate debate next month, if the candidates are pressed to talk about data centers and Flock cameras — two issues where Tiffany has, interestingly, moved to capture some of the energy that animated supporters of Francesca Hong, the democratic socialist candidate Crowley narrowly defeated at the end of the chaotic Democratic primary. Crowley has not taken as strong a stance as Hong opposing either AI data centers or Flock surveillance. Tiffany’s position sounds more assertive, but his record is complicated, since he voted for Trump’s ban on AI regulation in Congress and seems more concerned with blocking wind and solar development that might fuel data centers than the data centers themselves. On Flock, it would be interesting to hear him square his support for local law enforcement with his proposal that local government be forbidden from using state revenue for Flock contracts. 
None of those nuances are going to get much airtime. Instead we will have the barrage of political advertising by shady groups, featuring grainy images and ominous music, shedding more darkness than light. 
“To have something that isn’t about sloganeering … to try to have civil discourse … I think that’s what we’ll have less of,” says Geisler.
For most of us that’s a big loss.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bookman: Is Jackson’s plan just another attempt to kick the Medicaid expansion can down the road?
description: Georgians strongly support Medicaid expansion to provide health insurance to their lower-income neighbors, and they have done so for years.  Yet somehow, their clear policy preference has not yet been translated into action. The state remains one of only 10 that have not accepted the federal government’s offer to expand coverage. How do we know […]
text:
Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderGeorgians strongly support Medicaid expansion to provide health insurance to their lower-income neighbors, and they have done so for years. 
Yet somehow, their clear policy preference has not yet been translated into action. The state remains one of only 10 that have not accepted the federal government’s offer to expand coverage.
How do we know that public support for expansion is real?
Well, repeated polls have shown that between 70-75% of voters support extending coverage to hundreds of thousands of Georgians – most of them working people – who are currently uninsured. (Expansion would also draw billions of additional federal dollars to the state, strengthening our healthcare system and bolstering rural areas where doctors and hospitals are struggling to stay afloat.)
We also know Medicaid expansion is popular because for several years now, Republicans have offered lip service to some form of expansion, but without actually ever delivering it. Judging by their rhetoric, their internal polls deliver much the same message as public polls: Georgians believe access to healthcare is a right and see government as a legitimate, necessary means of providing it. 
But it never happens. The taboo against “Obamacare” remains too strong.
Consider Gov. Brian Kemp’s Georgia Pathways to Coverage program, which he touted as a conservative alternative to Medicaid expansion that would be so effective that it would serve as a national model for other red states. 
But if Pathways had been an actual healthcare proposal, you would have to consider it an expensive failure. Almost seven years after Kemp announced it, and three years after he signed it into effect, Georgia still has the second highest uninsured rate in the country, behind only Texas. (Not coincidentally, Georgia also has the fifth highest level of unpaid medical debt, which is a burden on patients and providers both.)
The Pathways program has been so ineffective – in part because of what appears to be purposeful bureaucratic neglect – that the Kemp administration recently announced that it may abandon it altogether. The number of Georgians enrolled in the program has never come close to initial promises, and the program has long been expensive to run.
However, the more accurate way to understand Georgia Pathways is as a distraction, as a proposal invented to sell an illusion of Medicaid expansion to voters, but without actually doing so. On those terms it has been somewhat of a success. No, it hasn’t reduced the demand for Medicaid expansion in Georgia; to the contrary, that demand has increased over the years. But it has succeeded in kicking the can a little bit further down the road.
So is Rick Jackson just another can kicker?
Like Kemp, the Republican candidate for governor balks at simply expanding Medicaid as federal law allows. Like Kemp, he’s telling Georgia voters that he has an even better idea. He’s not just offering an alternative to Medicaid expansion, he’s offering an intelligent alternative to Medicaid expansion.
Who could be opposed to that? It’s intelligent!
However, if you unwrap the intelligently tied bow from the intelligently gift-wrapped box and peer inside, what do we find? Honestly, not much. The Jackson campaign provides few details of its proposal. The plan is to use “better technology,” “cut out the middlemen” and “make Georgia a national model for high-quality, accessible and affordable healthcare.”
So intelligent.
To be fair, a big part of Jackson’s argument is that as someone who has made billions of dollars as a profitable “middleman” in the healthcare industry, he has special insight into how to do it better and cheaper. That’s certainly plausible.
It’s also plausible that the skill set, instincts and values required to wring billions from the system are different from those required to improve it. Those are two very different areas of expertise. And as demonstrated in our ongoing experience at the national level, government by billionaire doesn’t always work as well in reality as its paid advocates would have us believe.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Report accuses Ohio-based grocery giant Kroger of frequent overpricing
description: An analysis of government inspections and a survey of customers find that incorrect prices are frequent in the stores of Ohio-based grocery chain Kroger. It said they’re usually in the store’s favor. Cincinnati-based Kroger is the third-largest grocery chain by sales in the United States. It has been accused of using its size to avoid […]
text:
The Kroger Co. corporate headquarters is seen in downtown Cincinnati. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)An analysis of government inspections and a survey of customers find that incorrect prices are frequent in the stores of Ohio-based grocery chain Kroger. It said they’re usually in the store’s favor.
Cincinnati-based Kroger is the third-largest grocery chain by sales in the United States. It has been accused of using its size to avoid competition and to use other tactics to drive up prices.
For example, in a 2024 trial to block a proposed merger with Albertson’s, the Federal Trade Commission presented testimony from a Kroger executive who said the company hiked the price of milk and eggs above the rate of inflation. 
The case also involved testimony from a former employee who accused Kroger of jacking up prices in neighborhoods where it didn’t have much competition.
Last May, the Center for Responsible Food Business, a nonprofit that advocates ethical practices in the food industry, launched a campaign, Kroger’s Pricing Problem. 
As part of it, the group compiled reports from government inspections of Kroger stores to see if prices on the shelves were what customers were charged at the register. 
It “obtained government records covering 389 price inspections at 101 Kroger stores across nine Ohio jurisdictions between 2022 and mid-2026.”
Of those, 15% failed, and 474 were overcharges compared to 170 undercharges — nearly a three-to-one ratio. In Butler County, half of the stores failed, the report said.
It added that minorities and seniors seemed particularly likely to be victims of incorrect pricing.
“One Kroger on Siebenthaler Avenue in Dayton, for example, failed three separate government price inspections, and complaints in the same records allege ‘senior abuse’ over the storeʼs pricing,” the report said. 
“According to U.S. Census Bureau survey data, the storeʼs ZIP code is 77% Black, and one in four of its residents lives below the poverty line.”
Asked about the report, a Kroger spokesperson said the company places a priority on getting prices right. 
“Our customers know that Kroger associates work hard every day to provide great service and value,” the spokesperson said in an email. “Across millions of transactions in Ohio, we take pricing accuracy seriously and work quickly to correct any issue when it is brought to our attention.” 
The spokesperson added that the Center for Responsible Food Business cherry picked data and customer comments.
“This misleading report combines selective data with unverified claims and does not accurately reflect the experience of customers in our stores every day,” the email said.
Some who identified themselves as Kroger workers told the Center for Responsible Food Business that understaffing made accurate pricing nearly impossible.
“I work at Kroger and the problem with items ringing up wrong is because they cut hours they donʼt have enough people doing tags, meaning when a new ad comes out they have to take down the old ones and they (the company) only gives you 1 maybe 2 people to do the WHOLE STORE in 8 hrs,” a person identifying as a Kroger worker in Texas wrote as part of the group’s survey.
As part of its campaign, the group solicited complaints through TV ads and an online porthole.
“We’re tired of getting ripped off at the register,” the appeal said. “Aren’t you? Tell us your story.”
Many of the responses were from people who said that when they double-checked, they weren’t charged the price that was advertised.
“Among the most common grievances in the submission dataset is that the price on the shelf, in the weekly ad, or on a digital coupon is not the price charged at the register,” the report said. “Five hundred fifty seven testimonials (29%) describe this issue.”
It added, “These counts should be read as a floor rather than an estimate of prevalence. A shopper who does not compare the shelf price to the receipt has no way of knowing an overcharge occurred, and most shoppers do not make that comparison on a routine basis.”

title: 2,776 acres of Ohio’s Wayne National Forest leased for more than $11 million for fracking
description: Nearly 3,000 acres of Ohio’s only national forest were leased this week for more than $11 million by the Bureau of Land Management to out-of-state companies for fracking.  The BLM auctioned off 40 parcels in Monroe and Washington counties totaling 2,776 acres in Wayne National Forest for $11.09 million during a quarterly oil and gas […]
text:
Lake Vesuvius Recreation Area at Wayne National Forest in Ohio. (Getty Images file photo.)Nearly 3,000 acres of Ohio’s only national forest were leased this week for more than $11 million by the Bureau of Land Management to out-of-state companies for fracking. 
The BLM auctioned off 40 parcels in Monroe and Washington counties totaling 2,776 acres in Wayne National Forest for $11.09 million during a quarterly oil and gas lease sale. 
“Leasing is the first step in the process to develop federal oil and gas resources,” BLM said in a statement. 
“The BLM ensures oil and gas development meets the requirements set forth by the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and other applicable legal authorities. Oil and gas leases are awarded for a term of 10 years and as long thereafter as there is production of oil and gas in paying quantities.” 
These are the companies that are leasing the parcels:

Pennsylvania-based Apex Energy Operating III LLC leased 25 parcels for $7.97 million. 
Texas-based R&R Royalty LTD leased six parcels for $864,234.
Oklahoma-based Gulfport Appalachia LLC leased five parcels for $1.98 million. 
Texas-based Texas Independent Exploration Limited leased three parcels for $241,559. 
Pennsylvania-based Ohio Gasco LLC leased one parcel for $25,769. 

The BLM scoped out the parcels in January and announced the auction in July. 
Fracking is the process of injecting liquid into the ground at a high pressure to extract oil or gas.
Nathan Johnson, senior attorney for the Ohio Environmental Council, said the lease sale violates important environmental laws meant to protect endangered wildlife and the quality of the environment.
“The Wayne is Ohio’s only National Forest and one of the state’s best places for outdoor recreation,” Johnson said. “Fracking the Wayne will pollute the air, harm local streams, and industrialize the landscape. We are preparing to challenge yesterday’s leasing in federal court.”
The Wayne National Forest was established in 1935 and totals 244,000 acres spanning 12 counties with three units in Athens, Ironton, and Marietta in Southeast Ohio.
More than 200,000 people visit Wayne National Forest annually, which is known for its hiking, biking, horseback riding trails, and off-road vehicle trails. 
Spending by visitors to the Wayne National Forest is about $7.4 million annually, according to the United States Forest Service. 
This is the first lease sale in Wayne National Forest since March 2017 when 20 parcels in Monroe County were auctioned off.  
A national forest is managed by the U.S. Forest Service under the Department of Agriculture and blends conservation with public service and resource extraction like logging and mining. 
Wayne National Forest already has 1,200 conventional wells, but the BLM predicts new wells drilled in the Wayne will be horizontal, hydraulic fracturing natural-gas wells. 
There were approximately 2,000 incidents associated with oil and gas wells in Ohio from 2015-2023 — including 98 incidents in Monroe County and 85 incidents in Washington counties, according to FracTracker Alliance, a nonprofit that collects data on fracking pipelines. 
Washington County residents have been raising concerns that injection wells leaking brine waste could contaminate Marietta’s drinking water. 
Evidence shows increased exposure to fracking impacts health, in particular children’s health, including low birth weight, preterm births, congenital anomalies, and asthma, according to Yale School of Medicine.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Should the state of Ohio ban property tax incentives for data centers?
description: Earlier this month, a group of Ohio House members largely representing urban areas of the state introduced a bill to prohibit property tax exemptions for data centers. Property tax exemptions are a significant tool that can have a big impact on local government budgets. When evaluating whether prohibiting property tax exemptions for data centers are […]
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)Earlier this month, a group of Ohio House members largely representing urban areas of the state introduced a bill to prohibit property tax exemptions for data centers.
Property tax exemptions are a significant tool that can have a big impact on local government budgets. When evaluating whether prohibiting property tax exemptions for data centers are a good idea, it’s worth asking a few key questions that I like to ask about a range of policy issues: does it work, does it help, and who does it impact?
Okay, first, “does it work.” 
The point of a property tax exemption is to give an incentive for a company to develop a project at a given site. 
While older literature on economic development incentives says that only about 2-25% of economic development projects make their decisions based on incentives, newer studies that focus specifically on data center incentives imply this number could be closer to 33% for data centers. 
While my inclination was to think that property tax incentives would follow the path of past incentive programs, recent analyses of data centers seem to be saying otherwise.
Now for “are they good.” 
There are a few questions we need to answer for this. One is this: what is the opportunity cost of a property tax exemption? 
Exempting a data center from property taxes means less money available for schools, county government, townships, and municipalities. 
Even if data centers are highly sensitive to exemptions and one-third of them change decisions based on these incentives, this could still mean hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds left on the table for the two-thirds of data centers that aren’t making decisions based on incentives.
Another consideration is what the real social impact is of attracting data centers. 
We know data center construction leads to more construction spending, wages, and capital investment.
So do subsidies for sports stadiums, but the economic consensus is that these subsidies are an economic development shell game rather than creation of new economic value. 
Data centers could be similar: they could just displace other economic development that is bound to happen on its own.
Further social impacts that need investigation center on utility costs and environmental and public health. 
Energy-heavy data centers will either drive up electricity costs and water costs and lead to burning of fossil fuels if they pull energy from the grid and water from public water systems or lead to construction of new gas-fired power plants if their energy generation is pushed behind the meter. 
This will lead to higher carbon emissions and the degradation of air quality and associated asthma and lung disease that comes with emission of NOx, PM2.5, and SO2 into the air.
Lastly, the question of “who benefits” matters here. 
Much of the benefits of data center construction will accrue to investors and data users who live outside of the state. 
Carbon emission costs will generally be felt by people across the world as they exacerbate climate change. 
On the other hand, both economic development benefits like jobs and public health costs like asthma and lung disease will be felt by local communities.
A final consideration is this: the state tends to give local communities wide range to use economic development incentives because different localities have different challenges when it comes to economic development. 
A total ban on property tax exemptions for these purposes would potentially cut some communities off from economic development that could help them. 
But data centers are a big deal. It may be that making this policy at the state level is the most straightforward way to regulate an industry that is changing rapidly in the buckeye state.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The fight against Flock cameras in Ohio is just the beginning
description: Government surveillance isn’t new, but new wide-ranging technologies that can detect our faces and track our movements are making it more ubiquitous. While the tools have changed, the purpose remains the same: to chill independent thought, free speech, and dissent, bringing our country closer to 1984. Millions of Americans are being watched as the U.S. […]
text:
A police officer uses the Flock Safety license plate reader system. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)Government surveillance isn’t new, but new wide-ranging technologies that can detect our faces and track our movements are making it more ubiquitous.
While the tools have changed, the purpose remains the same: to chill independent thought, free speech, and dissent, bringing our country closer to 1984.
Millions of Americans are being watched as the U.S. ramps up mass surveillance with help from AI, data brokers, and partnerships with private tech companies.
Immigrants, people seeking reproductive health care, and activists are among the most intensely monitored, but tech like Flock cameras has brought the issue into communities across the country.
That includes people in Ohio — one of the most heavily surveilled states in the country, with 62.4 cameras for every 100,000 residents as of Aug. 17.
And the debate over these cameras in Ohio, which has drawn significant interest from locals as well as officials, reflects growing concerns nationally.
According to the ACLU, police departments have increasingly deployed automated license plate readers (ALPRs) powered by AI to track drivers “without a warrant, probable cause, or even reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing.” And they’re doing this with little to no oversight or regulation.
Flock Safety is one of the largest ALPR vendors in the U.S. Their solar-powered, teardrop-shaped cameras capture images of all passing vehicles, storing the car’s make, model, and other identifying features. Any law enforcement agency with a Flock contract can access the company’s nationwide database without a warrant.
Flock cameras also track people. Their “FreeForm search” feature has allowed police departments to search the database using phrases like “male with tattoos” and “person on skateboard,” according to data reviewed by 404 Media.
DeFlock, an open-source project that maps license plate readers, has identified over 128,000 ALPRs in the U.S. Even my small town of around 20,000 people in Southern California has at least 35 ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras.
No independent research has shown that ALPRs can reduce crime. But there’s mounting evidence of the technology’s alarmingly high error rate. An analysis by the Roseville, California police department found that 71 percent of Flock’s alerts to the Roseville police incorrectly flagged vehicles as stolen or used in a felony.
Far from promoting “public safety,” the tech has led to wrongful arrests, profiling, and countless other abuses.
Flock reportedly has shared license plate data with federal authorities, including ICE. Among other cities, Los Angeles recently suspended their use of Flock cameras amid mounting privacy concerns over who controls the data and how it’s shared.
Court records obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation show that Texas deputies searched 83,000 Flock cameras nationwide to track a Texas woman across state lines because she allegedly “had an abortion.” In Dunwoody, Georgia, a public records request revealed Flock employees accessing cameras in children’s spaces at a community center as part of sales demonstrations.
Other reporting has found cops repeatedly misusing the Flock system to stalk exes.
More communities are organizing and fighting back against this unregulated AI technology. As a result, at least 100 cities have now rejected ALPRs, most of them Flock cameras. But Flock is only one cog in the machine. Cities can easily replace their Flock cameras with those from competitors like Axon, Motorola Solutions, or Genetec, as some have already done.
Mass surveillance remains the fundamental problem. Ever more companies collect our data through cellular networks, facial recognition, surveillance cameras, and ALPRs, among other sources.
The U.S. government, in turn, purchases massive amounts of our data from commercial data brokers without obtaining warrants — bypassing our Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable searches and seizures. In tandem, multiple federal agencies now have sweeping access to Americans’ sensitive personal data through systems built by Big Tech company Palantir, following President Trump’s 2025 executive order that expanded data sharing across agencies.
This metastasizing mass surveillance state — what George Orwell called “Big Brother” in 1984 — is eroding our privacy, freedom, and Constitution.
As more communities wake up to the danger, the solution isn’t trading one brand of camera for another. We need oversight and regulation of the entire surveillance industry, as well as the government agencies that rely on it.
OtherWords columnist Farrah Hassen, J.D., is a writer, policy analyst, and educator. This op-ed was distributed by OtherWords.org.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Raise your voice about climate change
description: Why is virtually no one in political leadership or mainstream journalism talking about the existential threat of climate change?
text:
If you watched the news over the last days of August, you saw video of an almost inconceivable wave of destruction in Nepal. Untold numbers of people and both the infrastructure and cultural heritage of this ancient region were swept away.  
Glaciers in the mountains above a populated valley were weakened by rising global temperatures and came cascading down in a deadly tsunami.
It may have seemed a world away, but the reality is you and I caused that disaster as surely as if we had pushed a big red button that released the deluge. You may roll your eyes but it is literally true. Why? How?
We have failed over several years to take any significant action on climate change. Meanwhile we consistently produce the most carbon emissions of any country on earth — emissions that are causing the globe to get hotter.
Nepal may seem too far away. Put it aside for the moment. What about the weather forecasts seemingly day after day for the past several months putting literally millions of Americans on alert for extreme weather?
It’s been record-breaking weather of every description. Snowfall measured in feet instead of inches.  Rainfall amounts considered once in a thousand years occurring annually. Los Angeles burning down! There is no need to list them. The majority of Americans now recognize that this extreme weather is the result of human-generated climate change.
It’s also clear that at a time when “affordability” squeezes every household, climate degradation is getting costly. Maybe it’s just the added cost of running the AC more or having to crank the furnace higher. Millions of Americans have endured moderate to severe storm damage. The cost of repairs comes either from your own wallet, insurance companies, or some level of government. Inevitably we will all bear increased costs due to these continuing catastrophes.
Considering all this, why is virtually no one in political leadership or mainstream journalism talking about it! Why? You know what? It does not matter. As of today — right now — you and I have to start hollering. Imagine if your kids were in a locked car that rolled into the river. That is how loud, and frantically, and persistently we have to yell. Yell!
Do not grasp for a complacency based on today’s already eroded standards, thinking we can adjust to this “new normal,” because this is all only going to get worse. And all the data indicates that the rate of decline is quickening.
First target of our new-found rage: No candidate for office, either challenger or incumbent, should get our support unless they are committed to a strong position of climate safety action.
Complain to the media about their pathetic coverage of the most important story, maybe, in human history. How can they report the weather forecast every 10 minutes but fail to provide any analysis about how rapidly weather is becoming more severe, why that is happening and what the future holds unless we eliminate carbon emissions?
Get on your marching shoes.  We need to be gathering in large numbers to protest this lack of action by those who control the levers of power in this society. In government, that means both the federal and state leadership.  Those culpable include the executive and legislative branches of government for generally gutless lack of action across the board. True, more is happening on the state level than nationally, but not nearly enough.
The prime target of our ire ought to be the private sector, which continues to engorge itself at the profit smorgasbord while they kill the earth. They have so far successfully lulled most of the population into somnambulant acquiescence to their path of destruction. But no more. For God’s sake, no more.
At this moment, in the days after Labor Day, unions must take up the call: “Workers DEMAND a safe planet!” If unions’ primary role is to safeguard the rights of working people and ensure they enjoy a decent, stable quality of life, what could be more important, more urgent, than fighting to maintain and restore our climate? If the members do not understand it, teach them.
DO NOT Continue to be complacent.  Do not surrender the future of your children and their children. Complain. Confront. Holler, yell. Raise hell! DEMAND a safe planet.
John Harrity is the former president of the Connecticut State Council of Machinists. He lives in East Hartland.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Drop in Nebraskans receiving public food assistance hastens, drawing concern at hearing
description: LINCOLN — The number of Nebraskans receiving public food assistance continues a downward slide, punctuated by recent back-to-back record drops in monthly participation since the state began releasing public SNAP data in 2014. The latest figures show that about 7,600 fewer Nebraskans were enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in Jul[...]
text:
Together food pantry in downtown Omaha helps people in need pack up free grocery items   during a past holiday season. The number of Nebraskans receiving public food assistance has dropped since the Trump administration's stricter eligibility and work requirements were implemented in summer of 2025. Advocates are concerned, saying some who need help aren't getting it and that pressure is weighing on private pantries and food banks. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The number of Nebraskans receiving public food assistance continues a downward slide, punctuated by recent back-to-back record drops in monthly participation since the state began releasing public SNAP data in 2014.
The latest figures show that about 7,600 fewer Nebraskans were enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in July compared with the month before. Total participation was 116,703 Nebraskans, down from about 150,000 a year ago.
July beat June in terms of the biggest single-month loss of SNAP participants in more than a decade and since the summer of 2025, when Congress approved a massive tax-and-spending-cuts package described by President Donald Trump as big and beautiful.
In a legislative hearing Thursday, a Nebraska Appleseed nutrition advocate sounded further alarm.
Eric Savaiano, manager of food and nutrition access and economic justice for the nonprofit Nebraska Appleseed. (Courtesy of Nebraska Appleseed)
Records show that compared with July 2025, nearly 33,000 fewer people in Nebraska received public food assistance this July, a nearly 22% dip over the year. Eric Savaiano, the nonprofit Appeseed’s manager for food and nutrition access, said about half of that loss represents Nebraska youth and teens under age 19, with 13% of the total annual loss being infants and children under 5.
He called that shocking and said the decline does not mean “someone solved hunger last summer.”
“Fewer people on SNAP means hungry people, half of which are children, are experiencing more strain and struggle, more trips to limited food pantries and food banks, and more long-term pain for school nutrition programs and educators for the foreseeable future,” Savaiano said.
He laid out concerns during a hearing before the Legislature’s Health and Human Services Committee. Though the focus was an interim study on food insecurity for pregnant and postpartum women and their children in Nebraska, SNAP emerged as part of the discussion.
Call for ‘accountability’
The committee chair, state Sen. Brian Hardin of Gering, took a challenging stance and asked Savaiano if there should be “accountability” for people to work if they’re being provided public food benefits.
Recent declines in SNAP and other public benefits have been tied to eligibility changes and stricter work requirements called for in the 2025 tax and spending measure. The Trump administration said it wanted to curb waste, fraud and abuse and spend federal dollars wisely. The Department of Agriculture covers the cost of SNAP benefits. States administer the program and share those administrative costs with the federal government.
Hardin said much of the national debt is related to health “in some way, shape or form.”
State Sen. Brian Hardin of Gering. (Photo courtesy of Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“If we don’t go after something in the health space, we will never get a handle on that,” Hardin said after Savaiano’s testimony. “And if we don’t get a handle on that national debt, what happens to Nebraska?” 
Savaiano responded, “Are we doing that on the backs of people who need the support right now?”
Appleseed officials believe that Nebraska’s declining SNAP participation has been exacerbated by the state’s implementation in May of new eligibility verification requirements for all applicants. Savaiano said states have flexibility in their verification process and that Appleseed believes the tactics employed by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services are overly burdensome and have scared off some Nebraskans who need aid. He hopes for future legislation to rein in the process.
Savaiano said, for example, that Nebraska SNAP beneficiaries must certify the number of people who live in their household, and that can take the form of getting a neighbor to sign paperwork. Savaiano referred to the case of a rural Nebraskan who balked, saying her neighbors would laugh and make her life miserable. She no longer participates in the program.
 Protecting taxpayer dollars 

A spokesperson for Nebraska DHHS acknowledged that the state’s drop in SNAP participation is in part due to stepped-up verification requirements. Jeff Powell, the spokesperson, said the process was created in response to the federal law change and requirement that states maintain a SNAP payment error rate below 6%.
States with error rates above that threshold, beginning in October 2027, must pay a portion of federal benefit costs. Nebraska was one of only nine states with a reported error rate below 6%. Error rates measure the accuracy of  states in determining who is eligible for SNAP and how much they receive.
“The enhanced verification measures will ensure program integrity, error rates remain below 6%, and taxpayer dollars are protected,” said Powell.
The entrance to a Big Lots store in Portland, Oregon. (Stock photo by hapabapa/Getty Images)
He said Nebraska has reduced the instances when the “honor system” is used. He said that is “critical” to remaining below the error threshold.
“DHHS is working to streamline the new measures to achieve quicker benefit determinations and will ensure that all Nebraskans eligible for SNAP benefits can receive them,” Powell said.
State Sen. Victor Rountree of Bellevue, who had requested that the Legislature examine food insecurity particularly for women and their children, noted during the hearing that Gov. Jim Pillen signed a proclamation declaring Sept. 14-18 as Malnutrition Awareness Week.
Only two members of the committee were present at Thursday’s  hearing, though it was livestreamed and recorded. Rountree testified that many pantries and food banks have been running low on healthier items as Nebraska families are leaning more on private food providers. 
 Healthy brain development 

Among experts invited to speak was Abbie Raikes, a professor at the University of Nebraska Medical Center whose focus is on early childhood development. She said she was speaking as a private individual and noted that nutrition in early years is essential for healthy brain development.
She and other academics who spoke said food insecurity can negatively affect school readiness, academics and behavior. 
Rountree asked members to consider the testimony when acting on future legislation related to low-income Nebraskans.
“Develop well now so we can have our children in school able to learn and be productive members in our society,” he said.
 
Most recent Nebraska SNAP statistics reflect activity through July. (Courtesy of Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services)

name: Alaska Beacon
title: The Roadless Rule rollback is an opportunity not a threat
description: While environmentalists oppose the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule, which would remove prohibitions on road construction and logging on nearly 59 million acres of national forest, I see this as an opportunity for professional foresters to manage federal land, reduce wildfire risk and boost the economy.  I’ve spent 30 years in th[...]
text:
An Alaska Forest Practices Act compliant forest road is seen in what was previously an unroaded forest setting. (Photo courtesy of Keith Coulter)While environmentalists oppose the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of the Roadless Rule, which would remove prohibitions on road construction and logging on nearly 59 million acres of national forest, I see this as an opportunity for professional foresters to manage federal land, reduce wildfire risk and boost the economy. 
I’ve spent 30 years in the industrial logging sector of the Western U.S. in states such as Idaho, Washington, Oregon and Alaska. Environmental rhetoric is nothing new to those of us who have chosen to make working in western forests their career.
Recently, I read a commentary in the Alaska Beacon that argued for maintaining the Roadless Rule and I was not surprised to view the typical laundry list of doom from one side of the debate. Words like “threatened” and “imperiled” come up as authors weave their case for almost certain environmental ruin unless we curb industrial activities immediately for what can only be described as the “do-nothing alternative.”
As a professional forester with decades of boots-on-the-ground experience, a few obvious counterpoints come to mind. The rhetoric that forests are a stagnant sea of trees that do not grow or become more dense year after year is simply wrong. That’s a Forestry 101 issue. You’d think something this simplistic would be understood by the average environmentalist: forests do grow, year after year, becoming denser. In a warming climate with limited resources of water, nutrients, space, sunlight and dwindling snowpack, continued growth will inevitably lead to insect and disease issues, dying trees and catastrophic wildfire.
Look at the news. The wildfire epidemic appears to be growing year to year and lasting longer each year due to warmer winters and dwindling snowpack. Catastrophic wildfire events are real and increasingly common. People are dying. Whole communities are being lost.
Throughout my career I’ve watched the environmentalist movement become very successful. It has demonized building roads, tree cutting and forest management as a whole. Regions of the Western U.S. and Alaska that used to have large milling infrastructure are now idled and gone. There is no one left to do the work or send the logs to mills because they aren’t there. There are few ways to complete forest restoration work, because there are no longer markets for the material. Revenue from the logging industry that can support public schools is in decline. Had forest management activities been allowed to continue, forests could be managed and local economies supported in the effort.
One hundred years of fire suppression in the western forests means they are overstocked as the climate warms. From what you know about forests, even if it is just a little: what do you think is going to happen in those areas in the years to come?
I’m not sure what the environmentalists’ long-term goal is, other than “preserve the forests and the forests will take care of themselves.” The evidence does not support that message. Their messaging to “do nothing” seems reckless and misplaced.
The sediment contribution to nearby water bodies from a well- managed forest road is probably difficult to even measure when compared to the benefits of accessing areas that can be managed for forest health, wood products, jobs and long-term recreation, resulting in stronger regional economies. Now, let’s consider what the contribution to sediment loads in fish bearing creeks or watersheds that supply drinking water to scores of people are after a catastrophic wildfire burns through an area. 
Keep in mind that forest operations in the Western U.S. and Alaska have strict forest practices rules and regulations. Timber harvesting is inspected by not only State agency forestry professionals but also Dept of Fish and Game and the Dept of Environmental Conservation representatives. 
Western states have strict regulatory standards that the forest industry must adhere to while simultaneously creating fire resilient and healthy forest ecosystems. The forest products sector is largely our only hope for navigating our way out of the overstocked forest problem that blankets the Western U.S. There are thousands of professional foresters and land managers that have been trained by Society of American Foresters accredited universities working to improve forest health across the nation.
I disagree with environmental organizations that want to stop science-based management of forests in the name of preservation, regardless of the cost to local economies. Arguing for the preservation of the Roadless Rule puts mother nature in the driver’s seat — and few people will be able to tolerate how she’ll manage the forests if it happens through destructive wildfire events. We already know how to solve forest management issues: with roads and active forest management.
