name: WyoFile
title: Unionized Fremont County first responders say they’ll strike over rift with local officials
description:
The county commission voted to let a contract with the employer 30 EMTs and paramedics expire while negotiating a deal with a regional hospital where they can't organize.
The post Unionized Fremont County first responders say they’ll strike over rift with local officials appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Thirty unionized emergency medical technicians and paramedics who serve Fremont County say they will walk off the job Sept. 28 because county officials appear poised to allow a contract with their employer, Tennessee-based Priority Ambulance, to expire.
The first responders, organized under United Steel Workers Local 9012, had an understanding with the county, according to Local 9012 President Dominick Sapien. If voters approved a ¾-cent sales tax — a portion of which would be dedicated to funding ambulance and EMT services — the county would extend its contract with Priority Ambulance long enough to eventually take over responsibility for the service under the Fremont County Association of Governments. That would provide a more stable service, Sapien said, along with state-level salaries and benefits.
County voters approved the tax in the Aug. 18 primary election.
But the Fremont County Board of Commissioners voted Tuesday to instead negotiate with Cody Regional Health. The county’s contract with Priority Ambulance, which operates under the name Frontier Ambulance in Fremont County, is set to expire in October. Its tentative agreement with Cody Regional Health would begin Oct. 1 and last for about a year while the county considers a more permanent strategy.
If the county goes with Cody Regional, the EMTs would no longer be able to bargain as a union.
“We knocked on hundreds of doors to get this [tax] passed,” Sapien told WyoFile. “We find out that the county commissioners are now talking to Cody Regional Health to come in and take the ambulance service. They’re trying to bring in this third party that doesn’t recognize unions. It feels as though it’s a move to bust our union so, that way, we have no negotiating power.”
Ambulances at Cody Regional Health. (Madelyn Beck/WyoFile)
In response, 21 of the union’s members voted to strike, beginning Sept. 28. 
Two commissioners reached by WyoFile on Thursday said their beef is with Priority Ambulance, and that they had made no such deal with the union.
“Let ’em,” commissioner Jennifer Wilson said. 
“[Priority Ambulance] just didn’t want to play ball,” Wilson continued, adding that the company has continued for years to demand “exorbitant” fees. “We tried to negotiate, but they wanted to just sit there and put the gun back to our head again, and we’re sick and tired of it.”
Wilson, and Commission Chairman Larry Allen, told WyoFile there was never an agreement with the EMTs regarding the passage of the optional sales tax and eventually bringing them in as county employees, much less any other scenario to afford them the opportunity to remain unionized.
“My understanding,” Wilson said, “is Cody [Regional Health] is going to pay them even better. So what are they hollering about?”
Due to continual staffing issues, the EMTs frequently work 72 hours a week or more, Sapien said. Being able to organize for bargaining power is vital, no matter the employer, he added. Because EMTs are dedicated to saving lives, employers regard them as people who can be stretched to the breaking point, and they’ll still come to work.
“Our people are out here saving lives, helping others, and making less that I could going to work at McDonalds,” Sapien said.
The county isn’t giving up on the idea of eventually building a self-sustaining EMT service, Wilson said. But they don’t want to do it with Priority Ambulance. “They can go away, and I never want to hear about them again,” Wilson said. “We’re paying a company to use all of our stuff and [they keep asking for] more and more money.”
Meantime, the county needs Cody Regional Health’s help, she added.
“[Cody Regional Health has] got a really good reputation. We’ve got some bumpy roads coming ahead, you know, to get all this lined out and to get people to fill these ambulance spots.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama executes Jeffery Lee by lethal injection
description: The state of Alabama executed Jeffery Lee, 49, Thursday for the murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during a pawn shop robbery in Orrville in 1998. Lee was executed by lethal injection just over two months after a federal district court rebuffed Alabama’s attempt to put him to death by nitrogen gas, and after […]
text:
Jeffrey Lee, seen in an Alabama Department of Corrections photo, was executed Thursday evening for the murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during a pawn shop robbery in 1998. A trial jury voted 7-5 to sentence Lee to life in prison, but the trial judge overrode the jury and sentenced Lee to death. (Alabama Department of Corrections)The state of Alabama executed Jeffery Lee, 49, Thursday for the murders of Jimmy Ellis and Elaine Thompson during a pawn shop robbery in Orrville in 1998.
Lee was executed by lethal injection just over two months after a federal district court rebuffed Alabama’s attempt to put him to death by nitrogen gas, and after an unsuccessful campaign for clemency by death penalty opponents, who said a jury’s initial recommendation of sentencing Lee to life without parole should be respected.
“All is well, I just want to say to my family, I love them,” Lee said during his final statement. “To my brothers on life row, I love them.”
Media witnesses did not observe any complications during the execution. Lee was pronounced dead at 6:22 p.m.
It was the second execution conducted by the state this year. Jeremy Williams, 41, was put to death by lethal injection last month for his role in the sexual assault and murder of a 5-year-old girl in Russell County in 2021.
Gov. Kay Ivey said in a statement that she reaffirmed her commitment to justice by following through with Lee’s execution and that the “promise was fulfilled for his victims.”
“This case underscores exactly why the law passed in 2017 ending so-called ‘judicial override’ did not apply to existing death sentences like Mr. Lee’s,” Ivey said. “These victims have waited long enough, and I pray they can feel peace and have closure.”
Lee was convicted of the murders of Thompson and Ellis in 2000. During the trial, Lee’s attorneys sought to avoid the death penalty, noting Lee’s youth at the time; the fact he was a father to two children and what they described as an intellectual disability.
A jury voted 7-5 to recommend sentencing Lee to life in prison. However, Dallas County Circuit Court Judge Jack Meigs overruled the jury and imposed the death sentence, writing that Lee had “mercilessly” killed Thompson and Ellis.
Alabama allowed judges to impose the death penalty against a jury’s recommendation for decades. The practice, known as judicial override, was abolished by the Alabama Legislature in 2017, but the bill doing so did not apply retroactively.
Death penalty opponents petitioned Gov. Kay Ivey to commute Lee’s sentence, citing the original jury determination. Ivey earlier this year commuted the death sentence of Charles “Sonny” Burton,  sentenced to death for being present during the robbery of a Talladega AutoZone in 1991 in which Doug Battle, a customer, was killed.
Burton did not pull the trigger and was not in the store when Battle was killed, and opponents of Burton’s execution noted that Derrick DeBruce, who shot and killed Battle, had his death sentence commuted to life in prison.
Ivey also commuted the death sentence for Robin “Rocky” Myers in February 2025 amid questions about Myers’ conviction for the murder of Ludie Mae Tucker in 1991. There was no physical evidence that linked him to her death.
However, Ivey spokeswoman Gina Maiola said Wednesday that the 2017 law abolishing judicial override “made very clear that it would not apply retroactively.”
Lee’s attorneys said in a statement following the execution Thursday that Lee’s death sentence rested solely on judicial override. They wrote that it was “a moral failure, not just a legal formality.”
“A state that no longer stands behind the rule that condemned a man, but kills him under it anyway, has not delivered justice,” the statement said. “It has revealed how little its own standards constrain it when it is determined to carry out an execution.”
Lee was originally scheduled to be executed by nitrogen gas in June, but he sued to block the method, arguing that it would subject him to unconstitutionally cruel and unusual punishment and that the state could carry out an execution by firing squad.
Though other inmates subject to nitrogen gas had previously challenged the method, Lee’s suit led to an unprecedented bench trial over the state’s use of nitrogen gas, which witnesses to nitrogen gas executions described as leading to drawn-out deaths for those subjected to it.
U.S. District Judge Emily Marks in late May ruled that while the nitrogen gas process would produce air hunger, that did not rise to the level of cruel and unusual punishment.  However, a three-judge panel with the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals reversed Marks, saying air hunger went “over and above the mental distress that typically accompanies the knowledge of impending death by execution.”
The judges directed Marks to rule whether death by firing squad was a feasible alternative. Marks ruled that it was and blocked the state’s use of nitrogen gas, which the U.S. Supreme Court declined to overturn.
The following day, the state moved to execute Lee by lethal injection. Lee’s attorneys argued in federal court that a 2018 settlement of a lawsuit brought by Lee against lethal injection prevented the state from using the method, but Marks ruled in the state’s favor, saying circumstances had changed.
The state did not make any serious efforts to attempt an execution by firing squad, Lee’s preferred method, and his attorneys did not refer to it much.
The state plans to execute Michael Shannon Taylor in November.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland officials grapple with ‘bizarre’ Trump executive order on Chesapeake Bay
description: Just months after federal officials joined Chesapeake Bay states to renew their pledge to restore the nation's largest estuary, President Donald Trump on Wednesday rescinded an Obama-era executive order that called for federal leadership in the effort.
text:
The Chesapeake Bay Bridge, pictured from the Eastport section of Annapolis, in September 2025. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Just months after federal officials joined Chesapeake Bay states in December to renew their pledge to restore the nation’s largest estuary, President Donald Trump on Wednesday rescinded an Obama-era executive order that called for federal leadership in the effort.
Trump’s executive order also railed against stormwater management fees, which he labeled “rain taxes” — a refrain from Republican Larry Hogan’s successful 2014 campaign for governor — arguing that they “impose hundreds of dollars in annual financial burdens on residents and small businesses,” with “little to no measurable benefits to the Chesapeake Bay.”
Some jurisdictions in the bay region, including some Maryland counties, collect fees from property owners to fund projects like rain gardens, tree plantings and permeable pavement installations that slow down runoff.  
Maryland’s entire congressional delegation — including lone Republican Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) — released a statement Thursday opposing Trump’s executive order.
“The 2009 Executive Order that the Trump administration just revoked provided vital federal resources that support state-led efforts to improve the health and productivity of the Chesapeake Bay and its surrounding area,” read the joint statement. “This decision is shortsighted and harmful to our communities. Make no mistake: the Chesapeake Bay is a national treasure. And we will continue to fight for it.”
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore gifts Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro with a fishing hat on Dec. 2, 2025, as Shapiro took the helm of the Chesapeake Executive Council. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Maryland Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz said the timing of the order “is a little bit bizarre,” after December’s meeting.
“We just saw strong support from all of the partners involved to continuing the work that we’ve been doing,” Kurtz said.
Maryland officials are in a “wait-and-see” mode, he said, wondering precisely how Trump’s executive order could affect the federal government’s role in the decades-long effort to clean up the Chesapeake. Could some federal agencies step back from the restoration effort, rescinding personnel or funding?
“This now is going to require us to have individual conversations with each one of those agencies, get a sense for how they’re interpreting the [executive order], and then how they’re going to be turning that into their own policies,” Kurtz said.
Trump’s order also calls on federal agencies to “encourage the repeal or rescission of stormwater management fees imposed by States or localities.” But the power to levy fees — and consider rescinding them — rests with state and local governments, said environmental attorney Jon Mueller, who manages the University of Maryland’s Environmental Law Clinic.
“You can’t take away state sovereignty,” said Mueller, a former vice president for litigation at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. “The Clean Water Act recognizes state sovereignty — and the fact that states can do more than the federal government as far as pollution goes.”
Maryland Department of the Environment spokesperson Aimena Lipscomb said in a statement that, because Maryland’s stormwater programs are established under state law and the federal Clean Water Act, Trump’s rescission of the 2009 executive order “will not alter our goals — nor will it derail our momentum, having already completed nearly 50,000 acres of local stormwater restoration.”
Rep. Rob Bresnahan Jr. (R-Pa.), who joined Trump during the executive order signing, said in a news release that he believes Obama’s 2009 executive order “created” the “rain taxes.” He praised Trump for “listening to the people of Northeastern Pennsylvania.”
Maryland first required certain jurisdictions to collect stormwater remediation fees in 2012, a move that became a political flashpoint in the 2014 gubernatorial campaign when Hogan decried the “rain tax” on his way to a stunning defeat of then-Lt. Gov. Anthony Brown (D) in deep-blue Maryland.
In 2015, Maryland removed the requirement that certain jurisdictions collect the fees, instead requiring that they submit periodic plans for how they will handle, and pay for, stormwater improvements. The goal is to reduce harmful flows of nitrogen, phosphorus and sediment that can cause oxygen-poor “dead zones” in the bay, harming underwater wildlife.
Former Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan (R) railed against the “rain tax” during his successful 2014 campaign for governor. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters).
In fiscal 2024, seven Maryland counties were still levying the stormwater fees, out of the 10 largest counties in the state that were once required to do so, according to a state report. Two others were using tax revenue, and one — Baltimore County — repealed it altogether.
Most of the counties decided to keep the fees because they recognized the projects’ benefits, said Kristin Reilly, director of the Choose Clean Water Coalition, which represents 325 environmental organizations in the bay area, including riverkeepers, land trusts and park advocates.
“They help improve flooding issues, they help beautify communities, they address potential health challenges related to dirty water, and they are put toward fixing our water infrastructure — which is failing,” Reilly said.
Stormwater pollution is considered the fastest-growing category of pollution affecting the bay watershed, compared to categories such as agricultural pollution and discharges from sewage treatment plants and industrial facilities.
Bay states have struggled to curtail diffuse sources of pollution, including stormwater runoff, and they failed to reach a 2025 goal for reducing nitrogen, phosphorus and sediment by specific amounts.
New pollution goals, by way of a new computer model, are in the works. In the meantime, the bay states and the Trump administration signed a new bay agreement last year with a host of other goals for wildlife, coastal habitat restoration and more.
“The Bay states and federal partners just signed a new watershed agreement committing to bay restoration goals. There are a host of new challenges the bay is facing, from climate change to population growth and development. This is absolutely not a time to step back,” Chesapeake Bay Foundation President and CEO Hilary Harp Falk said Thursday.
She said the foundation, a leading nonprofit advocating for the bay, is “most concerned about the loss of federal leadership, accountability and cross-agency coordination that were flagships of the original executive order.”
Reilly said Trump’s executive order was another example of the administration’s “actions not reflecting” its approving words about the bay cleanup effort.
Stormwater runoff carries a wide range of pollutants into streams, rivers and, ultimately, the Chesapeake Bay. (Photo by Matt Rath/Chesapeake Bay Program)
“Repeatedly, the administration has proposed the termination of critical federal funding for the Chesapeake Bay region and now this Executive Order aims to strip away the right of local governments to make decisions based on the needs of their community,” Reilly wrote in a statement.
But Mueller argued there are reasons for optimism.
The president did not signal an attempt to rescind the TMDL, or Total Maximum Daily Load — the legally binding “pollution diet” that the Environmental Protection Agency established in 2010.
In fact, the president “doubles down” on the bay restoration effort, Mueller argues. In the order, Trump calls on his federal agencies to focus their resources on “more direct, on-the-ground projects, in areas of highest need, that would result in the most impactful water quality improvements.”
“In the past there have been a lot of best-management practices — both in agriculture and in urban, suburban settings — that look good on paper and they got credits for them, but … are not as effective as they could be,” Mueller said.
But Kurtz pushed back against what he called the “implication” in Trump’s order that cost-effectiveness isn’t a priority.
“That’s just patently inaccurate here in Maryland,” Kurtz said. “Cost-effectiveness is really central to what we do, because we know that the cheaper the projects are, the more projects we can do.”
Even if the exact long-term impacts of Trump’s executive order for Maryland remain unclear, Kurtz said that the order has a negative impact in the short-term.
“Any confusion is only going to slow us down, and I think we’ve all recognized that we need to be going faster,” Kurtz said.

title: Supreme Court finds Wyoming must spend more on teachers, strikes down other funding demands
authors: Rebecca Huntington and Owen Houtakker, Wyoming Tribune Eagle
description:
Mixed ruling from high court in school funding suit draws praise from both lawmakers and educators. Decision reverses requirements to pay for school safety officers, computers and student nutrition. 
The post Supreme Court finds Wyoming must spend more on teachers, strikes down other funding demands appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In a highly anticipated decision, the Wyoming Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state has failed to adequately fund K-12 teacher salaries and properly account for inflation. But the court struck down other portions of a lower court’s finding that Wyoming has a constitutional obligation to pay for school resource officers, student nutrition and computers.
The court’s decision to require more state funding for schools, but only for certain elements, largely drew praise and optimism from lawmakers, the governor and educators. 
The ruling is the result of a lawsuit filed in 2022 by the Wyoming Education Association, an educator advocacy group, against the state, alleging the Legislature was failing its constitutional obligation to provide a thorough and efficient education to every student. Eight school districts joined the lawsuit as intervenors.
Association President Kimberly Amen lauded the court’s careful consideration of the case in a statement Thursday. 
“The Court found that model salaries did not reflect the true costs of recruiting and retaining qualified teachers, which in turn created disparities among school districts,” Amen’s statement read. “For years, educators and school districts have told policymakers that Wyoming cannot provide the education our students deserve without the people who make that education possible.”
Rep. Scott Heiner, a Sweetwater County Republican and co-chair of the Wyoming Legislature’s Select Committee on School Finance Recalibration, was also pleased with the ruling but for different reasons. The court overturned the district court’s spending requirements for technology, nutrition and law enforcement in schools. 
“They’re not elements of proper education in the state of Wyoming,” Heiner said Thursday. 

Rep. Scott Heiner, R-Green River, during the first meeting of the House Special Investigative Committee on Thursday, Feb. 26, 2026, at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

Heiner, who also served as the House majority floor leader during the 2026 session, said the ruling validates the K-12 school funding recalibration bill that lawmakers passed this year overhauling how the state funds schools. This ruling means no additional funding would be required, Heiner said, referring to ongoing efforts to fund technology, nutrition and school resource officers. The 2026 school funding bill became law without Republican Gov. Mark Gordon’s signature because the governor said it disadvantaged smaller districts, usurped local authority and failed to address essential operational funding needs.
But like Heiner, the governor praised the high court’s ruling. Gordon lauded the decision as providing communities with flexibility to determine how to best serve their students. Different districts have different needs, and mandating spending is not a guarantee for better results, he said in a Thursday statement. 
“Funding is a means to an end; that end should be a Wyoming student who graduates prepared for further education, meaningful work, military service, and productive life in his or her community,” the governor’s statement read. Gordon also emphasized the need for a school finance model that is durable and does not require continual adjustment.
Heiner represents portions of Lincoln, Sweetwater and Uinta counties, which are home to four of the eight school districts that joined the lawsuit as plaintiffs. Sen. Evie Brennan, a Cheyenne Republican, also served on the School Finance Recalibration Committee and represents Laramie County, which also has a school district that joined the lawsuit. 
Although the Supreme Court struck down some elements that the recalibration committee was working on, Brennan said the research already done regarding technology, nutrition and school safety remains beneficial to understanding the needs of Wyoming schools. Not having a court mandate specific to spending on those programs could allow for more flexible solutions, Brennan said Thursday. 
“My hope is that we can move forward with some legislation that can help fund them, but that not so much of it needs to be done a certain way,” she said.

Steve Harshman speaks on Thursday, July 16, 2026, during a forum for candidates for the Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction at the Albany County Public Library in Laramie. (Molly Walters for WyoFile)

Rep. Steve Harshman, R-Casper, who’s the Republican nominee for state superintendent of public instruction, called the ruling a reasonable outcome for both sides, even though neither received everything it sought. 
Plus, he’s grateful the court provided clear guidance on how the Legislature should approach school funding in the next session. A high school coach, Harshman has served as House District 37 representative since 2003, including two terms as speaker of the House. If elected state superintendent, his job would be to lobby the Legislature for good policy, and ensure it is implemented, he said.
“I think the conversation is going to continue on food service. I think the conversation is going to continue on [school resource officers],” he said. “So those will be ongoing conversations.”
The ruling
The Wyoming Constitution requires the Legislature to provide a thorough and efficient education to every student in elementary and secondary school. But funding public education through local property taxes has led to disparities based on property values. 
“Efforts to purge the wealth-based disparities began in 1971 and focused on funding schools from statewide wealth to give all students, regardless of whether they lived in wealthier or poorer districts, an equal opportunity for a proper education,” Chief Justice Lynne Boomgaarden wrote in the majority opinion. 
Wyoming Supreme Court Chief Justice Lynne J. Boomgaarden delivers her State of the Judiciary address Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, at the Capitol. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
In the latest round of legal wrangling over whether the state has been meeting its constitutional obligations and correcting such disparities, Laramie County District Court Judge Peter Froelicher ruled in 2025 that the state had fallen short. Froelicher found that the Legislature had failed to adjust for inflation and to properly fund teacher and staff salaries, mental health counselors, school safety resource officers, nutritional programs and computers for students. Lawmakers also had not properly assessed school buildings, allowing inadequate facilities to remain in use for too long, he ruled. 
The high court agreed with Froelicher on salaries and inflation.
“The district court correctly ruled that the legislature failed to maintain a constitutional system for financing public school operations because it did not fund teacher salaries or make inflation adjustments to the [legislative model] at levels approximating the true costs of education,” the ruling states. The court found that the Wyoming Legislature’s approach to funding created a disparity among school districts that violated “students’ fundamental right to an adequate public school education.”
But the ruling reversed the district court’s requirement that the Legislature fund one-to-one technology, nutrition programs and school resource officer programs. 
“Applying our precedent, the record does not demonstrate that the failure to fund nutrition and school resource officer programs resulted in constitutional injury,” the ruling states. 
Teton County Sheriff’s Office School Resource Officer Andrew Roundy lets Jackson Hole High School seniors back into school during the lunch hour in March 2018. As a resource officer, Roundy was present at the school whenever students were in the building, as well as during special local events. (Ryan Dorgan/Jackson Hole News&Guide)
Although some of the plaintiffs’ arguments fell short in court, the education association said that more evidence could be presented in the future. 
“Although this was the Court’s holding for now, the Court also recognized that additional evidence or further developments could subsequently result in a finding that Wyoming must fund such important costs,” Amen’s statement read.
The Supreme Court also said the district court erred by ordering the state to conduct a statewide assessment of school facilities for educational suitability. “The administrative process adopted by the School Facilities Commission provides an acceptable means to identify and address concerns with the educational suitability of a school building,” the ruling states. 
The state did not appeal the district court’s requirement to fund elementary school mental health counselors. 
Justice Kari Gray  wrote a minority opinion, joined by Natrona County District Judge Joshua Eames, concurring in part and dissenting in part with the majority ruling backed by three justices. 
“I would reverse the district court’s decision in its entirety,” Gray wrote.
School officials were still processing the 74-page ruling. 
“We’re still in the process of reviewing the decision. So, at this point, we just feel like it’s premature to comment,” said Mary Quast, community relations director for Laramie County School District 1, the state’s largest K-12 district and a plaintiff in the case.
The post Supreme Court finds Wyoming must spend more on teachers, strikes down other funding demands appeared first on WyoFile .

name: VTDigger
title: Jason Eaton tries to fire his attorneys midway through his attempted murder trial
description:
The judge denied his motion, and a prosecution expert testified Thursday that Eaton was not legally insane at the time he is accused of shooting three Palestinian college students in Burlington.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Jason Eaton tries to fire his attorneys midway through his attempted murder trial.
text:
Jason Eaton attends his trial on charges of attempted second-degree murder in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, September 17, 2026. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe

BURLINGTON — A Burlington man accused of shooting and wounding three Palestinian college students told a judge midway through his trial that he wanted to fire his attorneys, contending that his lawyers failed to properly question witnesses and present evidence.
Jason Eaton’s request Thursday morning proved unsuccessful as Judge John Pacht rejected his bid to represent himself. 
“I vigorously object to your denial,” Eaton said to the judge after the ruling.  
The fourth day of Eaton’s trial continued in Chittenden Superior criminal court with a prosecution psychiatric expert rebutting the testimony of a defense expert a day earlier who said he found Eaton legally insane at the time of the shootings on Nov. 25, 2023.
Eaton, 51, faces three counts of attempted second-degree murder. He is accused of opening fire on the three students, who had been visiting Burlington for the Thanksgiving holiday, while they were out for a walk on North Prospect Street.  
Eaton, in a recording played in court Wednesday, said he had been hearing voices through his FM radio and had been directed by government intelligence agencies, including the CIA, to carry out the shootings. 
The court day started Thursday with Eaton, before the jurors entered the room, rising up and standing at the defense table. He said to the judge that his attorneys had been ineffective in trying to press his insanity defense.
“There are records that could be submitted,” Eaton said to Pacht, adding that the testimony and evidence in his trial so far “didn’t come out as a coherent mental health history.”
Eaton, represented by two lawyers assigned to him as public defenders, has tried unsuccessfully prior to the trial to seek new counsel.  
Pacht told Eaton that he had not presented enough information to warrant removing his attorneys from his case.
“We’re in the middle of a trial,” the judge said to Eaton, adding, “It’s awkward for the court to deal with this.”
Eaton repeatedly tried to engage in dialogue with the judge throughout Thursday, with Pacht rejecting many of the issues Eaton raised. 
At one point, when the judge appeared to agree with him, Eaton sat back and clapped his hands in an apparent round of applause for himself.
Dr. Jhilam Biswas, a forensic psychiatrist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston and the state’s expert, told jurors Thursday afternoon that in her opinion Eaton did not suffer a mental disease or defect needed to meet the legal standard for insanity in Vermont.
Biswas, under questioning from Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, said that although Eaton did meet the criteria for personality disorder, he did not suffer from a psychotic disorder.
The psychiatrist said she based her opinion on several factors, including a review of medical and court records as well as a three and half hour interview she conducted with him this summer. 
Biswas described Eaton in the days leading up to the shooting as overwhelmed with stress and anxiety, having recently lost his job and in jeopardy of losing his apartment in Burlington.
Biswas testified that Eaton had long struggled with maintaining employment as well as housing and relationships. 
In the past, Biswas added, Eaton has lost jobs after getting in arguments with his bosses. She said in her opinion that he starts to believe he knows more than his employers about what needs to be done, leading to disputes at the workplace and eventually costing him his employment.
Biswas testified that for five days prior to the shooting Eaton had been staying with his mother in Addison County and that his mother said it was the best the two had gotten along.
“She did not notice anything that was odd, except that he was very nice to her,” Biswas told jurors Eaton’s mother had said in an interview. 
Eaton’s mother drove him back to his Burlington apartment on the day of the shootings, and Eaton reported that he began smoking marijuana and tobacco as well as drinking alcohol, Biswas told jurors. 

Dr. Jhilam Biswas, a forensic psychiatrist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, testifies as the state’s expert witness during the trial of Jason Eaton in Chittenden Superior criminal court in Burlington on Thursday, September 17, 2026. Pool photo by Paul Heintz/Boston Globe

Biswas described Eaton as then having cannabis-induced paranoia, combined with the high levels of stress and anxiety he had already been experiencing. 
She said when a person like Eaton with “narcissistic-type personality traits” is walked out of a job it can overwhelm the person. “So that was playing a role in that moment along with using those substances,” Biswas said.
About an hour or two before the shootings, Biswas testified, Eaton reported hearing voices and a mix of messages through his radio from either the CIA, Israel’s Mossad or God.
“That’s when he got messages to go out and shoot,” Biswas said.
Margaret Jansch, an attorney for Eaton, on cross-examination raised Biswas’ limited experience testifying in court in insanity defense cases. “You never testified in Vermont on the issue of criminal responsibility in an insanity defense case?” Jansch asked. 
Biswas said that was correct. 
Also, the defense attorney pressed Biswas on Eaton’s marijuana use on the day of the shootings. Jansch said Eaton had reported that day he was out of marijuana and “scraped together a couple of roaches” to mix with tobacco to smoke. 
“You can have a paranoid experience on marijuana,” Biswas said, adding that Eaton was also under a great deal of stress and anxiety. 
The three men Eaton is accused of shooting — Hisham Awartani, Kinnan Abdalhamid and Tahseen Aliahmad — were all treated at hospitals. Awartani’s lower body remains paralyzed. 
In earlier trial testimony, forensic witnesses linked a handgun seized from Eaton’s apartment a day after the shootings to casings found at the shooting scene. 
Jury deliberations could begin as early as Friday after the close of testimony.

title: ICE agent in Jan. 14 Minneapolis shooting makes first appearance in Minnesota state court
description: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro, who is accused of unjustifiably shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the closed door of a north Minneapolis home in January, made his first appearance in Hennepin County District Court Thursday. Minnesota prosecutors fought for months to get Castro into court, unsuccessfully suing Texas Gov.[...]
text:
Christian Castro, an ICE agent charged with shooting and injuring Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis and then lying about the circumstances surrounding the shooting, stands for his first hearing Thursday, September 17, 2026. (Court sketch by Cedric Hohnstadt) U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro, who is accused of unjustifiably shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the closed door of a north Minneapolis home in January, made his first appearance in Hennepin County District Court Thursday.
Minnesota prosecutors fought for months to get Castro into court, unsuccessfully suing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott for blocking Castro’s extradition from Texas to Minnesota.
This week marks eight months into a winding saga that began on Jan. 14 and has involved four legal cases, including federal charges against the shooting victim and his roommate that were later dropped after prosecutors discovered Castro had lied about the incident; the extradition battle between Texas and Minnesota; and federal charges against Castro, who will make a federal court appearance Friday.
ICE agent Christian Castro turns himself in on federal charges

Hennepin County District Judge Paul R. Scoggin set bail at $200,000 if Castro agrees to not possess firearms, not contact witnesses and to be electronically monitored. Scoggin set unconditional bail at $400,000.
Castro also signed a waiver of extradition — an agreement to be extradited without a formal hearing in the future — and agreed to surrender his passport to state authorities immediately if he gets it back from federal authorities, who took his passport under federal legal proceedings happening simultaneously.
Castro appeared behind a glass partition in an orange uniform and handcuffs, his brows occasionally furrowed as he listened. He said only two words, after Scoggin asked him if he understood the requirement to surrender his passport: “100% sir.”
Minnesota prosecutors have said that Castro made 394 jail calls to a woman in Mexico, during which he expressed his intention to marry her and buy a house in Mexico to retire. County prosecutor Joshua Larson had asked for higher bail amounts at $350,000 and $500,000 respectively. He argued that Castro was a flight risk, citing the difficulty of extraditing Castro from Texas and Castro’s phone calls to the woman in Mexico.
Larson also said that Castro failed to turn himself into Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension headquarters as promised Wednesday, leading to BCA agents arresting Castro on the street in downtown Minneapolis.
“This did not strike me as an indication that this defendant is a man of follow-through,” Larson said.
Daniel Gerdts, Castro’s lawyer, offered a contradicting narrative: The BCA had agreed to take Castro into custody at Gerdts’ office but instead arrested Castro as he and his wife were looking for a place to park. After the court appearance, Gerdts said that the BCA’s arrest seemed like “political theater.”
Gerdts advocated for a $50,000 bail, arguing that Castro would have fled already if he wanted to, and that Castro would struggle to make a $200,000 bail. Gerdts also claimed that Castro, despite refusing to consent to extradition for 90 days, was “disappointed” in his then-legal counsel when he was in jail and would have preferred to be extradited to Minnesota than spend “all that time in jail” in Texas.
Confusion and misinformation surrounding the facts of what happened have plagued the case since it began.
On Jan. 14, during the peak of Operation Metro Surge, Castro engaged in a car chase with Sosa-Celis’s roommate, Alfredo Aljorna, ending at Sosa-Celis’s and Aljorna’s home in north Minneapolis. Castro and his fellow ICE agent had mistaken Aljorna for another Latino man, according to an FBI affidavit. Aljorna exited his car and slipped as he tried to get inside his house, at which point Castro attempted to arrest Aljorna. Sosa-Celis tried to help Aljorna, leading to an 11-second scuffle between the three. After both men escaped and ran inside, Castro’s shot passed through the front door and hit Sosa-Celis in the leg before coming to a stop in the wall of a child’s bedroom.
In an interview with FBI agents, Castro accused Sosa-Celis and Aljorna of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel in a three-minute fight before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.
The shooting took place between the Jan. 7 killing of Renee Good and the Jan. 24 killing of Alex Pretti by federal agents, both of which had ample witnesses and bystander footage. The details of the north Minneapolis shooting were far more shrouded, until aspects of that night were revealed over the course of several months.
In May, Minnesota prosecutors charged Castro with four counts of second-degree assault as well as one count of falsely reporting a crime, setting off the extradition battle in which Abbott declined to sign off on, and Castro was released from a Texas jail.
Castro finally turned himself in to federal authorities in early September after a federal grand jury indicted him with six charges of making false statements related to the shooting, stemming from six specific lies he told FBI investigators after the shooting. An assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota had been pursuing hefty civil rights charges against Castro, but was instructed by Justice Department officials in Washington, D.C. to downgrade the charges. The attorney, Matthew Evans, was fired, CBS News reported, citing four unnamed sources familiar with the matter.
Castro appeared in a federal court in Texas, and is set to appear in federal district court in St. Paul Friday morning. He drove up from Texas this week.
With Castro finally in state custody and having signed the waiver of extradition, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said Thursday that his office has dropped the lawsuit against Abbott.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Lawmakers mull cybersecurity concerns as they prepare for overhaul of Georgia’s voting system
description: Georgia seems poised to switch to a hand-marked paper ballot system for the 2028 election, but researchers and cybersecurity experts say there is a lot more to consider to ensure that voting stays secure and free from undue influence. Election security concerns have long been at the forefront of the conversation around election equipment. Georgia’s […]
text:
Members of Georgia's Election Equipment Specifications and Standards Committee are working to develop the guidelines that state lawmakers will use when selecting their next statewide voting system.. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderGeorgia seems poised to switch to a hand-marked paper ballot system for the 2028 election, but researchers and cybersecurity experts say there is a lot more to consider to ensure that voting stays secure and free from undue influence.
Election security concerns have long been at the forefront of the conversation around election equipment. Georgia’s current voting machines, which use a QR code to tally votes, have repeatedly faced criticism from advocates of hand-marked paper ballots, who say that ballots should be counted based on text that can be deciphered by humans. 
State lawmakers have passed legislation to phase out the use of QR codes on ballots, but are still developing the guidelines that state lawmakers will use when selecting their next statewide voting system.
Sen. Max Burns, a Sylvania Republican who is co-chairing a special committee tasked with helping select Georgia’s next statewide election system, said he is hoping to land on a system that is as secure as possible, while maintaining the convenience that he said Georgia voters have come to expect.
“100% [security] is a goal,” he said. “We have to get as close to that as we can, and then we have to build other processes and mitigation opportunities around it to ensure that we address any potential challenges that we find.”
At a Thursday meeting at the state Capitol in Atlanta, cybersecurity experts and researchers gathered to share their insights with members of the legislative panel. Here are some of the election security issues state lawmakers will have to consider.
Equipment maintenance
Georgia’s current ballot-marking devices were purchased under a 10-year contract, and used statewide in Georgia for the first time in 2020. More than half a decade later the machines are still in use, but experts say the lack of software upgrades has left vulnerabilities in the system. 
Lawmakers weigh seismic changes to Georgia’s voting equipment

Whichever system the state turns to next, state leaders say, will likely be in use for at least the next decade. However, Geoff Hale, a fellow at the nonpartisan Washington-based Center for Democracy and Technology, said technology and cybersecurity risks often evolve much more quickly, meaning that Georgia’s voting equipment will likely need to be updated several times over the course of its lifespan.
“Georgia is not purchasing something that will remain permanently secure,” Hale said. “Election security is a process and not a purchase.”
In addition to picking equipment that meets Georgia’s current specifications, Michael Barnes, the deputy director of information technology for voting systems for the secretary of state’s office, said lawmakers should ensure that the vendor they select has a plan to continue providing support, technology updates and spare parts for however long the state plans to keep using the system.
“What is the vendor providing, and what is their plan for providing that, not only for the initial deployment, but for five, 10, 15 years down the road?” he said.
Voter secrecy
The question of how to ensure that a voter’s selections remain private is another issue lawmakers will have to juggle. 
Georgia’s constitution mandates that voters’ ballots be kept secret. However, rapid developments in artificial intelligence and other technology can make that harder to guarantee, especially in smaller counties. Last month, a Princeton University researcher claimed that he was able to use AI to tie thousands of voters in Heard and Cherokee counties to specific ballots with relative certainty by putting publicly available data through an AI tool.
The intersection of privacy and accessibility is another challenge. Precincts are required to keep at least one voting machine on hand for voters with disabilities according to federal law. But in jurisdictions where most voters mark ballots by hand, it may be fairly easy to determine how voters who used accessibility software voted.
Verified Voting policy and strategy director Mark Lindeman addressed the committee on Sept. 17, 2026. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
Mark Lindeman, Philadelphia-based Verified Voting’s policy and strategy director, said that while he supported minimizing the role of ballot-marking devices in Georgia’s elections, there shouldn’t be restrictions on who gets to use the machines. 
He noted that many voters who don’t consider themselves disabled may benefit from using a machine-marked system. A larger pool of people casting ballots marked by voting machines will also give voters with disabilities an increased level of anonymity when casting their ballot.
“It doesn’t have to be hundreds in a polling place, but to protect voter privacy and dignity, it shouldn’t be just a handful,” he said.
Foreign interference
Federal cuts to election security systems and a recent spike in cyberattacks may also fuel the risk of foreign interference in the midterm elections. Already this year, several Georgia counties have been hit by cyber attacks targeting their water systems. States like Minnesota, Michigan and Wisconsin have also faced similar attacks, according to the FBI. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency put out an advisory in April warning that such attacks may be linked to Iran.
Expert says Georgia water system attack highlights critical security deficiencies

But experts say it’s impossible to implement a system that completely eliminates the risk of bad actors interfering with elections. According to Michael Specter, an assistant professor and cybersecurity researcher at Georgia Tech, the most secure systems assume that a breach will happen at some point and develop transparent protocols to disclose and adapt to such instances.
“A system is only secure if the adversary knows how the system works and it is still secure,” he said.
Switching to hand-marked ballots may lessen the risk of certain security breaches, but experts emphasized that no technology is impervious to manipulation.
“Ballot on demand [printing] does not remove software from the election entirely,” said Hale, the Center for Democracy and Technology fellow. “Instead, it changes where software sits in the process.”
Paulding County Elections Director Deirdre Holden said that she worries about bad actors trying to access voter data, but added that in her experience, state officials had been quick to respond in instances where counties had faced cyberattacks.
“We have a very, very robust state system that takes care of us that knows when things like that are going on and they alert us very quickly,” she said.

title: Growing revenue in airport assistance fund leads South Dakota commission to loosen spending policies
description: A South Dakota fund for airport projects is growing faster than the state Aeronautics Commission is spending it, which led the commission to approve two policy changes Thursday.  “We have this money. Let’s spend it on aviation,” said Chairman Robert Huggins, a pilot and retired air traffic controller from Sioux Falls. One change will raise […]
text:
A rendering of a Sioux Falls Regional Airport expansion project. (Courtesy of Sioux Falls Regional Airport/South Dakota Aeronautics Commission)A South Dakota fund for airport projects is growing faster than the state Aeronautics Commission is spending it, which led the commission to approve two policy changes Thursday. 
“We have this money. Let’s spend it on aviation,” said Chairman Robert Huggins, a pilot and retired air traffic controller from Sioux Falls.
One change will raise a cap on state Aeronautics Fund assistance for projects at smaller airports. The other change will make more state assistance available to ongoing expansion projects at the Sioux Falls and Rapid City airports. It replaces the existing maximum assistance for those projects with a formula tied to the size of terminal projects. The Sioux Falls and Rapid City projects are each expected to cost more than $100 million, with a mix of funding from federal, state and local sources.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Department of Transportation officials told the commission the Aeronautics Fund is at a record balance of nearly $20 million and was projected, without Thursday’s changes, to reach nearly $30 million by fiscal year 2032.
The fund receives revenue from aviation-related taxes and fees, including aircraft fuel taxes, aircraft registration fees and taxes on aircraft sales. Aircraft sales generated $5.8 million in fiscal year 2025 and about $3.3 million in fiscal year 2026, while fuel taxes have produced about $1 million annually in recent years, according to Transportation Secretary Joel Jundt. 
Jundt said revenues are outpacing expenditures by roughly 2-to-1, making it hard to justify continuing to grow the fund balance while airport projects need funding. He said lawmakers could choose to redirect unspent money to another purpose, and changing commission policies to spend more of the money would demonstrate to lawmakers that the commission is using the fund for its intended purposes.
The Department of Transportation later told South Dakota Searchlight that the changes do not need legislative approval.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho minister found guilty of trespassing at a protest of anti-trans bills to serve no jail time
description: An Idaho judge on Thursday ordered a Boise minister who was found guilty of misdemeanor trespass during a political protest to pay $357 in fines — but not serve more jail time.  The Rev. Sara LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, and eight others who were protesting bills restricting transgender rights were […]
text:
Trans advocate Nikson Mathews, center, listens to an Idaho State Police trooper moments before he and the Rev. Sara LaWall, right, were arrested in Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s office on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
An Idaho judge on Thursday ordered a Boise minister who was found guilty of misdemeanor trespass during a political protest to pay $357 in fines — but not serve more jail time. 
The Rev. Sara LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, and eight others who were protesting bills restricting transgender rights were arrested this spring after refusing to leave the lobby to the office of Idaho Gov. Brad Little, whom the protestors said they were hoping to meet with. LaWall’s defense attorney cast her actions during the protest as an act of civil disobedience, an act that involves intentionally breaking laws for moral reasons. 
In a statement before the judge delivered his sentence, LaWall, who has a transgender daughter, said she had repeatedly attempted to relay her concerns over anti-trans bills with elected officials. 
“We followed every available path of redress (grievenances) within our system. Our fears and concerns, and frankly, our begging and pleading, went unheard and unanswered,” LaWall said, citing legislators cutting off testimony early on an anti-trans bill where doctors planned to testify.
She said she understands her actions have consequences, and she said she accepts full responsibility for her actions.
“I do not take this lightly,” LaWall said. “I knew the risks when I chose to stay. But I was willing then and am willing now to accept the risks as an act of faithful witness and solidarity with my daughter, all the beautiful trans youth, and the incredible trans community here in Idaho. Many of whom I am blessed to call my friends and chosen family — all of whom must negotiate risk and their own safety every day, just by being who they are.”
Before issuing the sentence, Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball said he was weighing several factors — such as protecting society and deterring LaWall and others from violating the law. But he said he didn’t find probation necessary in this case.
“It’s my hope that you will be heard the way you wish, and that if you are not, that you do not break the law to be heard. But I don’t find that placing you on probation is necessary to achieve that end,” the judge said.
“Your conduct, whatever it may have been, waiting for an appointment, a protest, was peaceful, was considerate,” he added.
The judge’s sentence for LaWall was for the state’s recommended minimum $500 in fines, plus $170 in court costs, which the judge tacked on after the case went to a jury trial and one day in jail for which he granted LaWall credit. The judge also granted LaWall credit toward her fees for her $300 cash bail. 
The Rev. Sara LaWall drops hearts down the rotunda of the Idaho State Capitol Building. Protestors on April 2, 2024, dropped 48,000 handmade hearts — meant to represent LGBTQ Idahoans — in protest of anti-LGBTQ legislation. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Why she was protesting in the Idaho governor’s office

Earlier this month, LaWall was found guilty by a jury of the misdemeanor trespassing charge after hearing testimony from three people and being presented body camera footage from the Idaho State Police trooper who warned her to leave several times before arresting her. 
At her trial, the minister waived her right to remain silent, but did not speak to why she was at the protest. The judge had said he had restricted trial testimony related to the reason for the protest.
Beginning around 2 p.m., the protest was staged for several hours in the lobby of the governor’s office late the day on April 1 after he signed into law the transgender bathroom ban. At the time, the governor was waiting to weigh in on a bill that requires teachers and doctors to out transgender minors to their parents, or face lawsuits. The governor later signed the bill.

That day, LaWall didn’t know that the governor had been escorted out of work at 3:30 p.m. out of public sight, according to LaWall’s defense attorney, Katelyn Enterkine. The Legislature was still meeting by 8 p.m. that day. The governor’s office could not be immediately reached for comment. 
LaWall has said the jail sentence she could have received for trespassing was less than the amount Idaho judges can dole out for violations of Idaho’s new criminal transgender bathroom ban, which allows for up to one year sentences on first offenses.
LaWall’s is the first of four trespassing cases headed to trial stemming from the protest, where nine protestors were arrested.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Report: Federal judge says rule of law was threatened during Operation Metro Surge
description: A federal judge who issued several critical rulings of the Trump administration during Operation Metro Surge last winter told The New York Times in a rare interview that the federal government’s actions during the crackdown “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” The New York Times spoke to Judge Patrick J. Schiltz and […]
text:
Diana E. Murphy federal courthouse is shown in Minneapolis Friday, May 17, 2024. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A federal judge who issued several critical rulings of the Trump administration during Operation Metro Surge last winter told The New York Times in a rare interview that the federal government’s actions during the crackdown “created a grave threat to the rule of law.”
The New York Times spoke to Judge Patrick J. Schiltz and six other members of Minnesota’s federal bench about the immigration sweeps that flooded the court with over 1,000 habeas corpus petitions and led to tensions between the U.S. Department of Justice and federal judges who are typically “partners” in the criminal justice system, Schiltz said.
Schiltz is a noted figure in conservative legal circles and clerked for the late U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia.
In February, Schiltz threatened to hold Trump administration officials in contempt for violating court orders numerous times at the height of their mass deportation efforts. Immigration and Customs Enforcement had violated nearly 100 orders issued by Minnesota’s Federal District Court, the New York Times reported.
“I would say aloud to myself, ‘This just never happens,’” he said, referring to the orders.
The federal judges described to the Times a chaotic environment where the number of cases ramped up as more people challenged their detention in court. The judges described being constantly near their devices in case they missed a petition.
“The cost of me enjoying a movie could be somebody waking up in New Mexico the next day when they shouldn’t have,” Schiltz told the Times.
Career prosecutors in the Justice Department resigned over how the Trump administration handled the investigations into the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
Schiltz also quashed broad U.S. Department of Justice subpoenas issued to the offices of Gov. Tim Walz, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey and other elected officials, in stark language: “Initiating a criminal investigation in order to harass political opponents or to coerce them into taking official action — particularly official action that the federal government cannot directly require those political opponents to take — is a blatantly unlawful and unethical use of the grand-jury process.”
The judges dealt with violent threats. After high-profile rulings, the phones in judges’ chambers would continuously ring, and clerks logged hundreds of messages each day. One judge showed the Times an anonymous email: “kill u soon,” it read.
In response to the interviews, a Department of Justice spokesperson said it was “remarkable that sitting federal judges are giving on-the-record interviews” criticizing the administration and suggested that they recuse themselves on pending cases.
The spokesperson said the administration “will continue to fully comply with court orders.”

title: Iowa advocates call for attention on proposed income tax constitutional amendment
description: Advocates speaking for and against a proposed state constitutional amendment held events Thursday calling for more attention on the ballot measure, which would set a higher bar for state lawmakers to raise the income tax in future sessions. Iowa Republicans held a news conference Thursday in Grimes, where multiple speakers said they supported the measure, […[...]
text:
Rep. Dan Gehlbach, R-Urbandale, called for Iowans to support a constitutional amendment that would require two-thirds of state lawmakers to approve future income tax increases at a news conference in Grimes Sep. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Advocates speaking for and against a proposed state constitutional amendment held events Thursday calling for more attention on the ballot measure, which would set a higher bar for state lawmakers to raise the income tax in future sessions.
Iowa Republicans held a news conference Thursday in Grimes, where multiple speakers said they supported the measure, arguing it would serve as a needed protection for taxpayers. The amendment, which would be added to the Iowa State Constitution if approved by voters, would require a supermajority — two-thirds — of state lawmakers to approve increases to the state’s personal income or corporate tax rate in order for these tax changes to pass.
The Iowa Legislature had to approve the measure in two consecutive general assemblies to place it on the Nov. 3 ballot. At the news conference, Rep. Dan Gehlbach, R-Urbandale, said when the amendment language was discussed in 2024 and 2026, he and every Republican in attendance voted in favor of the measure, while Democratsin attendance voted against it.
“It strikes me as just common sense that if politicians want to raise our taxes, there should be wide consensus, not narrow support,” Gehlbach said. “So you’d think this would garner wide bipartisan support, but think again.”
Eric Klein, a Clive businessman who also spoke at the event, said he was in support of the proposed constitutional amendment “because I believe that Iowa families and taxpayers don’t need to worry about a future tax hike.”
“This common sense amendment to our state constitution ensures that politicians cannot indiscriminately raise taxes, because Iowa taxpayers deserve to keep more of what they earn,” Klein said.
But opponents of the measure said it will not prevent Iowans from facing increased taxes — it will only limit which taxes can be raised if the state is seeking more revenue. Anne Discher of Common Good Iowa said the goal of the amendment was to “lock in” conservative tax policies enacted in the past decade by a GOP-controlled Legislature, even if future lawmakers want to make changes.
Previously, Iowa had a “progressive” income tax system, in which higher earners paid a larger percentage of their income in tax than lower earners, Discher said, speaking Thursday at an online “Lunch & Learn” event hosted by the Iowa Farmers Union. When Iowa Republicans made tax cuts in recent sessions, they transitioned the tax system to a “flat” income tax rate, where all taxed entities pay the same percentage of their income, no matter how much they are earning.
“What happens when you do that is you give the biggest breaks to the richest folks and the most profitable corporations,” Discher said.
When the measure was discussed in previous legislative sessions, Democrats argued the proposed constitutional amendment would restrict future lawmakers from making changes to Iowa’s income tax system as a means to address a state budget crisis.
Discher said this would mean other forms of taxes would likely be raised — taxes she said would have a larger impact on low- and middle-income families.
“To be clear, they’re keeping a simple majority (approval to pass) in place for every other tax,” Discher said. “I think the most obvious, the most notable one is the sales tax, because that is the other major source of revenue for the state budget. But I will note, it would still only take a majority to raise the fuel tax to raise vehicle registration taxes to raise court fees and fines. It would take a simple majority of the Legislature to cut state aid to balance the budget and pass costs long in the form of college tuition.”
Republicans and supporters of the state constitutional amendment also criticized state Rep. Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, for voting against the amendment language in 2024.
“Josh Turek voted to make it easier for politicians to raise taxes on hardworking Iowans, and that’s just a preview of what he would do in the U.S. Senate,” Gehlbach said.
In order to amend the constitution, a simple majority of voters must approve the language in the November election. If the income tax amendment is not approved, there would be no other changes to the rules Iowa lawmakers must follow to increase income taxes. The current requirement for a majority of state legislators to approve changes would remain in place.
Turek is running against Republican Ashley Hinson in the November election.
A spokesperson for Turek’s campaign said during his time in the Iowa House, Turek “has repeatedly worked with Republicans to cut taxes for Iowans, lowering income and property taxes,” while Hinson “voted to cut health care for 110,000 Iowans just to give a tax break to her … billionaire donors,” referencing her support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that made cuts to Medicaid funding.
Other speakers at the GOP event Thursday argued Turek would reverse other portions of the OBBB Act, like cutting taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security. Turek said in August he agreed with President Donald Trump that “we should have no tax on tips and overtime” and said he would support keeping some portions of the law in place.
