name: Mississippi Today
title: UM Chancellor Glenn Boyce defends firing employee over social media post
description: Chancellor of the University of Mississippi Glenn Boyce, center, speaks during a Institutions of Higher Learning meeting Thursday, Jan. 16, 2020.
text:
In a Wednesday court filing, University of Mississippi Chancellor Glenn Boyce continued to defend his firing of former university employee Lauren Stokes over a social media post she made following the death of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk.

This is the latest legal development in Stokes’ First Amendment lawsuit that she filed against Boyce in October in response to her firing. U.S. District Judge Glen Davidson dismissed the lawsuit in March on the grounds that Stokes’ failed to make a plausible First Amendment violation claim.
Following the dismissal, Stokes filed an appeal in the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing that Davidson had improperly dismissed her lawsuit.
In his response, Boyce argues that Stokes’ complaint fails to allege a violation, that the chancellor is entitled to qualified immunity and the district court was correct in its dismissal of the lawsuit.
“She failed to plausibly allege that her interest in speaking on social media outweighed the University’s interest in promoting efficiency in the workplace.” Boyce’s filing states.
Boyce argues that the attention drawn to the university and the “disruption to the University’s operations” only stopped after Stokes was fired and he, as chancellor, issued an apology statement.
Read more: Former Ole Miss employee contends in appeal of dismissed lawsuit that Chancellor Glenn Boyce caved to hecklers
Boyce’s lawyers stated that the chancellor testified “he did not terminate Stoke’s employment based on his personal opinion about the viewpoint expressed in her Instagram post,” but he fired her due to the disruption and impact that it had on the university’s operation and reputation.
The filings also argue that Boyce has qualified immunity in his personal capacity. The filing largely mentions the Pickering test, a legal standard that courts use to determine whether the law was clear enough that a reasonable official would have known what they were doing was illegal.
“Even if Stokes could state a plausible First Amendment claim, the qualified immunity defense prevents pursuit of that claim against the Chancellor in his individual capacity,” Boyce’s response states.
On July 23, University of Mississippi faculty members J.T. Thomas, Wendy Goldberg and Graham Pitts, along with a freedom of speech organization, filed amicus briefings, or “friend of the court” briefings, in support of Stokes.
Next, Davidson will determine whether an oral argument is necessary. Stokes’ lawyers requested one, while Boyce’s said it was not necessary.
Stokes served as the executive assistant for Charlotte Parks, UM vice chancellor for development. Following Kirk’s death, Stokes reposted a social media comment critical of Kirk’s activism to her private Instagram account. By the next morning, Stokes was terminated from her position and the university released a statement condemning Stokes’ actions.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas reports fewer failing schools and school districts in 2025-2026
description: The percentage of Arkansas schools and districts receiving failing or low grades from the state for their performance has decreased, according to data released by the state Department of Education Thursday. Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and education officials touted the numbers as validation for her signature 2023 education law, the LEARNS Act. Educa[...]
text:
From left: Arkansas Education Secretary Jacob Oliva and Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders tout the improvements in public school students' test scores at a press conference at the Arkansas Capitol on June 18, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)The percentage of Arkansas schools and districts receiving failing or low grades from the state for their performance has decreased, according to data released by the state Department of Education Thursday.
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and education officials touted the numbers as validation for her signature 2023 education law, the LEARNS Act. Education Secretary Jacob Oliva told reporters Thursday that “the improvements that we’ve made by building out this blueprint and this system are showing more students are performing at or above grade-level.”
Arkansas public and charter schools are assigned an A-F ranking by the education department, based on Arkansas Teaching, Learning & Assessment System standardized testing scores, individualized growth targets for students and, for high schools, post-graduation readiness. 
Arkansas schools evaluated under new accountability system 

The percentage of schools receiving a D or F during the 2025-2026 academic year decreased, according to data released Thursday. One hundred and nine schools that previously received a D or F improved to at least a C in 2025-2026. 
Schools receiving a B saw the largest increase, with 350 receiving the ranking, 58 more than the previous year. 
However, 80 schools lost ground. Of the 613 schools that scored a B or C last year, 68 scored a D or an F this year, and 12 of last year’s D schools received an F this year. The majority of those 80 schools were given C grades last year.
Schools that received an A grade last year mostly maintained high grades this year, though nearly a third of them fell from an A to a B. Schools that received a B saw similar patterns. While 39 schools improved from a B to an A, 79 fell to a C grade. 
School district grades showed similar results. Seven of the 11 districts that scored an F last year were given at least a C this year — though the remaining districts did not improve. However, 11 districts that receivved a B or C saw their grades fall to a D or an F. 
In all, nearly 45% of Arkansas’ 1,047 schools neither improved or worsened. At the district level, 58.5% of the state’s 258 districts neither improved or worsened.
Oliva said struggling districts that took advantage of the support offered to them for improvement saw the biggest gains. 
“Every D and F school got assigned a literacy coach. Every D and F school had access to high-impact tutoring,” Oliva said. “Whenever we focus on students’ needs, those schools saw outstanding increases in achievement and learning gains.”
Oliva pointed to the North Little Rock, Crossett, and Fordyce school districts as examples. All three increased their grades from an F to a C this year.
“Those districts acted with intentionality and saw significant gains in overall student performance,” Oliva said.


Let us know what you think...


 

This year is the second year the education department has graded school districts, Oliva said. Arkansas has provided letter grades for schools for several years, but revised the formula for how those grades were assigned after the LEARNS Act.
Arkansas has made several educational changes as a result of the LEARNS Act, which Sanders, a Republican, signed in 2023. The overhaul of the state’s K-12 education system included an increase in the state’s minimum teacher salary to $50,000 and the creation of a school voucher program.
“Three years later, the results continue to speak for themselves: test scores are up, and more school districts are improving than falling behind, building on the historic gains we saw in this year’s ATLAS scores,” Sanders said in a press release. “Arkansas teachers and schools are helping students achieve more, our schools are getting better and LEARNS is working.”
The law has faced criticism from Democrats and some Republicans who have raised concerns about the impact of the voucher program on public schools and its cost to the state. Democratic Sen. Fred Love, who is challenging Sanders in the governor’s race, has promised to sign an executive order ending the voucher program if he’s elected.
Arkansas school rating system should consider additional factors, superintendents say

April Reisma, the president of the Arkansas Education Association, criticized the letter grades, saying it was “questionable to measure schools using the current method.” 
She said judging public schools by a “rigid test-based A-F system” undermines claims of transparency when private schools receiving taxpayer dollars through the school voucher program do not have to be graded, release standardized test results or meet comparable accountability rules.
Education officials created the new formula to go along with the new state test, the Arkansas Teaching, Learning & Assessment System, also known as ATLAS, which replaced the discontinued ACT Aspire and was first administered to students in spring 2024.
“Our schools deserve to be measured on everything they provide for children, with the weight of what they face with limited resources counted in that mix, not just results from end of year tests that do not fully measure the growth of a child or the ability of an educator,” Reisma said in a statement.
Oliva said during the press call that differences in standardized test scores in schools with higher poverty rates or with more students with disabilities was accounted for during the letter grade redesign, which was why some schools or districts with more of those students may still be given an A.
“So all those mitigating factors, regardless of programs that you’re in, demographics, regions of the state, are calculated for in building out a very statistically significant growth model,” Oliva said. “If kids are learning, you’re going to get a good grade.”
Last year was the first year schools were fully assessed under the new grade system, with grades in the 2023-2024 academic year being simulated based on the first administration of the ATLAS test.

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: With vote-by-mail court fight settled, attention shifts to protections at the polls
text: Voting rights groups and Democratic officials are looking to defend against what they see as possible election interference from the Trump administration ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, now that they’ve won a major battle over mail ballots.Common Cause, a nonpartisan pro-democracy organization, announced a “voter protection” campaign Thursday that would place thousands of volunteers at polling sites in 25 states.The initiative is designed to counter potential administration moves to intimidate voters, such as ordering troops or law enforcement officers to polling places.The Democratic Party is also upping its voter protection efforts, launching its own initiative this week to deploy 10,000 volunteers to assist voters at polling locations in all 50 states plus seven U.S. territories.Both efforts are described as preemptive efforts to head off any possible attempts by President Donald Trump to skew election results. Trump for years has alleged, without evidence, U.S. elections are beset by myriad attempts at fraud.He has used that pretext in attempts to enact policies to restrict voting, including the order limiting vote-by-mail that the U.S. Supreme Court blocked for this election. ‘Breathing down our neck’Voting rights advocates say they are preparing for more efforts to dissuade voters from casting ballots. Voters are “facing aggressive and deliberate threats from this administration and anti-voter forces that are tied to this administration,” Common Cause CEO Virginia Kase Solomón said. “Whether it be voter intimidation at the polls, the attacks on mail-in voting or attempts to collect your personal data, the barriers that voters are facing right now … are not only real, they are urgent. And they are intentionally designed to make everyday Americans give up.”The Democratic plan, led by the Association of State Democratic Conferences, a coalition of the 57 state and territorial party leaders, was also in part a reaction to Trump, ASDC Chair Jane Kleeb said in an interview.“We had to react to the threat that was breathing down our neck,” Kleeb, who is also the chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party, said in an interview.Trump has broadly accused Democrats of trying to cheat, and has placed particular focus on the possibility of noncitizens voting.White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis wrote in a Thursday email that the administration would continue to guard against that possibility.“Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of non-citizens registering and voting in our elections continues to pile up,” Bis wrote. “Any non-citizens found registering and voting in our elections will be arrested and held accountable. Only Americans should be electing American leaders.”The Justice Department has charged a handful of voter fraud cases of foreign nationals in recent months. The administration has also argued a software glitch in New Jersey that registered 6,600 noncitizens showed why tighter regulations on voting are needed.“There continues to be a narrative and a concern that noncitizens are voting,” Ari Mittelman, the executive director of the civic education group Keep Our Republic, said, adding that examples like the New Jersey glitch kept the issue “on the minds of many.”Troops at the polls?Common Cause officials and Kleeb highlighted the possibility of federal troops or law enforcement, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, at polling places as a strong concern.“We don't know exactly what Donald Trump is going to do,” Kleeb, whose interview was conducted before the Supreme Court’s mail voting decision on Sept. 14, said. “But if we take him at his word, he will disrupt the vote-by-mail process, and he will have people outside of polling locations to intimidate voters.”Administration officials have dismissed the idea of sending federal agents to the polls, but have not completely ruled it out. FBI Director Kash Patel repeatedly dodged the question during a U.S. Senate hearing Wednesday.At a press conference this month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said ICE would not have a sizable presence at election sites, but could deploy as part of the agency’s routine duties.“ICE isn't there to patrol the polling places,” Mullin said. “We're there to enforce specific threats. The only reason why we would be at polling places: Because there is a threat to that polling place or we are serving a warrant on someone we are actively tracking down.”And then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt called a question about sending ICE agents to the polls “disingenuous” at a February press briefing.“I can't guarantee that an ICE agent won't be around a polling location in November. I mean, that's frankly a very silly hypothetical question,” she said. “But what I can tell you is I haven't heard the president discuss any formal plans to put ICE outside of polling locations.”Disinformation, distrustTrump’s relentless focus on election regulations has contributed to a distrust of elections. Only 34% of adults in a AP-NORC and USAFacts poll this month said they trust government certifications of election results “a great deal” or “quite a bit.”Solomon said on the Thursday press call announcing the voter protection drive that the administration and its allies were seeking to sow distrust in the election.The program, which the group said was the country’s largest nonpartisan election protection effort, hopes to counter that narrative by installing voter advocates at polling stations.Volunteers will receive about an hour to 90 minutes of training on their state’s voting laws and how to help voters. ASDC volunteers will also receive about an hour of training. “They are trained to check for things like signage, polling place accessibility, long lines,” Common Cause Director of Policy Carol Evans said. “They are trained to be a positive and joyful presence at the polls to make the experience better for voters. And importantly, they are our eyes and ears on the ground to alert us to serious issues.”In another voter education initiative, Keep Our Republic has launched a series of town hall-style events in the five states in which it operates — Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — to give election officials a platform to speak to voters and increase trust in the election process, Mittleman said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Fraudsters hit Missoula College in national financial aid ‘ghost student’ scheme
description: A fraudulent enrollment scheme drained $673,745 in federal money from the University of Montana’s Missoula College in 2025, according to a new report from the Legislative Audit Division. The report says UM returned all the money to the federal government in the 2026 fiscal year, and the university’s net cash loss was $377,937. UM Vice […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.A fraudulent enrollment scheme drained $673,745 in federal money from the University of Montana’s Missoula College in 2025, according to a new report from the Legislative Audit Division.
The report says UM returned all the money to the federal government in the 2026 fiscal year, and the university’s net cash loss was $377,937.
UM Vice President of Communications Dave Kuntz said UM has submitted an insurance claim to recover the money lost to theft.
The scheme has hit nearly every academic institution in the country in some way, according to U.S. Department of Education Deputy Undersecretary James Bergeron.
Bergeron said an estimate of the total dollars stolen isn’t yet available but will be in the tens of millions.
Generally, the theft has taken place when AI bots steal identities, apply to multiple institutions at one time, and in some cases, receive federal aid, Bergeron said.
But when it comes time to connect with institutions in any variety of “touch points,” such as a one-on-one meeting with a professor, they disappear, earning them the name “ghost students,” he said.
Bergeron said the Department of Education is working to recover funds and combat the fraudsters, and at least a few prosecutions are underway. As of April, he said, so is a new verification system to access federal loans.
“We calculated we saved about $400 million from falling into the hands of fraudsters in just those four months since the new technology went into effect,” Bergeron said.
Other Montana University System campuses have seen similar attempts at theft, but a limited volume, according to an MUS spokesperson.
The audit report said UM has since strengthened its fraud detection through “enhanced monitoring,” more review of suspicious activity across departments, and expanded identity verification.
The Trump administration has a goal to dissolve the Department of Education and transfer control to the states.
But Bergeron said the effort to ensure taxpayer dollars are spent effectively remains a priority for the White House irrespective of the status of the Department of Education.
He said as student aid moves to the Department of the Treasury, the work to protect funds will be a focus for those officials as well.
“The staff there are very engaged and interested in combatting fraud,” Bergeron said.
Montana Legislative Auditor Angus Maciver said online scams are constantly changing and growing more sophisticated, and UM should continue to strengthen its security measures.
He said the Legislative Audit Committee would take up the report, intended to increase public trust in state government, at its meetings this week.
“We expect the Audit Committee discussion to provide additional context about these risks, how they are affecting universities, and what institutions are doing specifically to respond,” Maciver said.
‘Ghost students’ cost UM
The Legislative Audit Division outlined the scheme in Montana as part of a comprehensive review of the state budget.
The audit counted 70 identity theft instances from the 2024 to 2026 fiscal years that led to improper federal disbursements. UM became aware of the fraud when an individual reported their identity had been stolen to enroll in online courses, the audit said.
UM then reviewed all summer 2025 online enrollments and identified 94 that were fraudulent, of which 63 received federal aid, the report said. It said seven additional cases have been found since.
The report says UM had controls in place, but “the sophistication and evolving nature of the fraud schemes exceeded the effectiveness of controls commonly used across higher education at the time.”
Kuntz said UM has put the following safeguards in place:

It is conducting identity verification checks on select populations prior to admission. This prevents potentially fraudulent students from being admitted, so they never receive access to federal aid. UM selects populations based on historical fraud activity, primarily students applying for distance-only programs.
Once admitted, UM has seen “ghost students” switch from in-person to distance modality. UM has established an identity verification check step for students who were admitted into an in-person program and attempt to switch to a distance program (or switch to exclusively distance-only courses).
Even after admitted and registered for courses, UM is flagging all new distance-only students for federal aid verification, which means they are subject to closer scrutiny by the Department of Education in order to receive financial aid.

Kuntz said the university has had extensive communication with the Department of Education, “including notifying them of the situation the moment we uncovered it.”
But the audit said a lack of resources at UM means it hadn’t yet uncovered the full scope of fraudulent enrollments. Kuntz said the resource challenge remains.
“A lack of staffing resources continues to prevent us from doing a comprehensive, retroactive look backwards,” Kuntz said in an email. “As a result, we have not uncovered any additional bad enrollments beyond what was disclosed in the audit.”
Auditors suspect the college was targeted because of its higher volume of online enrollment and lower tuition costs, which result in greater cash disbursements to schemers after tuition and fees are paid.
Montana University System spokesperson Galen Hollenbaugh said the college has a high number of online enrollments, but it isn’t the largest in the system, and the university system doesn’t “necessarily conclude that one institutional feature” is the reason it was attacked.
Hollenbaugh said the MUS does not have a record of whether any fraud attempts at other campuses have been successful, but it is working to thwart attacks across the system.
“Other Montana University System campuses have seen similar attempted fraudulent activity in varying forms,” Hollenbaugh said in an email. “We are working with a vendor across campuses to share information about known fraudulent identities, patterns, and methods of attack, with the goal of closing potential points of entry as quickly as possible.”
Bergeron said the Department of Education’s Office of Inspector General already conducted investigations on student aid fraud rings before 2025 and recovered $35 million, including in restitution, settlements and fines.
“This is a fraction of what we think it will be” for the ghost student scheme, Bergeron said.
He said international investigations also are underway and found crime rings overseas, including in the middle of Africa and eastern Europe, stealing the identities of Americans.
For a solution, Bergeron said the Department of Education approached a handful of colleges that already were vigilant with identity verification, and they pointed the DOE to a tool used in the private sector.
He said the result is the DOE is using a “best in class” private sector tool that 19 of the 20 largest financial institutions in the country use to be sure federal resources go where intended.
Academic institutions can override the federal system and still award federal aid, Bergeron said, but the DOE is auditing them to be sure those dollars aren’t going to thieves.
“It’s intended to serve students, not fraudsters,” Bergeron said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: UNI receives regents’ approval to form center housing Grassley papers
description: The University of Northern Iowa is furthering its work into civic education and stewardship of historical government resources through two centers, one created from a directive by the Iowa Board of Regents and the other approved by it Thursday. The board of regents approved the formation of a “center for public engagement, leadership development and […]
text:
The University of Northern Iowa is bringing civic education and political archives to campus with two centers. (Photo courtesy of University of Northern Iowa)The University of Northern Iowa is furthering its work into civic education and stewardship of historical government resources through two centers, one created from a directive by the Iowa Board of Regents and the other approved by it Thursday.
The board of regents approved the formation of a “center for public engagement, leadership development and archival stewardship” at UNI during its Thursday meeting, with the vote amended to clarify that once U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley retires, the center will be named for him and his wife, Barbara.
UNI President Mark Nook told the board the center has been in development since before he arrived in 2017, and the university has spent “many years” working on it with the knowledge the university would receive Grassley’s documents once he leaves the Senate.
The board approved the center on its future namesake’s 93rd birthday.
“The center will be a nationally recognized resource for civic engagement, leadership development, archival stewardship, and public program programming that connects Iowa to the nation through learning, dialog, scholarship, and public service,” Nook said. “To accomplish that, the mission that will drive this center is to preserve and provide access to Sen. Grassley’s historic career while advancing civic education, student leadership development, public engagement, and educational programming that strengthens the understanding of American government and representative democracy.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Regent Christine Hensley voiced her support for the center, but said she “feel(s) strongly” that the board needs to have a fundraising update from the university at its November meeting. According to a news release from UNI, the university is creating a fundraising and implementation strategy for the center and expects funding to come from donations, endowment earnings, grants, sponsorships, program revenue and support from UNI.
Board documents stated the center will launch a scholarship and leadership development program, host events like lectures and exhibits for both students and the public, preserve and provide access to the Grassley Collection and work with partners to “expand civic learning opportunities.”
One of these partnerships will be with the UNI Center for Civic Education, the document stated, though their missions are distinct. The center for civic education is focused on educational outreach and programming in support of civic learning.
UNI civics education center receives federal grant
Allison Rank, director of the center for civic education, presented to the board of regents Wednesday about its work and priorities. Over the past 15 months, Rank said the center has put on events to introduce students to diverse viewpoints, group activities to learn more about civic culture at UNI and other training and activities off campus and across the state.
“We want to be a nationally recognized leader in research, teaching, and public outreach in free speech and civic education,” Rank said.
The center is focused on civic engagement on and off campus related to free speech, Rank said, as well as providing professional development and civic learning to current and future Iowa educators and promoting civic education through curricular changes with faculty across the state.
The first year of the center’s “Challenging Perspectives Series” focused on the “future of the American family,” an event Rank said more than 60 students attended. From student-led brainstorming sessions with small groups came 17 solutions for bolstering UNI civic culture, which Rank said they used to apply for and receive a national grant to become an anchor campus for deliberative dialogue focused on faith-based institutions “and service provision.”
Another challenging perspectives event, as well as deliberative dialogues, will take place this academic year.
Rank said the center also received a $1.2 million grant from the U.S. Department of Education to create the “Iowa Civic Educators Institute” for Iowa standards-based civic education professional development for pre- and in-service teachers. A focus of this work is providing primary resources that are “connected to politics, but not politicized.”
“It’s hard to find content-rich information that they can trust, and we see ourselves as being able to fill that gap for faculty or for faculty in K-12,” Rank said.
Training sessions have already been held with the support of the three-year grant, Rank said, and she is working to find spaces in other areas of the state so educators don’t have to make their way to Cedar Falls. She’s also completed professional development and curriculum work both at UNI and at Iowa community colleges.
When asked by Hensley about what percentage of the student body is aware of the center, Rank said probably less than one-fifth. However, her goal isn’t to ensure every student knows her and her work but to ensure that the ones who need her can find her.
Rank provided the example of running a program with residence assistants in student dorms “to help them understand that what they’re doing is building students’ neighborhoods,” saying that it doesn’t matter if every student on the floor knows her as long as their leaders know to turn to her when they have questions or concerns.
“I care about reaching students where they are,” Rank said. “I don’t need them to know me, I need them to want to do civics.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC drivers can take UTVs to the roads later this year. Until then, DMV says to keep them home.
description: COLUMBIA — Owners of utility task vehicles can start driving the small, enclosed vehicles on public roads this year under a new law. The vehicles, which are popular among farmers, hunters and other outdoor enthusiasts, have existed for years in a legal gray area, without clear requirements or bans on where they can operate, legislators […]
text:
Sen. Russell Ott, D-St. Matthews, shows senators a photo of a utility task vehicle at the Statehouse in Columbia, S.C., on Thursday, April 16, 2026. (Screenshot of SCETV legislative livestream)COLUMBIA — Owners of utility task vehicles can start driving the small, enclosed vehicles on public roads this year under a new law.
The vehicles, which are popular among farmers, hunters and other outdoor enthusiasts, have existed for years in a legal gray area, without clear requirements or bans on where they can operate, legislators said. Starting Nov. 18, drivers will have to register the vehicles and meet certain requirements to take them off their property.
Until then, drivers should keep the vehicles home, according to the Department of Motor Vehicles.
“Our priority is the safety of all South Carolinians, whether they will be riding in a UTV on a public road or in a passenger vehicle next to a UTV,” DMV director Kevin Shwedo said in a statement.
Registration, which includes a license plate, will cost $10 and last two years under the law, which passed in May.
To run on public roads, the vehicles must have four wheels, a top speed over 55 miles per hour and a width of 80 inches or less. They also need to have similar features to cars, including seatbelts, headlights, brake lights, taillights and turn signals.
Drivers have to be 17 or older and have a diver’s license. No UTVs will be allowed on public roads with a passenger who is 8 years old or younger, and anyone in the vehicle who is under the age of 21 must wear a helmet with a face shield.
UTV drivers must also carry insurance.
The vehicles won’t be allowed on roads with a speed limit above 55 miles per hour, and they can’t travel on any interstates. Drivers also can’t take their vehicles further than 10 miles from the address where the UTV is registered.
Cities and counties can put additional restrictions on driving UTVs, including where and when they can operate.
The rules are, by design, similar to those about taking golf carts and all-terrain vehicles on public streets, legislators said. Similar to ATVs, UTVs are typically enclosed and have a steering wheel instead of handle bars.
“We do have a lot of different vehicles that are allowed to be on our roads, from bicycles to mopeds to motorcycles to cars and trucks,” said Sen. Russell Ott, who sponsored the bill. “This is just another one that essentially has evolved over time.”
People in rural areas use the vehicles to manage large swaths of property, since they can get to places where many cars can’t, said Sen. Chip Campsen, who noted he drives a UTV of his own.
“When I’m burning timber, when I’m planting food plots, sometimes I don’t have any option but to get out on the road and come back in,” the Isle of Palms Republican told senators during debate on the bill earlier this year. “For rural South Carolina, that needs to happen.”
Ott, a Democrat from rural St. Matthews, has seen more UTVs on the road since he started introducing proposals to allow them on public roadways six years ago, he told senators during debate on the bill.
“I certainly see UTVs on the roads back home where I live every week, if not every day,” Ott said. “It’s just a common occurrence.”
If legislators did nothing, the number of UTVs on the roads would likely continue to grow without any regulation, Ott said.
Many drivers believed they could register their UTV in a different state and legally drive it in South Carolina, Ott said. The vehicles are legal in some capacity in 33 other states, according to data tracking site World Population Review.
Other people believed they weren’t allowed to drive on public roads in any instance. Police shared in their confusion, said Sen. Greg Hembree, who leads the transportation committee.
Because South Carolina had no laws specifically addressing the vehicles, drivers and police were left to wonder what was legal and what wasn’t, he said.
“They’re kind of in no man’s land,” said the Little River Republican.
That could create major issues in the case of a crash, Hembree said. If an uninsured UTV driver hit a car, for instance, the driver could end up out of luck in an attempt to recoup their money, he said.
Some legislators raised safety concerns about driving smaller, slower-moving vehicles on roads alongside cars and trucks. The law passed the Senate in a vote of 26-18 and the House by 109-3.
The Department of Public Safety, which tracks car crashes, doesn’t release the types of vehicles involved. Golf carts, which are slower, are estimated to be involved in nearly 4,000 annual injuries nationwide, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
“I’ve seen so many times where a vehicle would pop over a hill and not see” a slower-moving vehicle, said the Prosperity Republican, who voted against the bill.
Putting restrictions on when and how people can drive the vehicles is meant to help prevent those problems, Ott said.
“A lot of people are using these and enjoying them,” Ott said. “There’s nothing wrong with that, and we just need to try to put some safeguards and rules and regulations around it.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi college board sets spring goal to name MUW’s next president
description: Mississippi University for Women in Columbus, Miss., Tuesday, Nov. 11, 2025.
text:
The state college board plans to name the next president of the Mississippi University for Women by early spring 2027.
The board of trustees for the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning announced the plans Thursday. The board also formed a committee of six trustees to oversee the national president search with support from a search firm that has not yet been selected. 
Mississippi University for Women in Columbus, Miss., Tuesday, Nov. 11, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The search committee members are:

Teresa Hubbard, chairwoman
Amy Arrington
Jerry Griffith
Charlie Stephenson, IHL board vice president
Gregg Rader 
Steve Cunningham, IHL board president 

Cunningham said he chose the search committee members in part because of their proximity to MUW, their familiarity with the university and ties to Columbus and the surrounding region. Once selected, the search firm will help develop a timeline and candidate profile incorporating feedback gathered from MUW stakeholders during previous listening sessions, he said. 
The board aims to keep stakeholders updated throughout the process, Cunningham said. A group of MUW alumni and Columbus residents asked trustees to disclose a timeline and details about how the board will conduct the leadership search. Some people have also suggested names of leaders they want IHL trustees to consider to lead the university.
“It always works out better when you can involve the constituency groups in this whole process,” Cunningham said. “They’re a really big part of that portion of the search because they’re boots on the ground on the campus, and they know what’s needed.” 
The board is expected to issue a request for proposals for search firms within the next few weeks, Cunningham said. 
Nora Miller, who had served as MUW’s president since 2018, retired on June 30. Scott Tollison, the university’s former provost and executive vice president of academic affairs, has served as interim president since July 1. 
Read more: Will MUW’s next president be an alumna?
In April, the trustees held listening sessions for MUW stakeholders to gather feedback from the public on preferred traits for the W’s next leader. At the listening sessions, some speakers suggested Sally Burchfield Doty, who graduated from the W’ in 1988 and directs Broadband Expansion and Accessibility of Mississippi. Doty, who lives in Brookhaven, also served in the state Senate from 2012 to 2020. 
In August, the Citizens Coalition for MUW and Mississippi School for Mathematics and Sciences sent the college board a letter endorsing another alumna, Doris Taylor of the class of 1977, who is a biotechnology researcher. 
The Citizens Coalition for MUW and Mississippi School for Mathematics and Sciences includes alumni and Columbus residents. The group is asking the state’s college board to consider a prominent alumna as the institution’s next president. Credit: Keith Gaskin
Neither suggestion makes Doty or Taylor an official candidate in the search. Candidates must apply for the role to be considered.
Coalition chairman Bruce Hanson said the group will continue to engage alumni, students, faculty and the community to become involved in the leadership search process. 
 “We will continue to work on strategy to ensure the best candidate gets the job and can support our region and institutions and our community at large,” Hanson said. 
While the group endorsed Taylor as a potential candidate, a national search can open up the possibility for additional strong candidates to lead the university, said Keith Gaskin, former mayor of Columbus and coalition member. 
Gaskin said he wants trustees to move quickly with the search process because he’s grown weary of recent legislative proposals and discussions about merging MUW with Mississippi State University and moving the Mississippi School for Mathematics and Science, a residential school for gifted high school juniors and seniors, to Starkville. But it’s important to find the right pick for MUW’s next leader, he said. 
“My hope is that we find a strong leader who can support and serve this region,” Gaskin said. “That’s the most important thing that matters to me.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Supreme Court rejects 2 Project Jupiter challenges, allows permitting process to resume
description: The New Mexico Supreme Court on Thursday unanimously shot down two environmental groups’ challenges to regulatory proceedings for the Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County. In the orders, which offered no further comment on the court’s rulings, justices unpaused the regulatory proceedings that have been frozen since August.
text:
The New Mexico Supreme Court on Sept. 17, 2026, allowed regulatory proceedings to proceed for the Project Jupiter data center, pictured on June 26, 2026. (Courtesy of Alexa Reynaud, Food & Water Watch, with aerial support provided by LightHawk)The New Mexico Supreme Court on Thursday unanimously shot down two environmental groups’ challenges to regulatory proceedings for the Project Jupiter data center under construction in Doña Ana County.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In brief orders, the court denied August requests from the Santa Fe-based New Energy Economy and the national Center for Biological Diversity that challenged the data center’s pending air quality permit application with the New Mexico Environment Department and its use of an emergency water well for construction.
The New Mexico Supreme Court in August paused regulatory proceedings for Project Jupiter while it evaluated the environmental groups’ complaints. The air quality permit hearing was initially scheduled to begin Monday in southern New Mexico.
In the orders, which offered no further comment on the court’s rulings, justices also unpaused the regulatory proceedings that have been frozen since August.
“I don’t know what to say,” Colin Cox, a New Mexico-based attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity, told Source NM Thursday. “I’m a little surprised that they granted both stays, which was pretty extraordinary and then pulled them without any explanation.”
In a statement, New Energy Economy Executive Director Mariel Nanasi said the plaintiffs were “terribly disappointed,” but acknowledged they had asked the state’s highest court “for extraordinary relief.”
“We went to the Supreme Court because we believed the rules of this proceeding were stacked against meaningful public participation,” she said. “We sought a fair opportunity for the public to obtain the evidence, test the claims being made by the applicant and present its case before New Mexico decides whether to authorize an enormous new source of pollution.” 
The New Mexico Environment Department’s hearing officer who presided over the air quality permit application abruptly recused himself from the matter in August. The department has yet to appoint a replacement or hold a scheduling conference to set a new hearing date.
NMED spokesperson Drew Goretzka told Source NM that department officials will follow the guidance of the new hearing officer.
State environment officials will decide whether to grant the data center developer’s request to issue an air quality permit for its proposed on-site energy source, a natural-gas powered fuel cell system. Projections show that, if approved, it would emit as many greenhouse gases annually as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.

name: WyoFile
title: Immigration attorney notes ‘shift in tactic’ after ICE arrests Turkish woman at Jackson bus stop
authors: by Jenna McMurtry, Evan Robinson-Johnson and Sophia Boyd-Fliegel, KHOL 89.1
description:
The 26-year-old was targeted for overstaying her yearlong visa, DHS says.
The post Immigration attorney notes ‘shift in tactic’ after ICE arrests Turkish woman at Jackson bus stop appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Feride Bardakci worked three restaurant jobs in Jackson. The 26-year-old from Turkey was on her way from a morning shift at Picnic cafe to her evening job at Teton Tiger on Tuesday afternoon when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested her at a bus stop. 
Officers wore visible badges that said “ICE,” an unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said via email. Other than the badges, officers wore plain clothes, according to bystander reports posted online. The spokesperson said Bardakci resisted arrest. 
As officers handcuffed her and put her into a vehicle for transport to Casper, Bardakci yelled out the name of her manager and asked someone to let her know she would miss her shift, said Teton Tiger General Manager Monica Rozzi. 
Rozzi got a phone call from Teton Area Rapid Response Network –  a newly formed hotline about ICE activities — with a report from a bystander. 
“My heart dropped,” said Rozzi. “It’s just shocking and scary because she’s definitely a friend to all of us, and she’s a wonderful person and not somebody I would consider a danger to society.”
Rozzi said she was unaware that ICE would have any reason to pursue Bardakci, whom she hired about five months ago. 
The targeted street-level operation marked a departure from how ICE usually works in Teton County. Under the second Trump administration, ICE has picked up about 200 people from the county jail. Most were first arrested for driving-related offenses, a May KHOL analysis found.
A woman was arrested at the bus stop near the Jackson Target by officers in plain clothes who used zip ties, according to the Teton Area Rapid Response Network. (Evan Robinson-Johnson/KHOL)
“This is a shift in tactic, it appears, that ICE is now going to stop people on the street,” said Jackson immigration attorney Elisabeth Trefonas. She advised other immigrants to get their documents in order.
A leadership team member from the Persephone and Picnic cafe team declined to comment. Coworkers say she also worked for Annie’s Thai Kitchen, which could not be reached for comment in time for this story.  
A search of state and federal courts did not return a criminal record. Reports show Bardakci is now in Natrona County jail. Bardakci was targeted for overstaying her yearlong visa, which she first obtained in 2023. 
“In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her welcome and refused to depart. Bardakci will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending the outcome of her immigration proceedings,” the statement from DHS said. “Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App.”
It’s common for many young Jackson hospitality workers to have arrived on a J-1 student visa, as Bardakci did. 
“I bet if you walked into any restaurant right now and asked how many of them had J-1s when they first got here, if they weren’t born here, you’d get an overwhelming percentage, if not all of them,” Trefonas said. 
Teton County Sheriff Matt Carr said he’s never seen such a publicly visible operation without any advance notice to local law enforcement, which he described as a violation of protocol. DHS did not respond to a question about the lack of notice.
Bardakci will likely be transferred to a detention center in Aurora, Colorado, Trefonas said. 
Many of Trefonas’ other clients have been denied bond and deemed a flight risk, forcing lawyers to use habeas corpus to try for release, she said. If a release is secured, cases can still take two to 10 years to process.
WyoFile contributed editing to this report. — Ed.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Mail trouble canceled some Alaska primary votes in Western Alaska
description: About 1 in 30 absentee ballots cast in Alaska’s August primary election were rejected for procedural errors, according to data published this month by the Alaska Division of Elections. The 3.4% rejection rate for absentee ballots was almost double what it was in the 2024 general election but it was below the record high 4.5% […]
text:
Members of the Alaska State Review Board are seen reviewing precinct ballot counts following the primary election on Aug 26, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)About 1 in 30 absentee ballots cast in Alaska’s August primary election were rejected for procedural errors, according to data published this month by the Alaska Division of Elections.
The 3.4% rejection rate for absentee ballots was almost double what it was in the 2024 general election but it was below the record high 4.5% seen during the 2022 special primary election held after the death of Congressman Don Young. 
The top reason for disqualification this year was late postmarking, a change from prior elections when witness signatures were the No. 1 reason for rejection. It isn’t clear why late postmarking was the top issue. A comparison with the 2020, 2018 and 2016 primaries indicates that absentee ballots did not, in general, arrive later this year than they did in previous years.
There were some notable exceptions.
The disqualification rate in parts of rural Alaska was significantly higher than the state as a whole. In House District 40, which covers the North Slope and Northwest Arctic Borough, 32 of 81 absentee ballots — almost 40% — were rejected. 
Seventy-five absentee ballots cast in person ahead of election day, including 28 from Kotzebue in the Northwest Arctic Borough, failed to reach the Division of Elections regional office in Nome before Aug. 31, the deadline to be counted. 
The ballots arrived so late that they couldn’t even be included in a list of ballots that were disqualified for arriving late. 
In addition to Kotzebue, ballots from Naknek, King Cove, Nikolski, Igiugig, Quinhagak, and Pitkas Point failed to arrive on time and weren’t counted.
Michelle Sparck, director of Get Out the Native Vote, called the issue a “slap in the face.” Her organization has been working to promote absentee voting as a way to boost turnout among Alaska Natives who live in rural Alaska.
“For us to have pushed absentee (voting) as a way of good practice … it builds that deep callus of voter apathy when we have to worry about whether or not this exercise even works,” she said.
One of the rejected ballots from Naknek was cast on Aug. 5, almost two weeks before the primary.
That vote was cast by Sallyann Hughes, who contacted the Alaska Beacon after getting a letter from the Division of Elections on Sept. 14. That letter said her ballot was not counted.
By email, Hughes said she remembered the election worker being so excited because her vote was the first she had processed in Naknek.
Hughes said that since receiving her rejection notice, she has sent a series of letters to find out what happened to her vote.
“I am not alleging voter fraud, manipulation of voting equipment, intentional misconduct, or responsibility by any particular person or agency. I do not yet know where in the custody or transportation process the failure occurred. I am seeking a documented accounting of what happened after these ballots were placed into the custody of election personnel,” she said.
Hughes said she’s particularly worried because she plans to be out of state in November and needs to vote absentee again. 
Most of the 19,760 absentee ballots cast during the primary came from voters who sent them individually by mail.
To be counted, absentee ballots first go to review boards at regional offices across the state, where workers verify that the ballots were cast legally.
The 75 extra disqualifications, including Hughes’ ballot, were cast at in-person absentee polling stations set up by the Division of Elections in rural Alaska.
In Alaska, rural mail generally travels first to Anchorage for processing, then to its end destination. 
In this case, slow delivery meant the ballots didn’t arrive in Nome before the election’s certification deadline at the end of the month. 
On Wednesday, the Division of Elections announced that it is changing its policy for the general election and for upcoming rural school board elections to prevent a repeat of the problem. 
Absentee ballots from in-person polling stations will now be “rerouted to the Region II Office in Anchorage to prevent unexpected mail delays.”
Sparck said it’s a good idea. “Cutting out a middleman is pretty smart here,” she said.
While the U.S. Postal Service’s handling of absentee ballots received extensive attention ahead of the primary, data published by the Division of Elections and reviewed by the Alaska Beacon indicate that on a statewide basis, absentee ballots didn’t arrive later this year than they did in prior primary elections.
Alaska law allows primary ballots to be counted as long as they arrive no later than 10 days after election day. This year, the busiest day for ballot returns was the day after election day.
That matches what happened in the 2020, 2018 and 2016 primaries — in each of those elections, the busiest days for absentee ballot returns were the days immediately after election day. 
Altogether across the state, 627 absentee ballots were disqualified for all reasons; more than 19,000 were accepted in part or whole.
Of the disqualified, 169 ballots were rejected because they were postmarked after election day and another 110 ballots weren’t counted because they were received too late. 
That latter figure may be an undercount, since it only includes the 75 late-arriving in-person absentees and 35 absentee ballots that reached officials between Aug. 28 and Aug. 31. 
In Alaska, anyone can vote absentee for any reason, but completing an absentee ballot requires a voter to provide ID information, sign the ballot and find a second person, a witness, to sign it as well. 
In every primary election since 2020, the lack of a witness signature was the No. 1 reason for rejections. This year, it’s No. 2. 
In this year’s primary election, 29.2% of absentee voters were registered Republicans. Registered Democrats made up 21.7% of absentee voters.
Sparck said there were positive signs for rural voting in the primary. Turnout was up 48.8% over the 2024 primary in tribally affiliated precincts, she said.
The annual Alaska Federation of Natives convention, scheduled for late October, will include a big voting push, she said, and because it is taking place a week later than normal, participants will be able to vote early in Anchorage and avoid any problems with absentee voting.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Auditor: Employee salaries rose for governor’s and secretary of state’s offices
description: Employee salaries in the Iowa governor’s and secretary of state’s offices increased by double-digit percentages over the past decade, a report released Thursday by Iowa Auditor Rob Sand shows. The report shows that in inflation-adjusted figures, executive branch salaries declined over the past 10 years by 7.6%, but when looking at individual offices within t[...]
text:
The Iowa Capitol on Feb. 25, 2025. (Photo by Kathie Obradovich/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Employee salaries in the Iowa governor’s and secretary of state’s offices increased by double-digit percentages over the past decade, a report released Thursday by Iowa Auditor Rob Sand shows.
The report shows that in inflation-adjusted figures, executive branch salaries declined over the past 10 years by 7.6%, but when looking at individual offices within the branch, the governor’s and secretary of state’s offices increased employee salaries over the period. 
“With deficits of more than a billion dollars every year over the state, and inflation adjustment cuts to education and Medicaid, as well as incoming cuts from the Big Beautiful Bill, we think it’s important to take a fact-driven look at aspects of state spending, including employment in the executive branch,” Sand, who is running for governor in the 2026 election, said at a news conference Thursday. 
According to the report, inflation-adjusted salaries in the governor’s office increased 35% during the time period and salaries in the secretary of state’s office increased 10% over the same time. 
The report analyzes executive branch compensation, employment trends and travel reimbursements for the fiscal years between 2016 and 2025. While this time frame coincides with Gov. Kim Reynolds’ time in office, Sand said that was not intentional. The time frame, he said, was chosen to show a 10-year trend and to include “a good amount” of time before and after the COVID-19 pandemic. 
The report compares pre-pandemic averages, encompassing fiscal years 2017 through 2020 and post-pandemic averages, fiscal years 2022 through 2025. When comparing average salaries, in inflation-adjusted figures before and after the pandemic, the salaries at the governor’s office increased 16%, and 7% at the secretary of state’s office. Salaries at the other analyzed branches decreased between 1% and 9%. 
In 2024, Reynolds’ office received a higher standing appropriation from the Legislature. Public records requests analyzed by Bleeding Heartland found Reynolds subsequently raised the salaries of top officials in the office. 
Reynolds’ office, in a statement about Sand’s report, said “the most important investment any organization makes is in its people.” 
“Government should be no different,” the statement said. “Governor Reynolds has built a strong team of experienced professionals, recruiting executive branch leaders from other states and members of her own staff from the private sector. She’s prioritized hiring senior level staff members with expertise in relevant areas.” 
A graph from a state auditor report shows salary increases across executive branch offices. (Graph courtesy of Iowa Auditor of the State)
Sand said Reynolds’ 2023 plan to reorganize and consolidate state agencies made it “really difficult” to track numbers at individual departments, as some employees moved departments under the reorganization plan. 
The report notes that it “attempted” to adjust for changes in department names by recoding the salary book data set. With these figures, the auditor report found that the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Corrections, and the Department of Transportation have accounted for 54% to 57% of all full-time executive branch employees since fiscal year 2021. 
While these departments account for more than half of executive branch employees, the report said the reorganization changes made it “infeasible” to make “department-specific comparisons from one period to another.” 
Instead, the report compares employee salaries at offices with statewide elected officials, as it said these offices — attorney general, auditor, governor, secretary of agriculture, secretary of state and treasurer, were “widely unaffected by the state government reorganization.” 
Based on this comparison, the report concludes that all offices aside from the governor’s office and secretary of state’s office paid inflation-adjusted salaries to employees that were “roughly equal to or slightly lower than the salaries paid a decade earlier.”
A statement from the secretary of state’s office said that while the office had not been given a copy of the report to review, it “navigated significant crises” like the pandemic and “rising cyber threats” during the examined period.
“While we don’t have all of the facts in front of us as to how the report was generated, we are confident that our staff is paid fairly and competitively,” the statement said. 
The spokesperson for the office also noted that Secretary of State Paul Pate has not had a raise over the period and that the office has “invested significantly” in full-time, specialized IT and cybersecurity roles that “many similar agencies have contracted” to other agencies or vendors.
The spokesperson said the office has also invested in training and development divisions to account for an increased turnover in election workers and county auditors. 
More temporary workers and more turnover
The report detailed an increase in the number of seasonal, temporary, or intern positions, which also caused an increase in the overall number of salaried staff in executive branch offices. According to the report, in 2016 employees with these titles accounted for 1% of total staff numbers and about 9% of total staff numbers in 2025. 
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship and the auditor’s office had the highest increase in part-time or seasonal employee figures of the analyzed offices. IDALS increased staffing in the category by about 43 when comparing pre-pandemic and post-pandemic averages. Sand’s office increased by about 6. The secretary of state’s office decreased its use of interns, part-time or seasonal employees by 2 and the governor’s office remained at an average of 0 temporary employees before and after the pandemic. 
State Auditor Rob Sand speaks Sept. 17, 2026 in his office about a report on executive branch employment trends. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Sand said the increase in temporary employees likely contributed to the increased turnover rates seen across the executive branch. He also said it “definitely impacted the salary increases” since temporary employees would not be eligible for the same salary increases or benefits as full time employees. 
“At the end of the day, if you see an increase in turnover, you have to ask yourselves whether or not the increase in turnover is costing you what you might have saved by not hiring full-time employees,” Sand said. 
Executive branch spending on travel and subsistence has also declined during the period, which Sand said “isn’t surprising” since the pandemic opened up more opportunities for remote work and meetings. Comparing pre-pandemic spending to post-pandemic spending in the category, the report notes a more than 21% decline in inflation adjusted dollars. 
Sand said Thursday he had not consulted other offices in the executive branch about the increases shown in the publicly available data. 
“When we saw the numbers, we just thought that this is an important conversation to be having,” Sand said. 
He said while an overall reduction in salaries “can be a good thing” the “taxpayer’s watchdog” needs to look at how dollars are being spent in state government. 
“We really need to think about balancing, making sure we’re balancing the prudent use of taxpayer resources, while also actually delivering to Iowans what they need from their own government in a timely manner too,” Sand said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma CareerTech board to vote on request for funding increase
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A state board governing vocational learning centers could ask for a $67.87 million budget increase next year with the goal of expanding workforce training. The Oklahoma Department of Career and Technology Education on Thursday presented a $249.56 million budget request for the 2028 fiscal year. The agency’s board is expected to vote […]
text:
An entrance to an Oklahoma CareerTech office in Stillwater is pictured on Dec. 6, 2024. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A state board governing vocational learning centers could ask for a $67.87 million budget increase next year with the goal of expanding workforce training.
The Oklahoma Department of Career and Technology Education on Thursday presented a $249.56 million budget request for the 2028 fiscal year. The agency’s board is expected to vote next month on whether to send the proposal to the state Legislature for consideration.
“What we need is everybody to understand the confidence that we have in our system and the state should have in our system,” state CareerTech director Brent Haken said while presenting the budget proposal. “There is nobody still, even though we’ve got a lot of work to do, that shows the return on investment that we do when we get students into the program.”
Brent Haken, state director of Oklahoma CareerTech, speaks to attendees of an open house at the Metro Tech Aviation Campus on June 21, 2024. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma’s 29 CareerTech centers count more than 500,000 enrollments across the state in job skill programs, adult education and K-12 courses. The state agency has asked for significant funding increases in recent years to reduce waitlists, which in 2024 counted 7,500 students.
State lawmakers appropriated more than $185 million to the CareerTech system for the current fiscal year, tens of millions of dollars less than the agency had requested.
With his latest budget ask, Haken suggested Oklahoma needs to invest far more than its current CareerTech funding levels to keep pace with other states.
“We are seeing other states make significant advancements in (CareerTech education) above what Oklahoma is doing,” he said during the meeting. “So we’re going to have to figure out how we want to play ball in that arena if we want to continue to have the system that we do.”
His proposal includes a $27.65 million increase to postsecondary workforce training, including $18.65 million in recurring funding to remove waitlists.
An additional $20 million would help “build a statewide approach” to giving more students in grades 5-12 career exposure at vocational technology centers, according to the agency’s proposal.
The agency reported 35% of all Oklahoma students in fifth through 12th grade had enrolled in a CareerTech class. Among high school juniors, that number recently surpassed 50%, Haken said.
His budget request would seek a one-time appropriation of $10 million to add more CareerTech centers in areas that don’t yet have one. 
Haken said the state took a similar approach when it expanded into Beaver County. It offered funds to start programs and support the new center for its first year so “they didn’t have to wait on tax money to come in,” he said
CareerTech centers rely on local tax revenue, state appropriations and federal funds.
“We still have significant white space across the state where we could use those dollars to bring people into the system,” Haken said. “If they do decide to come into the system, then we have a tax base that sustains it, but this would be a one-time request.”
An added $6.7 million would support curriculum costs, new programs and CareerTech student organizations, according to the proposal.
The cost of employees’ insurance benefits is expected to rise by $3.72 million, which the state is obligated to pay, Haken said.

title: Lincoln residents seek public hearing as state board weighs proposed airstrip
description:
Lt. Gov. John Rodgers hosted a forum in Lincoln as some residents continue to press their concerns about the proposed airstrip’s impact on safety, the surrounding environment and the character of the area.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Lincoln residents seek public hearing as state board weighs proposed airstrip.
text:
Vermont Lt. Gov. John Rodgers speaks to the crowd at a Sept. 14 forum at Burnham Hall focused on the proposed airstrip Lincoln residents Kyle and Katie Clark have been seeking approval to site at their property since 2022. Photo by Marin Howell/Addison Independent

This story by Marin Howell was first published in the Addison Independent on Sept. 17, 2026.
LINCOLN — The fate of a proposed personal aircraft strip in Lincoln no longer rests in the hands of that municipality, but some residents are seeking another opportunity to weigh in before the quasi-judicial Vermont Transportation Board decides the project’s future.
“I’m here tonight because I believe the people of Lincoln, and especially those who will be affected by this proposed airstrip, deserve a full and fair public process,” Lincoln resident Coco Moseley said at a forum held in Burnham Hall on Monday.
Moderators at the meeting clarified that the gathering was an informational forum and was not being hosted or sponsored by the town of Lincoln or any government agency. The meeting is not part of the decision-making process for the landing strip, which Lincoln residents Kyle and Katie Clark have been seeking approval to operate at their property since 2022. Kyle Clark is CEO of the electric airplane manufacturer Beta Technologies, where Katie Clark serves as head of brand, creative, culture and spaces.
The forum was hosted by Vermont Lt. Gov. John Rodgers after a group of around a dozen Lincoln residents sent emails to state officials last month sharing concerns about impacts the proposed airstrip could have on safety, the surrounding environment and the character of the area, among other things.
Project history
The group of residents has expressed such concerns since 2022, when Lincoln’s former zoning administrator issued the Clarks a permit to build the landing strip on their Orchard Road North property. The decision to issue that permit was appealed by Lincoln resident Marilyn Ganahl. Following a series of public hearings, the town’s Zoning Board of Adjustment denied the Clarks’ the permit.
Lincoln’s zoning board was dissolved soon after and replaced by the Development Review Board, which in 2023 denied a separate conditional use permit application submitted by the Clarks for a proposed personal landing area.
The Clarks appealed those decisions to the Vermont Environmental Court. Although the court ultimately OK’d the land-use portion of the Clarks’ application, it stated noise and safety aspects of aircraft operations “are preempted by federal law” and would thus not be considered when analyzing the personal landing area’s compliance with Lincoln’s zoning regulations.
Such questions were expected to be addressed by the Federal Aviation Administration and the Vermont Transportation Board. The FAA issued a conditional determination to the Clarks for the airstrip last year and denied a petition for reconsideration this summer. Vermont Agency of Transportation officials recommended “operational approval and certification” of the restricted landing area to the Transportation Board following a visit to the site in June.
Thus, a decision from the Vermont Transportation Board could mark the last step in the approval process for the airstrip. In their emails to state officials, Lincoln residents said they were told that process would include a public hearing and that without one, residents haven’t had a chance to be heard on concerns around safety and the public interest as the application has made its way through various channels.
“My perspective and the reason I’m here is because I believe when a town and a selectboard have asked a state agency for a public hearing that the agency can clearly have, that they should have it, and I’m going to keep asking them to have it on your behalf,” Rodgers said at the meeting. “I have said from the beginning, I don’t want to put my thumb on the scale either way. I want to make sure the process has been carried out and the public and the town officials have had their say before a decision is made.”
Regulatory gap?
That process and how it’s unfolded have been viewed in different ways. Some note that the project has made its way through the necessary channels and say issues like safety have been addressed. Others argue that questions around safety and the public interest remain and that the project being weighed by different entities has created a regulatory gap.
“Sometimes in government, the best intentions run into the fact that some people, some courts do something, some agencies do something else,” Roy Goldberg said at the meeting. He is an aviation attorney based in Washington, D.C., who’s represented Lincoln residents opposed to the airstrip.
“Safety is obviously very important, so we just want to make sure the tires on safety have been kicked by all the necessary parties, and that this aircraft operation … will be fully vetted before operational.”
A statement provided to the Independent by a spokesperson for the Clark family noted the project has been deemed safe by state and federal agencies.
“Over four years, the Clark family has followed the required permitting, safety review, and approval processes to construct a safe, limited use personal landing area at their home,” the statement reads. “They are disappointed by opponents’ attempts to usurp the official processes and take away the Clarks’ freedom and liberty to enjoy the use of their private property. … Their hope is that there will be a resolution through the official process soon.”
“The Clarks have prevailed at the state’s environmental court because this is a permitted land use under Vermont law,” the statement continues. “The FAA has deemed the landing area safe and permissible. And, the Vermont Agency of Transportation completed a site inspection and deemed it safe, and recommended approval to the Transportation Board. We hope to have resolution from the Transportation Board promptly because this permitted use has undergone years of inspection and process, as required, for approval.”
Sept. 14 forum
The Clarks did not attend the Sept. 14 forum, which saw over 70 people gather in Burnham Hall. Among those in attendance were state Sen. Ruth Hardy, D-Middlebury, Addison-4 Reps. Karen Lueders and Herb Olson, and Franklin-4 Rep. Matt Walker, who chairs the House Committee on Transportation.
Along with a presentation by Goldberg, attendees also heard from Lincoln Selectboard Chair Tim McGowan and Lee Moak, a national aviation expert and consultant hired by Lincoln residents to conduct a safety assessment of the proposed airstrip. Moak summarized his report Monday, highlighting concerns such as operations being described by the FAA as “highly challenging” because of the terrain and runway length.
In his remarks, McGowan offered his understanding of the town’s role in the process, saying that the selectboard has “maintained a neutral monitoring posture” and focused on supporting the work of its local boards.
More recently, the town has participated in the process as an interested party. McGowan said the town’s participation is intended to request a public hearing “so that the interested parties have an opportunity to address the application,” provide information on the town’s concerns and seek clarification on “inconsistencies or ambiguities within the application and related documents.”
“The town recognizes that certain subjects, including aircraft safety, pilot operations and noise, are outside the scope of local zoning regulations and must be addressed through state and federal processes,” McGowan said. “In other words, Lincoln is not attempting to usurp the Transportation Board’s role. Rather, the town is requesting that the appropriate state process be fully vetted and that Lincoln residents are granted a fair opportunity to be heard on matters currently before the state.”
The Independent reached out to Vermont Transportation Board Executive Secretary Rachel Dimitruk, asking if the board planned to hold a public hearing and when a decision from the board could be expected. Dimitruk said the board does not comment on ongoing cases and referred to the process for personal restricted landing areas outlined in state statute (5 VSA 207) and the Aeronautics Rules and Regulations.
At the Sept. 14 forum, Hardy said she believes the process needs to be clarified, specifically around whether there should be a public hearing.
“One of the things that I had introduced as part of a bill was to create a sort of advisory committee on aviation issues that includes members of the public that are impacted by aviation facilities,” she said. “So, I’m hoping that Rep. Walker … if we’re both back in the Statehouse, that we can work together on this to make sure that there’s a clearer public process when there’s a proposed new facility or something that might impact the public and the broader public good, which has been part of the conversation tonight.”
Monday’s forum featured about an hour of public comment and questions. Multiple residents used that opportunity to reiterate concerns about the proposed airstrip’s impact on nearby farms, residents and the surrounding environment.
While residents at times shared differing opinions, Rodgers encouraged attendees at the start of the meeting to keep discussion respectful.
“We’re neighbors, and no matter how this ends, you’re all going to be neighbors when it ends, and so we hope we can all be good neighbors,” he said.
